topics.t: Meet the story: Daudet, Alsace and a late morning
topics.h: Imagine waking up to find that from tomorrow your school may not teach in your own language. That is the morning Franz walks into.
p: Author: Alphonse Daudet, a French novelist and short-story writer of the 19th century.
Background: the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–71. Prussia, led by Bismarck, defeated France and took the border districts of Alsace and Lorraine.
Narrator: Franz, a young schoolboy in a village of Alsace, tells the story in the first person, looking back on that day.
Opening: Franz is late and dreads being questioned on participles, which he has not learnt at all.
Temptation: the warm bright day, birds chirping at the edge of the woods and Prussian soldiers drilling in the field behind the sawmill pull him outdoors, but he resists and hurries to school.

ex.q: Why does Daudet open the story with Franz being late and unprepared?
st: Franz's fear of the participle test shows how little he cares for French lessons.
This careless attitude sets up a strong contrast with his deep regret later.
So the opening prepares the reader for the change in Franz.
ex.a: It shows Franz as a careless boy at first, so that his later remorse over losing French lessons feels sharper.

topics.rl: Many Indian students skip a regional-language class thinking it is 'easy marks later'. Franz learns, too late, that a language can be taken away.

rv.summary: Alphonse Daudet's story is set after the Franco-Prussian War, when Prussia took Alsace and Lorraine. Franz, the narrator, is late and dreads the participle test, but resists the bright day and hurries to school.
focus: How the opening prepares for his later change
remember: Author: Alphonse Daudet (French, 19th century)
Franco-Prussian War 1870–71; Alsace and Lorraine taken
Narrator: Franz, first person
traps: The narrator is Franz, not M. Hamel
Franz feared the participle test, not the soldiers

topics.t: An unusual morning at school
topics.h: Picture your noisy classroom gone silent like a Sunday, and your strictest teacher smiling at you. Something is very wrong.
p: At the town hall a crowd stands before the bulletin board; for two years all the bad news (lost battles, the draft, the commanding officer's orders) had come from there.
Usually school begins with a great bustle: desks banging, lessons repeated aloud in unison, the teacher's ruler rapping on the table. Franz had hoped to slip in unseen under that noise.
That day it is as quiet as a Sunday morning. Franz expects a scolding, but M. Hamel kindly tells him to go to his place.
M. Hamel is in his Sunday best: his beautiful green coat, frilled shirt and little black silk cap, all embroidered, worn only on inspection and prize days.
Village elders sit silently on the back benches: old Hauser with his old primer, the former mayor and the former postmaster.

ex.q: List three things that were unusual at school that day.
st: Recall the normal routine: noise, bustle, ruler on the table.
Compare: it was silent, M. Hamel was gentle, he wore his special clothes.
Add the villagers sitting on the back benches.
ex.a: The silence, M. Hamel's kindness and best clothes, and the village elders on the back benches.

topics.rl: When something big happens, Indians crowd around notice boards, from exam results to railway charts. In Franz's village, the notice board brought news of war.

rv.summary: That morning a crowd stood at the bulletin board, the source of bad news. School was silent instead of bustling, M. Hamel was kind and in his best clothes, and village elders sat on the back benches.
focus: What was unusual at school that day
remember: Bulletin board: two years of bad news
Hamel's green coat, frilled shirt, black silk cap — worn on inspection and prize days
Old Hauser with his old primer
traps: The elders did not come on official duty
The 'Sunday' quiet is a comparison, not the actual day

topics.t: The order from Berlin and Franz's regret
topics.h: One line on a notice can change a whole people's future. M. Hamel reads it out in a trembling voice.
p: M. Hamel announces the order from Berlin: only German is to be taught in the schools of Alsace and Lorraine.
This is their last French lesson; the new master arrives the next day.
Franz is shocked that he can hardly write French. He regrets hunting birds' eggs and sliding on the Saar; his grammar and history books now feel like old friends.
When Franz fails to recite the participle rule, M. Hamel does not scold him. He says that Alsace's great trouble is putting off learning till tomorrow.
He blames everyone: parents sent children to work on farms or in mills for a little more money, and he himself sent pupils to water his flowers or gave a holiday when he wanted to go fishing.

ex.q: How did the order from Berlin change Franz's feelings about his books?
st: Before: the books were a nuisance and heavy to carry.
After the order: he could lose French lessons forever.
So the books suddenly felt like old friends he could not bear to give up.
ex.a: His once-boring grammar and history books became like old friends he could not give up.

topics.rl: Families sometimes pull children out of school to help earn money, as M. Hamel says Alsatian parents did. Laws like the Right to Education Act in India try to stop exactly this loss.

rv.summary: M. Hamel announces the order from Berlin: only German will be taught, and this is the last French lesson. Franz regrets wasted time, and Hamel blames everyone, including himself, for putting off learning.
focus: The order and its effect on Franz
remember: Only German in schools of Alsace and Lorraine; new master the next day
Alsace's trouble: putting off learning till tomorrow
Hamel blames parents and himself (flowers, fishing)
traps: Franz was not happy about the order
Hamel did not blame only the students

topics.t: The last lesson itself
topics.h: Ever noticed you understand a lesson perfectly on the day you know it is the last revision? That is what happens to Franz.
p: M. Hamel calls French the most beautiful language in the world, the clearest and the most logical, and asks them to guard it.
His key idea: when a people are enslaved, holding on to their language is like holding the key to their prison.
Grammar, then writing and history follow. Franz understands everything. New copies saying 'France, Alsace' hang from the desks like little flags.
Pigeons coo on the roof, and Franz wonders whether they too will be made to sing in German.
At twelve the church clock strikes, the Angelus rings and Prussian trumpets sound. Too moved to speak, M. Hamel writes 'Vive La France!' on the board and dismisses the class.

ex.q: Explain: 'as long as they hold fast to their language it is as if they had the key to their prison' (paraphrase).
st: Prison here means being ruled by a conqueror.
Language keeps a people's identity, culture and unity alive.
So a people who keep their language can one day win back their freedom.
ex.a: Language preserves identity, and with it the hope and means to regain freedom; it is the key to escaping foreign rule.

topics.rl: India's freedom struggle used songs, newspapers and slogans in many Indian languages to unite people. Language kept the idea of freedom alive, just as M. Hamel says.

rv.summary: In the last lesson M. Hamel praises French and says keeping one's language is like holding the key to one's prison. Franz understands everything; at noon, too moved to speak, Hamel writes 'Vive La France!'.
focus: Hamel's view of French and language
Key images: copies, pigeons, final words
remember: French: most beautiful, clearest, most logical
Language = key to the prison of an enslaved people
Copies: 'France, Alsace'; 'Vive La France!' = Long live France
traps: Don't confuse the copies ('France, Alsace') with the board words ('Vive La France!')
Hamel wrote because he was overcome, not because he was forbidden to speak

topics.t: Characters, mother tongue and linguistic chauvinism
topics.h: Some people learn the value of something only when it is snatched away. Every main character in this story does.
p: Franz: careless and playful at first; then remorseful, sensitive and suddenly eager to learn.
M. Hamel: strict but devoted teacher of forty years; patriotic and deeply emotional at the end.
Villagers: they come to the class full of regret for not learning their language when they had the chance.
Mother tongue: it carries a people's identity, memory and culture; losing it is losing a part of oneself.
Linguistic chauvinism: forcing one's language on others, or treating other languages as inferior. Here the conquerors impose German on Alsace and Lorraine.

ex.q: Is the Prussian order an example of linguistic chauvinism? Give a reason.
st: Define it: aggressive pride in one's language and imposing it on others.
The order bans French and forces German on a conquered people.
So it fits the definition exactly.
ex.a: Yes. The conquerors force German on Alsace and Lorraine and deny people their own language.

topics.rl: India has 22 languages in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution. Respecting every language, rather than forcing one, keeps such a diverse nation together.

rv.summary: Franz changes from careless to remorseful and keen; M. Hamel is strict but devoted and patriotic; villagers regret not learning. The story shows a mother tongue carries identity, and the order is an example of linguistic chauvinism.
focus: Character sketches of Franz, M. Hamel and the villagers
remember: M. Hamel taught for forty years
Linguistic chauvinism = forcing one's language on others or calling others inferior
traps: Praising your own language is not chauvinism — imposing it is
Hamel was not only strict; he was also devoted and kind

topics.t: Themes and craft: delay, patriotism, irony and symbols
topics.h: 'Kal kare so aaj kar' (do tomorrow's work today) runs Kabir's famous doha. Daudet's whole story is a painful lesson in that line.
p: Procrastination: the habit of putting off learning till tomorrow; M. Hamel calls it the great trouble of Alsace.
Patriotism and loss: the pain of war appears in the bulletin board, the silent class and Hamel's breakdown.
First-person narration makes Franz's feelings direct and personal.
Irony: the 'last' lesson turns out to be the best lesson Franz ever had; he understands everything only when it is too late.
Symbols and pathos: the bulletin board (bad news), the pigeons (absurd imposition), 'Vive La France!' (undying patriotism), with vivid, moving description.

ex.q: Explain the irony in the title 'The Last Lesson'.
st: Irony is a contrast between what is expected and what happens.
Franz never cared for lessons, yet the final one is the one he understands best.
The people value French only when it is about to be taken away.
ex.a: The last lesson becomes the most meaningful one; value is realised only at the moment of loss.

topics.rl: Exam toppers often say, 'Start revision early.' Board students who delay till the last week feel exactly what Franz felt about French.

rv.summary: The story's themes are procrastination, patriotism and loss. First-person narration makes it personal; its central irony is that the last lesson is the best; symbols like the bulletin board, pigeons and 'Vive La France!' add pathos.
remember: Procrastination = putting off learning till tomorrow
Irony: the last lesson is the best one
Bulletin board = bad news; pigeons = absurd imposition
traps: Franz did not always love his lessons
The story is first-person, not third-person

topics.t: Words from the lesson and the past perfect
topics.h: 'Tycoon' comes from Japan and 'robot' from Czech. English is a borrower, and this lesson asks you to trace its loans.
p: Phrases from the text: 'in great dread of' (very afraid of), 'counted on' (relied on), 'thumbing the pages' (turning pages with the thumb), 'a great bustle' (busy noise), 'reproach ourselves with' (blame ourselves for).
Word origins: tycoon (Japanese, 'great lord'), tulip (Turkish word for turban), logo (Greek 'logos', word), zero (Arabic 'sifr'), trek (Dutch/Afrikaans, to travel), robot (Czech), bandicoot (Telugu).
Choose a meaning from context: read the whole sentence and pick the sense that fits.
Past perfect (had + past participle) shows the earlier of two past actions, e.g. 'I had counted on the noise to reach my desk unseen.'

ex.q: Combine using the past perfect: Franz reached school. The lesson began before that.
st: Identify the earlier action: the lesson began.
Put the earlier action in the past perfect: had begun.
Keep the later action in the simple past: reached.
ex.a: When Franz reached school, the lesson had already begun.

topics.rl: Many English words come from Indian languages too: 'jungle', 'shampoo', 'bungalow', 'pyjamas'. Language borrowing shows how cultures meet.

rv.summary: The lesson teaches phrases like 'in great dread of', 'counted on' and 'reproach', words of foreign origin such as tycoon and zero, choosing meanings from context, and the past perfect for the earlier of two past actions.
focus: Meanings of phrases from the text
remember: Past perfect = had + past participle (had rung, had begun)
Tycoon – Japanese; zero – Arabic 'sifr'; tulip – Turkish; robot – Czech; bandicoot – Telugu
Counted on = relied on; reproach = blame
traps: Don't write 'had rang' or 'had ring'
'Counted on' does not mean adding up

topics.t: Board exam practice: The Last Lesson
topics.h: Board examiners love this story. A sharp 40–50 word answer on M. Hamel or Franz can be your easiest marks.
p: Short answers (40–50 words): make one clear point, support it with one detail from the text, and end with its significance.
Common 'think as you read' questions: what Franz expected, what was unusual, what was on the bulletin board, what changed after the order, how Franz's feelings changed.
Long answers (120–150 words): for 'importance of mother tongue', use the key-to-the-prison idea, the villagers' regret and the theme of identity.
Discussion questions: peoples who lost their languages, problems of linguistic minorities, and whether pride in language can go too far (linguistic chauvinism).

ex.q: Draft a 40–50 word answer: How did the people realise the value of their language?
st: Point: they realised its value only when it was being taken away.
Evidence: villagers sat in the class; Franz regretted wasted time.
Significance: they understood language is their identity.
ex.a: When the order from Berlin banned French, villagers came to the last lesson full of regret and Franz wished he had studied. Losing French made them see that their language was their identity and the key to their freedom.

topics.rl: Debates on mother-tongue education in India, as in the NEP 2020 emphasis on home language in early years, echo the questions this story raises.

rv.summary: Board answers need a point, a text detail and its significance. Common questions cover Franz's expectations, the unusual day, the order's effects and the value of mother tongue, using the key-to-the-prison idea and linguistic chauvinism.
focus: Structure of short and long answers
remember: Short answer: 40–50 words; long answer: 120–150 words
Mother tongue answer: key to the prison, villagers' regret, identity
traps: Don't open a long answer with plot detail
Don't write a one-sided character sketch

topics.t: Saheb of Seemapuri: garbage and wonder
topics.h: Every morning, before most of Delhi wakes, children with sacks on their shoulders are already searching through the city's garbage. Anees Jung asks them why.
p: Author: Anees Jung, an Indian journalist and writer. The chapter is an extract from her book 'Lost Spring: Stories of Stolen Childhood'.
Form: a two-part reportage on child labour and poverty: Part 1 on Saheb, a ragpicker in Delhi; Part 2 on Mukesh, a bangle-maker's son in Firozabad.
Saheb-e-Alam's family came from Dhaka, Bangladesh, after storms swept away their fields and homes.
They live in Seemapuri, on the outskirts of Delhi, in mud structures with roofs of tin and tarpaulin, without sewage, drainage or running water.
For the elders ragpicking is a means of survival; for the children garbage is wrapped in wonder, because they may find a coin or even a ten-rupee note.

ex.q: Why does the author say garbage means different things to children and to elders?
st: Elders depend on what they collect to feed the family: survival.
Children are thrilled by the chance of finding a coin: wonder.
So the same garbage is a hard job for one and a treasure hunt for the other.
ex.a: For elders it is a means of survival; for children it holds the wonder of a possible find, like a coin.

topics.rl: India's National Child Labour Project and the Right to Education Act (free schooling for ages 6–14) aim to move children like Saheb from rag sacks to school bags.

rv.summary: Anees Jung's reportage tells of real children in poverty. Saheb's family fled storms in Dhaka to Seemapuri near Delhi, where they live in mud and tin homes; for elders ragpicking is survival, for children garbage holds wonder.
focus: Author, form and structure of the chapter
remember: Author: Anees Jung, from 'Lost Spring: Stories of Stolen Childhood'
Seemapuri: mud houses with tin and tarpaulin roofs, no sewage or water
Garbage: survival for elders, wonder for children
traps: Saheb lives in Seemapuri, not Firozabad
His family left Dhaka because of storms, not for jobs

topics.t: Barefoot, a grand name and a lost freedom
topics.h: A boy named 'Lord of the Universe' cannot afford a pair of chappals. Anees Jung lets that irony speak for itself.
p: Many children walk barefoot. Some say it is a tradition, but the author suspects this explains away constant poverty.
Saheb-e-Alam means 'lord of the universe', ironic for a barefoot boy who picks rags.
The author jokingly asks if he would go to school if she started one; days later he asks if her school is ready, and she feels embarrassed by her empty promise.
Later Saheb works at a tea stall for 800 rupees and all his meals. He now carries a steel canister instead of his plastic bag.
He has lost his freedom: the bag was his, but the canister belongs to the tea-stall owner. He is no longer his own master.

ex.q: Is Saheb happier at the tea stall? Explain.
st: He earns 800 rupees and gets meals, so he is better fed.
But his carefree look is gone; the steel canister feels heavier than the bag.
The bag was his own; now he works for a master.
ex.a: No. He earns more, but he has lost his freedom and carefree spirit; he is no longer his own master.

topics.rl: Thousands of children still work at dhabas and tea stalls in India. Their wages may seem like progress, but the cost is their childhood and schooling.

rv.summary: Children walk barefoot in the name of tradition, which hides poverty. Saheb-e-Alam's grand name is ironic. When he takes a tea-stall job for 800 rupees and meals, he loses his freedom: the canister is his master's, not his.
focus: Why Saheb is not happier at the tea stall
remember: Saheb-e-Alam = lord of the universe
Tea stall: 800 rupees and all meals
Steel canister (master's) replaces plastic bag (his own)
traps: More money did not make Saheb happier
The canister is not a sign of progress

topics.t: Firozabad: the bangle makers
topics.h: Bright glass bangles jingle at weddings across India. Few buyers think of the dark rooms where they are made.
p: Mukesh lives in Firozabad, the centre of India's glass-bangle industry.
About 20,000 children work near high-temperature furnaces and glass-blowing units in dingy cells without air and light; many lose their eyesight before they become adults.
Child labour is illegal, yet it thrives; families have made bangles for generations.
Savita, a young girl in a drab pink dress, solders pieces of glass beside an elderly woman.
Bangles symbolise a married Indian woman's auspiciousness (suhaag); Savita may not yet know the sanctity of what she is making.

ex.q: Why is there irony in Savita making bangles?
st: Bangles are a symbol of a married woman's good fortune.
Savita is a young girl working in grim conditions, not enjoying any such fortune.
She makes symbols of joy while her own childhood is lost.
ex.a: She makes the symbols of a happy married life while her own life is joyless labour.

topics.rl: Studies of the Firozabad glass industry have long reported eye and lung problems among workers. Safety rules and bans on child labour exist, but enforcement is the real challenge.

rv.summary: Mukesh lives in Firozabad, India's glass-bangle centre, where about 20,000 children work in dark cells by hot furnaces and many lose their eyesight. Child labour is illegal but continues; Savita makes bangles, symbols of suhaag, without knowing their meaning.
focus: Irony of Savita and the bangles
remember: About 20,000 child workers
Main hazard: loss of eyesight
Bangles = suhaag of a married woman
traps: Don't confuse 20,000 with other figures
Child labour continues despite being illegal — the law has not changed

topics.t: The vicious circle and Mukesh's dream
topics.h: Imagine making something beautiful all your life and never once eating a full meal. An old bangle maker lives that truth.
p: An elderly woman says she has not enjoyed even one full meal in her whole life, though she has made bangles throughout it.
The workers are trapped in a vicious circle of sahukars (moneylenders), middlemen, policemen, keepers of the law, bureaucrats and politicians.
They cannot organise: if they did, they fear being hauled up by the police, beaten and jailed; there is no leader and no cooperative.
Mukesh is different. He dreams of being a motor mechanic and driving a car, a dream that breaks away from the family tradition of bangle making.

ex.q: Why does the author see Mukesh's dream as hopeful?
st: Everyone around him accepts bangle making as destiny.
Mukesh wants to be a motor mechanic and learn to drive a car.
Choosing his own path shows courage to break the circle.
ex.a: His dream to be a motor mechanic breaks away from the inherited trade, showing courage and hope.

topics.rl: Self-help groups and cooperatives, like those under India's DAY-NRLM mission, help artisans sell without middlemen. That is exactly what the bangle workers lacked.

rv.summary: Bangle makers like the elderly woman never escape poverty, trapped by sahukars, middlemen, police, bureaucrats and politicians, and afraid to organise. Mukesh breaks away by dreaming of becoming a motor mechanic.
remember: Sahukars = moneylenders
No leader, no cooperative; fear of police
Mukesh: motor mechanic, wants to drive a car
traps: Teachers are not part of the vicious circle
There is no cooperative in Firozabad

topics.t: Themes, the title, and answer writing
topics.h: Spring is the season of new leaves. Childhood is the spring of life. What happens when a child never gets one?
p: Child labour and the loss of childhood: children like Saheb and Savita work instead of playing and learning.
Poverty and exploitation, made worse by the burden of tradition and fate (karam), which people accept without question.
Hope: Mukesh's dream and Saheb's interest in school show that the wish for a better life survives.
Title metaphor: 'spring' stands for childhood; 'lost spring' means childhood stolen by poverty and work.
Answer writing: short answers (40–50 words) on Saheb or Mukesh need one key point plus a detail; a long answer on child labour should cover causes, effects and solutions.

ex.q: Explain the title 'Lost Spring' in about 40 words.
st: Spring = youth, freshness, growth = childhood.
Saheb and Mukesh lose this stage to labour and poverty.
So their 'spring' is lost.
ex.a: Spring symbolises childhood. Saheb and Mukesh lose the joys of childhood, like play and school, to poverty and labour, so the title means 'stolen childhood'.

topics.rl: India's 2011 Census counted about one crore working children aged 5–14. Every one of those numbers is a 'lost spring'.

rv.summary: The chapter's themes are lost childhood, poverty, exploitation and the burden of tradition and karam, with hope in Mukesh's dream. 'Spring' stands for childhood, so 'Lost Spring' means stolen childhood.
remember: Spring = childhood
Karam = destiny or fate
Long answer on child labour: causes, effects, solutions
traps: Poverty is not the only cause — tradition and exploiters matter too
Don't mix Saheb's story with Mukesh's

topics.t: Craft and questions: reportage, irony, and the role of society
topics.h: A news report gives numbers. A reportage like this gives names, faces and voices, and that is why you remember it.
p: Reportage technique: first-hand observation, real names, dialogue ('Is your school ready?') and vivid imagery.
Irony: Saheb's grand name against his poverty; bright, colourful bangles against the grim lives of their makers.

Think-as-you-read answers: Saheb looks for coins in garbage; he lives in Seemapuri because storms drove his family from Dhaka; children go barefoot because of poverty; Saheb is not happy at the tea stall because he has lost his freedom.
Understanding the text: Mukesh dreams of being a motor mechanic; the bangle industry harms eyesight; workers cannot organise for fear of the police and lack of a cooperative.
Society's role: enforce child-labour laws, provide schools, form cooperatives and spread awareness among buyers.

ex.q: How does the author make the reader feel Saheb's reality, not just know about it?
st: She uses his real name and its meaning.
She quotes his words and her own.
She describes Seemapuri in concrete detail: mud, tin, tarpaulin.
ex.a: Through real names, dialogue and vivid concrete detail, typical of reportage.

topics.rl: Campaigns like Bachpan Bachao Andolan, founded by Nobel laureate Kailash Satyarthi, rescue child workers. Public pressure is part of society's role.

rv.summary: Jung's reportage uses real names, dialogue and vivid detail. Irony appears in Saheb's name and in bright bangles from grim cells. Ending child labour needs laws, schools, cooperatives and public awareness.
remember: Reportage: first-hand observation, real people, dialogue, imagery
Irony: 'lord of the universe' ragpicker; bright bangles, dark lives
traps: The government alone cannot end child labour
Irony needs a contrast — a plain fact is not irony

topics.t: Douglas and the first fear of water
topics.h: A future judge of the most powerful court in the USA was once a skinny boy who froze in a swimming pool. This is his true story.
p: Author: William O. Douglas, a Judge of the US Supreme Court and an environmentalist. 'Deep Water' is an extract from his autobiography 'Of Men and Mountains'.
Form: an autobiographical, first-person account of a childhood fear of water and how he conquered it.
First fear: at three or four, on a California beach with his father, the waves knocked him down and swept over him; he was buried in water and frightened.
At ten or eleven he decided to learn to swim at the YMCA pool in Yakima, because it was safer than the river his mother warned him about. He used water wings at first.
The pool's shallow end was about three feet deep; the deep end was about nine feet.

ex.q: Why did Douglas choose the YMCA pool and not the Yakima River?
st: His mother kept warning him that the river was treacherous.
The pool was considered safe, with a shallow end of about three feet.
So the YMCA pool was the sensible place to begin.
ex.a: The river was dangerous and his mother warned him against it, while the YMCA pool was safe.

topics.rl: Many Indian children first learn to swim in a municipal pool, often with floats like Douglas's water wings, before trying rivers or the sea, which are much less predictable.

rv.summary: In 'Deep Water', from his autobiography 'Of Men and Mountains', William O. Douglas recalls a fear of water that began when waves knocked him down on a California beach. At ten or eleven he began learning at the safer YMCA pool.
focus: Why he chose the YMCA pool
remember: Author: William O. Douglas, US Supreme Court judge
Source: 'Of Men and Mountains'
Pool: shallow end about 3 feet, deep end about 9 feet
traps: The first fear came from the California beach, not the pool
Don't confuse ages: 3–4 at the beach, 10–11 at the YMCA

topics.t: The misadventure at the YMCA pool
topics.h: A big boy's idea of a joke at a swimming pool can leave a scar of fear for years.
p: A big bruiser of a boy, about eighteen, called him 'Skinny', picked him up and tossed him into the deep end.
Douglas swallowed water and sank. On the way down he planned to make a big jump from the bottom, come up and paddle to the edge.
The nine feet felt like ninety. He rose slowly and sank again; this happened three times.
Stark terror: his legs felt paralysed, he tried to scream but no sound came out, and he saw only yellowish water.
At last he stopped struggling, felt calm and peaceful, and blacked out. He woke up lying beside the pool, vomiting.

ex.q: Trace the change in Douglas's state of mind while he was drowning.
st: First: frightened but still able to plan a jump from the bottom.
Then: panic and terror as the plan failed and his legs froze.
Finally: he stopped struggling, felt peace, and blacked out.
ex.a: Fear with a plan, then sheer panic and terror, then calm peace before he lost consciousness.

topics.rl: Lifeguards in Indian pools are trained to watch for 'silent drowning': a drowning person often cannot shout, just as Douglas could not scream.

rv.summary: An eighteen-year-old bruiser tossed Douglas into the deep end. He planned to spring up from the bottom but went down three times, frozen with terror, then felt peace and blacked out, waking beside the pool.
focus: Stages of his feelings while drowning
remember: Bruiser of about eighteen called him 'Skinny'
Plan: jump from bottom, paddle to edge
Down three times; 'nine feet more like ninety'
traps: The terror did not last till the end — he felt calm before blacking out
An adult instructor did not throw him in

topics.t: A fear that stayed, and a teacher with a rope
topics.h: Some fears pass in a day. Douglas's lasted for years, until he decided enough was enough.
p: A haunting fear of water stayed with him for years; whenever he entered water, his legs would freeze and terror would grip him.
It spoiled his joys: whenever he waded in the Tieton or the Bumping River, or bathed in Warm Lake, terror gripped him; it also ruined his fishing trips and the fun of canoeing, boating and swimming.
He resolved to conquer the fear because it was ruining his enjoyment of life.
He hired an instructor who trained him for months, five days a week, an hour a day.
The method: a belt around his waist, attached to a rope that ran through a pulley on an overhead cable. The instructor held the rope and walked him back and forth across the pool.

ex.q: Why did Douglas finally decide to hire an instructor?
st: The fear stopped him from canoeing, bathing and fishing.
It was ruining the fun of outdoor life he loved.
So he resolved to overcome it with expert help.
ex.a: Because his fear was spoiling activities he loved, like canoeing and fishing, he resolved to conquer it.

topics.rl: Indian swimming coaches still use similar methods, like a rope or a pole held by the coach, so that a frightened learner feels safe while building skill.

rv.summary: The fear haunted Douglas for years, freezing his legs in rivers and lakes and spoiling his outdoor joys. He hired an instructor who trained him for months using a belt, rope and pulley to keep him safe.
focus: Why he decided to conquer it
remember: Wading in the Tieton and the Bumping River brought terror
Training: five days a week, an hour a day, for months
Belt + rope + pulley + overhead cable
traps: He was not already an expert swimmer when he hired the instructor
The rope was for safety, not speed

topics.t: Building a swimmer, piece by piece
topics.h: Big skills are built from small parts. Douglas's instructor broke swimming into tiny steps.
p: Step-by-step training: put the face under water and exhale; raise the nose and inhale; repeat many times.
Next: hold the side of the pool and kick with the legs; then combine arms, legs and breathing into a whole stroke. 'Piece by piece he built a swimmer.'
Even after training, small traces of terror returned when he swam alone, so he kept swimming to beat them.
Test 1: at Lake Wentworth in New Hampshire, he dived off a dock and swam two miles across the lake. The terror tried to return once, but he swam on.
Test 2: at Warm Lake he dived in, swam across to the other shore and back, and shouted with joy. The terror was gone.

ex.q: Why did Douglas test himself at Lake Wentworth and Warm Lake after the training?
st: The instructor's work was done, but traces of fear remained.
He needed to be sure he could swim alone in deep, open water.
Swimming across and back at Warm Lake proved the terror was gone.
ex.a: To be sure the last traces of fear had gone, he swam alone in open lakes; at Warm Lake he knew he had won.

topics.rl: Cricketers practise in nets ball by ball before facing a real match. Douglas did the same with breathing, kicking and strokes before facing open lakes.

rv.summary: The instructor built a swimmer piece by piece: breathing, kicking, then full strokes. Traces of fear remained, so Douglas tested himself by swimming two miles across Lake Wentworth and across and back at Warm Lake, where the terror was gone.
focus: Why and how he tested himself
remember: 'Piece by piece he built a swimmer'
Lake Wentworth, New Hampshire: two miles
Warm Lake: across and back, shouting with joy
traps: Training alone did not remove all fear
Lake Wentworth is in New Hampshire, not California

topics.t: Themes: fear, the will to live and freedom
topics.h: 'All we have to fear is fear itself.' Douglas borrowed a president's words to sum up a boy's victory.
p: Fear can paralyse a person, but it can be overcome by willpower, patience and practice.
Douglas quotes US President Franklin D. Roosevelt: 'All we have to fear is fear itself.' The fear of something is often worse than the thing.
Near death he felt peace; afterwards his will to live grew stronger. He says there is terror only in the fear of death.
Victory over fear brings freedom: he could enjoy rivers, lakes and mountains again.

ex.q: Explain 'All we have to fear is fear itself' with reference to Douglas.
st: The real enemy was not water but his fear of water.
That fear froze his legs and spoiled his life for years.
Once he faced and beat the fear, the water held no danger for him.
ex.a: His fear, not the water, was his real enemy; by conquering it, he was free.

topics.rl: Top Indian athletes often talk about beating nerves before a big final. Mastering the fear is often the real contest.

rv.summary: Douglas shows that fear can be conquered by will and practice. Quoting Roosevelt, 'All we have to fear is fear itself', he says the terror lies in fearing death, and victory over fear gave him freedom.
focus: Douglas's reflection on death and life
remember: 'All we have to fear is fear itself' – Franklin D. Roosevelt
Terror is only in the fear of death
Will to live grew stronger
traps: Douglas did not feel terror right up to death
The lesson is not that swimming is dangerous

topics.t: Craft and vocabulary of Deep Water
topics.h: Read the drowning scene and you almost hold your breath. That is the power of sensory writing.
p: Sensory description: yellowish water, choking, frozen legs; repetition of going down and coming up builds suspense.
Tone: reflective; the adult Douglas looks back calmly. Strong contrast between helplessness in the pool and triumph at Warm Lake.

Vocabulary: bruiser (big, tough person), flailed (waved wildly), paralysed (unable to move), misadventure (unlucky accident), stark terror (sheer fear), vestiges of fear (small traces), residual doubt (doubt that remains).
Think as you read: the 'misadventure' is being thrown into the deep end; he planned to spring up from the bottom; the experience left him with a fear of water for years.
Extract-based MCQs often ask about the meaning of a phrase, the narrator's feeling, or a device in the drowning scene.

ex.q: Extract (paraphrased): He thrashed wildly at the surface, gulped water and choked; his legs would not rise and dangled, heavy and frozen. Identify the feeling.
st: Thrashing wildly (the text's word is 'flailed') shows helpless movement.
Choking and frozen legs show physical failure.
Together they convey panic.
ex.a: Panic and helplessness.

topics.rl: Sports commentators use vivid sensory words, 'the ball skids, the crowd roars', to make you feel a match. Douglas does the same for drowning.

rv.summary: Douglas's vivid sensory detail and repetition build suspense in the drowning scene, while the reflective adult voice contrasts helplessness with triumph. Key words include bruiser, flailed, misadventure, vestiges and residual.
remember: Misadventure = unlucky accident; flailed = waved wildly
Vestiges = small traces; residual = remaining
Tone: reflective
traps: 'Residual doubt' means doubt that remains, not no doubt
The tone is reflective, not comic

topics.t: Board exam practice: Deep Water
topics.h: The examiner asks: 'How did the instructor build a swimmer?' You have 40 words. Ready?
p: Why he was determined: fear was ruining fishing, canoeing and outdoor joy.
How the instructor built a swimmer: belt-rope-pulley, then breathing, kicking and strokes, piece by piece.
How he tested himself: two miles at Lake Wentworth; across and back at Warm Lake.
Short answers (40–50 words) on the YMCA incident and the training method should give sequence and one key detail.
Long answer (120–150 words) on courage: cause of fear, its effects, the determined effort, the tests, and the lesson about fear itself; link to your own life.

ex.q: Write a 40-word answer: How did the experience in the pool affect Douglas?
st: Immediate effect: near drowning and blackout.
Long-term effect: a haunting fear of water for years.
Result: missed joys, then a decision to conquer it.
ex.a: Nearly drowning left Douglas with a haunting fear of water; his legs froze in any river or lake. For years he missed canoeing and fishing until he resolved to hire an instructor and overcome it.

topics.rl: Many Olympians speak openly about stage fright and anxiety. Talking about fear, as Douglas does, helps others face theirs.

rv.summary: Board answers on 'Deep Water' cover why Douglas was determined, how the instructor built a swimmer, how he tested himself, and the lesson about fear. Short answers need sequence and a detail; long answers trace cause, effort and result.
focus: Planning a long answer on courage
remember: Determined because fear ruined fishing and canoeing
Tests: Lake Wentworth (two miles) and Warm Lake
Courage is facing fear, not lacking it
traps: Don't open a long answer with a plain fact
Don't say training alone ended the fear

topics.t: The peddler and his big idea
topics.h: A poor man selling wire traps decides the whole world is one giant trap. Is he bitter, or is he on to something?
p: Author: Selma Lagerlöf, a Swedish writer and the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in Literature (1909).
Setting: the iron-mining area of Värmland in Sweden, with its forges, mines and forests.
The peddler sells small rattraps of wire; his trade earns too little, so he begs and steals now and then to keep body and soul together.
His big idea: the world is a rattrap. Its riches and joys, shelter and food, heat and clothing are baits, and whoever touches them is caught.
He takes a bitter pleasure in this idea, amused at people who fall into the trap.

ex.q: Explain the peddler's 'rattrap' philosophy in your own words.
st: A rattrap offers cheese or meat as bait.
The world offers wealth, comfort and joy as bait.
People who grab them lose their freedom, like rats in a trap.
ex.a: The world tempts people with material things, and those who reach for them get trapped by greed.

topics.rl: Online 'easy money' scams and lucky-draw tricks in India work exactly like the peddler's rattrap: a tempting bait, then a trap.

rv.summary: Selma Lagerlöf's story, set in Sweden's iron-mining Värmland, follows a poor peddler of rattraps who begs and steals. He believes the world is a rattrap whose riches are bait, and enjoys thinking of others caught in it.
remember: Selma Lagerlöf: first woman Nobel laureate in Literature, 1909
Setting: Värmland, Sweden
Bait: riches, joys, shelter, food, heat, clothing
traps: The bait is the world's riches, not punishment
The peddler did not gain money from his idea

topics.t: The lonely crofter and the thirty kronor
topics.h: A lonely old man is so glad of company that he shows a stranger exactly where he keeps his money.
p: One evening the peddler is welcomed into a little grey cottage by an old crofter who lives alone with no wife or child.
The crofter gives him porridge for supper, a big slice of tobacco, and plays mjölis, a card game, with him till bedtime.
He proudly says his cow's milk earned him thirty kronor last month, and shows the three ten-kronor notes kept in a leather pouch on a nail in the window frame.
Next morning the peddler comes back, smashes a pane, steals the money and hangs the pouch back. To avoid capture he takes a forest road, gets lost and realises he too is caught in a rattrap.
The crofter: lonely, generous and trusting.

ex.q: How does the peddler realise he is caught in a rattrap?
st: He took the bait: the thirty kronor.
Now he is lost in a big, dark forest, unable to find his way out.
Like a rat, he has been tempted and trapped.
ex.a: After stealing the bait (the money), he is lost in the forest and sees that he himself is trapped.

topics.rl: Police in India often warn senior citizens living alone not to show cash or share bank details with strangers; loneliness can make trust risky.

rv.summary: A lonely old crofter welcomes the peddler with porridge, tobacco and cards, and proudly shows the thirty kronor he earned from his cow's milk. The peddler steals it, flees into the forest, gets lost and feels trapped himself.
remember: Thirty kronor: three ten-kronor notes in a leather pouch
Card game: mjölis
Lost in the forest = caught in the rattrap
traps: The crofter was trusting, not suspicious
The money came from cow's milk, not rattraps

topics.t: A case of mistaken identity at Ramsjö
topics.h: Lost, cold and hungry, the peddler wanders into a forge, and the ironmaster greets him as an old army friend.
p: Lost in the forest, the peddler reaches the Ramsjö ironworks and is allowed to warm himself in the forge.
The ironmaster, on his night round, mistakes him for an old regimental comrade, Captain von Stahle, and invites him home for Christmas. The peddler does not correct him.
He declines, fearing that going to the manor house with stolen money would be like walking into the lion's den.
The ironmaster's daughter, Edla Willmansson, comes and persuades him with kindness to come.

Next morning, after he has been bathed, shaved and dressed, the ironmaster sees in daylight he is not the captain and wants to throw him out; he even threatens the sheriff. The ironmaster is impulsive and proud.

ex.q: Why did the peddler first refuse the ironmaster's invitation?
st: He had stolen thirty kronor and still had it.
A grand house full of people meant more risk of discovery.
He compared it to throwing himself into the lion's den.
ex.a: He feared being found out with the stolen money; going to the manor felt like walking into the lion's den.

topics.rl: Indian cinema loves mistaken identity, from twin brothers to look-alikes. Lagerlöf uses the same device, but to test human goodness.

rv.summary: At the Ramsjö ironworks the ironmaster mistakes the peddler for Captain von Stahle and invites him home; fearing the 'lion's den', the peddler refuses until Edla persuades him. In daylight the ironmaster sees his mistake and threatens him.
focus: Why the peddler refused and then accepted
remember: Ramsjö ironworks; Captain von Stahle
'Lion's den' — fear of being caught with stolen money
Ironmaster: impulsive and proud
traps: The peddler kept quiet hoping for money, not out of confusion
The ironmaster discovered the truth in daylight, not from the money

topics.t: Edla's kindness and the Christmas gift
topics.h: Treat a man like a captain and he may start behaving like one. Edla's kindness proves it.
p: When her father wants to throw him out, Edla insists he stay: they had promised him Christmas cheer, and he should have one day of peace.
He spends Christmas Eve with the family and is treated with kindness and respect.
On Christmas morning, while the family is at church, he leaves. He leaves a small package for Edla: a rattrap holding the crofter's three ten-kronor notes and a letter.
In the letter he asks her to return the money to the old crofter, says he would have been caught in the world's rattrap had he not been treated like a captain, and signs it 'Captain von Stahle'.
The peddler: poor and bitter but redeemed by kindness. Edla: compassionate and mature; her goodness transforms him.

ex.q: Why does the peddler sign the letter as 'Captain von Stahle'?
st: Edla had treated him with the respect due to a captain.
That respect awakened his self-respect and goodness.
Signing as the captain shows he wants to live up to that respect.
ex.a: Edla's respect raised him to the dignity of a captain; signing so shows his moral change.

topics.rl: Many Indian NGOs that work with former offenders say the same thing: respect and a fresh chance often change lives faster than punishment.

rv.summary: Edla insists the peddler stay for Christmas. Treated with kindness and respect, he leaves her a rattrap with the stolen money and a letter asking her to return it, signed 'Captain von Stahle'. Her goodness redeems him.
remember: Gift: a rattrap with three ten-kronor notes and a letter
Signed 'Captain von Stahle'
Edla: compassionate and mature
traps: Edla did not want him to leave
Kindness, not fear of the sheriff, changed him

topics.t: Themes, metaphor and symbols
topics.h: A rattrap catches rats. In this story, the same rattrap ends up setting a man free.
p: Theme 1: the world as a rattrap. Greed and temptation trap people, as they trap the peddler.
Theme 2: human goodness and the power of kindness to redeem; Edla's trust makes the peddler honest.
Theme 3: loneliness and the need for company, seen in the crofter and in the peddler's own life.
Devices: an extended metaphor of the rattrap; irony (a man is mistaken for a captain and then acts like one); gentle humour.
Symbols: the rattrap as temptation; the rattrap returned with the money as a Christmas gift symbolises his escape from the trap and his redemption.

ex.q: Why is the peddler's Christmas gift ironic?
st: The rattrap stood for his bitter view that the world traps people.
Now he uses a rattrap to return stolen money.
The symbol of being trapped becomes a symbol of his release.
ex.a: The rattrap, once his symbol of the world's cruelty, becomes the vehicle of his honesty and freedom.

topics.rl: Festivals like Diwali and Eid are times of sharing. Lagerlöf sets her story at Christmas, the season of goodwill, to make the redemption feel natural.

rv.summary: Themes are the world as a rattrap of greed, the redeeming power of kindness and loneliness. The extended rattrap metaphor, the irony of a tramp acting like a captain, gentle humour and the Christmas setting support them.
focus: The rattrap as extended metaphor and symbol
remember: Rattrap = temptations of the material world
Irony: mistaken for a captain, he acts like one
Returned rattrap = escape and redemption
traps: The story is not entirely gloomy
Edla stands for kindness, not greed

topics.t: Words from the ironworks and reflexive pronouns
topics.h: Trudge, plod, stumble: English has a dozen ways to say 'walk wearily'. The peddler uses most of them.
p: Phrases: 'keep body and soul together' (just survive), 'plods along' (walks slowly and heavily), 'unwonted joy' (unusual happiness), 'nodded a haughty consent' (agreed proudly), 'fallen into a line of thought' (begun thinking along one track).
Labels for the peddler: vagabond, stranger, tramp, ragamuffin (person in ragged clothes), guest.
Weary movement: lurch (sudden unsteady movement), stumble (trip), slog (work hard and long), trudge and plod (walk slowly and heavily).
Ironworks terms: hammer strokes, pig iron (crude iron from a furnace), coal dust, anvil (iron block on which metal is hammered).
Reflexive pronouns (myself, himself, themselves) refer back to the subject: 'He found himself caught.' Used for emphasis: 'The ironmaster himself came.'

ex.q: Identify the use of 'himself' in: (a) The peddler saw himself in a trap. (b) The ironmaster himself opened the door.
st: In (a), 'himself' is the object and refers to the subject (the peddler).
In (b), 'himself' only stresses who did it; removing it keeps the sentence complete.
So (a) is reflexive, (b) is emphatic.
ex.a: (a) reflexive use; (b) emphatic use.

topics.rl: Indian steel plants at Bhilai or Jamshedpur still use terms like pig iron, ladle and anvil, words that would make sense to the forge workers of Ramsjö.

rv.summary: The chapter's vocabulary includes phrases like 'keep body and soul together' and 'unwonted joy', names for the peddler, words of weary movement and ironworks terms. Reflexive pronouns refer back to the subject or add emphasis.
remember: Unwonted = unusual; ragamuffin = person in ragged clothes
Anvil = iron block for hammering metal
Reflexive: 'He hurt himself'; emphatic: 'The ironmaster himself came'
traps: 'Unwonted' is not 'unwanted'
'Hisself' is non-standard

topics.t: Board exam practice: The Rattrap
topics.h: Ironmaster vs Edla is a favourite board question. Know the contrast and you have the answer.
p: Think as you read: the rattrap idea came while thinking about his own traps; he was amused because people are caught; the crofter was talkative because he was lonely; he declined the invitation out of fear and accepted because of Edla's kindness.
How the peddler read kindness: at first he thought the crofter foolish and the ironmaster easy to fool; Edla's genuine kindness finally changed him.
Ironmaster vs Edla: he is impulsive, proud and quick to judge; she is observant, compassionate and generous.
Discussion: is the world a rattrap? how does loneliness affect people?
Long answer on kindness: show how goodness, not punishment, redeems the peddler.

ex.q: Write a 50-word answer contrasting the ironmaster and Edla.
st: Ironmaster: impulsive, mistakes identity, then threatens the sheriff.
Edla: observant, sees his fear, persuades him gently, insists he stay.
Result: her kindness redeems him.
ex.a: The ironmaster is impulsive and proud; he invites the peddler by mistake and then threatens him with the sheriff. Edla is observant and compassionate; she senses his fear, insists he stay for Christmas, and her kindness transforms him.

topics.rl: The idea of reform through compassion appears in India's open jails, like Sanganer in Rajasthan, where trust is given to change behaviour.

rv.summary: Board answers cover the origin of the rattrap idea, the crofter's loneliness, why the peddler declined and then accepted, the contrast between the impulsive ironmaster and compassionate Edla, and how kindness redeems him.
remember: Idea came while thinking of his own rattraps
Accepted because of Edla's kindness
Ironmaster impulsive; Edla compassionate
traps: The ironmaster is impulsive, not cruel
Don't fill a long answer with background details

topics.t: Fischer, Champaran and a persistent peasant
topics.h: A poor, unlettered farmer follows Gandhi from city to city until he agrees to come. That stubbornness changed Indian history.
p: Author: Louis Fischer, an American journalist. 'Indigo' is an extract from his book 'The Life of Mahatma Gandhi'.
Fischer heard the story from Gandhi himself when he visited Gandhi's ashram at Sevagram in 1942.
Subject: Gandhi's Champaran movement of 1917 in Bihar for the indigo sharecroppers.
Rajkumar Shukla, a poor sharecropper from Champaran, met Gandhi at the annual Congress session at Lucknow in December 1916 and begged him to come.
Shukla was resolute: he followed Gandhi to Cawnpore and to his ashram near Ahmedabad until Gandhi named a date and asked him to meet him in Calcutta.

ex.q: What quality of Rajkumar Shukla made the Champaran movement possible?
st: Gandhi was busy and kept putting him off.
Shukla followed him from Lucknow to Cawnpore to Ahmedabad.
His persistence finally won Gandhi's promise.
ex.a: His persistence and determination; he did not give up until Gandhi agreed to come.

topics.rl: Ordinary citizens still move change in India through persistence: from RTI petitions to repeated letters that finally get a village road built.

rv.summary: 'Indigo', from Louis Fischer's 'The Life of Mahatma Gandhi', tells of the 1917 Champaran movement. Gandhi told Fischer the story in 1942. The poor sharecropper Rajkumar Shukla met Gandhi at Lucknow in 1916 and followed him until he agreed to come.
focus: Author, source and how Fischer knew the story
remember: Louis Fischer, American journalist
Champaran movement 1917, Bihar
Shukla met Gandhi at the Lucknow Congress, December 1916
traps: Fischer was not an eyewitness in 1917
Shukla first met Gandhi at Lucknow, not in Champaran

topics.t: The road to Champaran and the tinkathia system
topics.h: Three parts in twenty: that tiny fraction of land kept thousands of families in misery for years.
p: From Calcutta they went to Patna. At Rajendra Prasad's house (he was away), the servants took Gandhi for another poor peasant and would not let him draw water from the well, fearing he was an untouchable.
At Muzaffarpur, Professor J.B. Kripalani received him at the station at midnight with students; lawyers came to meet him too.
Tinkathia system: Champaran's sharecroppers were bound by contract to grow indigo on 15 per cent (3 parts in 20) of their land and give the whole crop to the British landlords as rent.
When Germany developed synthetic indigo, the indigo crop lost its value. Landlords then got the peasants to sign agreements to pay compensation for being released from the 15 per cent arrangement.

Gandhi met the secretary of the British landlords' association, who refused information to an 'outsider', and the British commissioner of the Tirhut division, who bullied him and told him to leave Tirhut.

ex.q: Why was the landlords' demand for compensation unfair?
st: Synthetic indigo had made the crop worthless to the landlords anyway.
They still made the peasants pay to be released from growing it.
So they profited twice from the peasants' ignorance.
ex.a: Indigo was no longer valuable, yet landlords made peasants pay compensation to end an obligation that had lost its worth.

topics.rl: Exploitative contracts with poor farmers are not just history. India's debates on contract farming still ask how to protect sharecroppers from unfair terms.

rv.summary: At Patna, Rajendra Prasad's servants took Gandhi for an untouchable; Kripalani met him at Muzaffarpur. Under tinkathia, peasants grew indigo on 15% of their land as rent; after synthetic indigo, landlords demanded compensation. Officials rebuffed Gandhi.
remember: Tinkathia: 3 parts in 20 = 15% of land under indigo
Germany developed synthetic indigo
Tirhut commissioner told Gandhi to leave
traps: Tinkathia was 15%, not 25%
Indigo lost value because of synthetic dye, not peasant resistance

topics.t: Motihari: the first civil disobedience
topics.h: An order says 'Leave'. A man writes back, politely, 'I will not.' Thousands of peasants arrive to watch what happens next.
p: Gandhi went to Motihari, the capital of Champaran. On his way to see a maltreated peasant, he was stopped and served an official notice to quit Champaran immediately.
He signed the receipt and wrote on it that he would disobey the order. He was summoned to court the next day.
In court he pleaded guilty, saying he had disobeyed not out of disrespect for the law but in obedience to the 'higher law of our being, the voice of conscience'.
Thousands of peasants gathered spontaneously at the court; the officials felt powerless. Gandhi helped them control the crowd.
Some days later the case was dropped on the orders of the Lieutenant-Governor. Civil disobedience had triumphed for the first time in modern India.

ex.q: What does 'the higher law of our being, the voice of conscience' mean?
st: Ordinary law is made by rulers.
Conscience is a person's inner sense of right and wrong.
When the two clash, Gandhi obeys conscience and accepts the penalty.
ex.a: Gandhi placed his moral sense of right above an unjust official order, and was willing to bear the punishment.

topics.rl: Peaceful protest is part of India's democratic heritage. Civil disobedience means breaking an unjust law openly and accepting the penalty, not violence.

rv.summary: At Motihari Gandhi was ordered to leave Champaran; he wrote that he would disobey, pleaded guilty and said he obeyed his conscience. Thousands of peaceful peasants gathered, and the case was dropped — the first civil disobedience in modern India.
remember: Motihari = capital of Champaran
'Higher law of our being, the voice of conscience'
Case dropped by the Lieutenant-Governor
traps: Gandhi pleaded guilty, not not guilty
Civil disobedience was open, not secret

topics.t: The 25 per cent settlement
topics.h: Why would a leader accept only half of what he asked? Because the real prize was not money.
p: An official commission of inquiry was set up; Gandhi was the sole representative of the peasants. Evidence went against the planters, and they agreed in principle to refund money to the peasants.
Gandhi asked for 50 per cent. The planters' spokesman offered 25 per cent, and Gandhi accepted, breaking the deadlock.
His reason: the amount was less important than the fact that the landlords had been forced to surrender part of the money and, with it, part of their prestige.
The peasants learnt that they had rights and defenders. Within a few years the British planters abandoned their estates, which went back to the peasants; indigo sharecropping disappeared.

ex.q: Why did Gandhi accept a 25 per cent refund?
st: He had asked for 50; the planters offered 25.
What mattered was that the landlords had to give back money at all.
That broke their prestige and showed peasants they had rights.
ex.a: Because the act of refunding broke the landlords' prestige and gave peasants courage; the amount was secondary.

topics.rl: In negotiations, from wage talks to cricket board disputes, winning the principle often matters more than the exact amount. Gandhi knew this in 1917.

rv.summary: An official inquiry, with Gandhi as the peasants' representative, found against the planters. Gandhi asked for a 50% refund but accepted 25%, since the planters' loss of prestige mattered more. Soon the planters left and sharecropping ended.
remember: Asked 50%, accepted 25%
Surrender of money = surrender of prestige
Estates reverted to the peasants
traps: Accepting 25% was not a defeat
Don't confuse the 25% refund with the 15% tinkathia share

topics.t: Beyond politics: schools, health and self-reliance
topics.h: Most leaders would leave after winning. Gandhi stayed on to open schools and teach villagers to keep clean.
p: Gandhi saw the deeper problems of cultural and social backwardness and opened primary schools in six villages.
Teachers included his disciples Mahadev Desai and Narhari Parikh with their wives, his youngest son Devdas, and his wife Kasturba.
Kasturba taught personal cleanliness and community sanitation. A doctor volunteered for six months with three medicines: castor oil, quinine and sulphur ointment.
Gandhi refused the help of C.F. Andrews, an English follower, because relying on an Englishman would show weakness; Indians had to rely on themselves.
Self-reliance and courage: the Champaran movement taught Indians to stand on their own feet.

ex.q: Why did Gandhi refuse to let C.F. Andrews stay in Champaran?
st: The lawyers wanted an Englishman on their side in an unequal fight.
Gandhi said this showed the weakness of their hearts.
The cause was just, so they had to rely on themselves.
ex.a: Depending on an Englishman would show weakness; Gandhi wanted Indians to be self-reliant.

topics.rl: Swachh Bharat Abhiyan, launched in 2014 on Gandhi's birth anniversary, echoes what Kasturba taught in Champaran: sanitation is part of freedom.

rv.summary: Gandhi also tackled social backwardness: he opened primary schools in six villages, Kasturba taught sanitation, and a doctor treated people. He refused C.F. Andrews's help so that Indians would learn self-reliance.
focus: The C.F. Andrews episode and self-reliance
remember: Schools in six villages; teachers included Mahadev Desai, Narhari Parikh, Devdas, Kasturba
Medicines: castor oil, quinine, sulphur ointment
Andrews refused to teach self-reliance
traps: C.F. Andrews was not kept on as a helper or teacher
Gandhi's work was not only political

topics.t: Themes: non-violence, rights and freedom from fear
topics.h: 'The British could not order me about in my own country.' Gandhi called this a very ordinary thing. It was revolutionary.
p: Civil disobedience and non-violence: Gandhi broke an unjust order openly and peacefully, and accepted the penalty.
Peasants' rights: for the first time the peasants saw that they could stand up to the planters and win.
Freedom from fear: Gandhi told the lawyers that relief lay in freeing the peasants from fear, not in law courts.
Civil disobedience today: peaceful, lawful protest is part of democracy; it differs from violence or vandalism, and it means accepting legal consequences.

ex.q: Why did Gandhi say law courts were not the answer for the peasants?
st: Lawyers charged the peasants high fees.
Court cases did not end their fear of the planters.
Real relief was to free them from fear.
ex.a: Courts drained their money; what they needed was freedom from fear.

topics.rl: The Constitution of India protects the right to assemble peacefully and without arms (Article 19(1)(b)); non-violence remains the core of lawful protest.

rv.summary: Champaran shows non-violent civil disobedience, peasants discovering their rights, and Gandhi's belief that relief lay in freedom from fear, not law courts. Peaceful protest that accepts legal consequences remains part of democracy.
remember: Civil disobedience: open, non-violent, accepts the penalty
Real relief = freedom from fear
'The British could not order me about in my own country'
traps: Civil disobedience does not allow violence
Gandhi did not see law courts as the answer

topics.t: Board exam practice: Indigo
topics.h: 'Why is Champaran called a turning point in Gandhi's life?' This question appears again and again. Here is how to nail it.
p: Shukla's persistence: he followed Gandhi from Lucknow to Cawnpore to Ahmedabad.
The 25 per cent refund: the principle and the surrender of prestige mattered more than the amount.
Impact on peasants: courage, rights, the end of indigo sharecropping; schools and sanitation in villages.
Turning point: Gandhi said it was the moment he decided the British could not order him about in his own country; it began freedom from fear for ordinary Indians.

Short answer on tinkathia: 15 per cent (3/20) of land under indigo, given as rent; compensation demanded after German synthetic indigo. Long answer on self-reliance: the Andrews episode, schools, sanitation.

ex.q: Write a 50-word answer: Why did Gandhi consider Champaran a turning point?
st: Point: he defied British authority openly for the first time in India.
Detail: refused to leave, pleaded guilty, case dropped.
Significance: showed Indians could win by non-violence, free of fear.
ex.a: At Champaran Gandhi first declared that the British could not order him about in his own country. His successful civil disobedience freed peasants from fear and proved that non-violent resistance could win, shaping the whole freedom struggle.

topics.rl: Champaran's centenary was marked in 2017 across Bihar, a reminder that a district's fight for fair farming grew into a national movement.

rv.summary: Board answers on 'Indigo' focus on Shukla's persistence, the tinkathia system, the 25% refund, the impact on peasants, self-reliance through the Andrews episode, and Champaran as the turning point when Gandhi defied British rule.
remember: Turning point: first open defiance of British rule in India
Tinkathia: 15% (3/20) under indigo as rent
Self-reliance: refusing Andrews; schools and sanitation
traps: The movement was not only about money
Don't give background trivia in a definition answer

topics.t: Gemini Studios and the make-up room
topics.h: Make-up bought by the truckload, a room once said to be a British general's stables, and lights hot enough to fry an actor. Welcome to Gemini Studios.
p: Author: Asokamitran, a Tamil writer who worked at Gemini Studios, Madras, from 1952 to the mid-1960s. The chapter is an extract from his memoir 'My Years with Boss'.
Tone: a humorous memoir. 'The Boss' is S.S. Vasan, the founder of Gemini Studios.
Pancake: the brand of make-up material that Gemini Studios bought by the truckload for its actors.
The make-up department was upstairs in a building said to have been Robert Clive's stables.
Incandescent lights and large mirrors made it like a hair-cutting salon turned torture chamber; the heavy make-up turned decent-looking actors into crimson-hued monsters.

ex.q: Explain the title 'Poets and Pancakes'.
st: 'Pancakes' refers to Pancake, the make-up brand used at Gemini.
'Poets' refers to the many poets and writers who worked there, like Subbu.
Together they sum up the studio: glamour and literature side by side.
ex.a: Pancake is the make-up brand; poets are the studio's writers. The title captures the two worlds of Gemini Studios.

topics.rl: Today's film sets in Hyderabad's Ramoji Film City or Mumbai's Film City still have make-up vans and hot lights, but cooler LED lighting has made the 'torture chamber' far gentler.

rv.summary: Asokamitran's humorous memoir 'My Years with Boss' recalls Gemini Studios, Madras, run by S.S. Vasan. Pancake was the make-up brand; the make-up room in 'Clive's stables' had hot lights that turned actors into crimson-hued monsters.
remember: Asokamitran at Gemini 1952 to mid-1960s
The Boss = S.S. Vasan
Pancake = make-up brand; room in 'Robert Clive's stables'
traps: Pancake is not food
The Boss is Vasan, not Subbu

topics.t: National integration and the frustrated office boy
topics.h: A Bengali, a Maharashtrian, a Kannadiga, an Andhra, an Anglo-Burmese and local Tamils, all in one make-up room. The author calls it 'national integration', with a wink.
p: The make-up department showed 'national integration': a Bengali chief (later succeeded by a Maharashtrian), with a Dharwar Kannadiga, an Andhra, a Madras Indian Christian, an Anglo-Burmese and local Tamils.
Strict hierarchy: the chief made up the main actors, his assistants the lesser players, and the office boy the crowd players.
The office boy, in his early forties, had joined the studio hoping to become a star actor, screenwriter, director or lyricist. He was a bit of a poet, but stayed in a dead-end job.
Frustrated, he blamed Kothamangalam Subbu, the No. 2 at Gemini, for his failure and poured out his anger to the author.

ex.q: How does the author create humour with the phrase 'national integration'?
st: National integration is a grand political ideal.
He applies it to a small, noisy make-up room.
The mismatch between the big phrase and the small setting is funny.
ex.a: By using a serious national ideal to describe a mixed group of make-up men; the mock-grand phrase is humorous.

topics.rl: Indian film crews today still bring together people from every state. A single Bollywood or Tollywood set may hear five languages before lunch.

rv.summary: The make-up department showed 'national integration' with staff from many regions and a strict hierarchy. The office boy, a man in his forties, had dreamt of stardom, stayed stuck doing crowd make-up and blamed Subbu.
remember: Chief – main actors; assistants – lesser players; office boy – crowd
Office boy: early forties, wanted to be a star or writer
He blamed Kothamangalam Subbu
traps: The 'office boy' was not young
The staff were not all from Tamil Nadu

topics.t: Subbu the genius and 'the opposition'
topics.h: One man is cheerful, loyal and endlessly creative. Another, nicknamed 'the opposition', ends a career with a tape recorder.
p: Kothamangalam Subbu: the No. 2 at Gemini, a poet and the Boss's loyal aide; always cheerful, and able to suggest many ways of shooting a scene.
He wrote poetry and the novel 'Thillana Mohanambal', acted well, and supported many dependants with great generosity.
The legal adviser, nicknamed 'the opposition' by others, was the only one in pants, tie and sometimes a coat, while others wore khadi.
He once secretly recorded an actress's angry outburst on the set and played it back to her; she was stunned into silence, and her career ended.

ex.q: Why was the legal adviser called 'the opposition'?
st: A legal adviser should help the studio.
Instead, his actions, like taping the actress, harmed the studio's work.
So, ironically, he worked like the opposition.
ex.a: Because instead of helping, he often created problems, as when he ended a talented actress's career.

topics.rl: Many Indian film studios have had creative all-rounders like Subbu: writer, lyricist and actor in one. Tamil cinema still celebrates such multi-talented artists.

rv.summary: Subbu, Gemini's No. 2, was a cheerful genius: poet, novelist, actor, idea man and generous host. The legal adviser, called 'the opposition', ended an actress's career by playing back her recorded outburst.
focus: The legal adviser and the irony of his nickname
remember: Subbu wrote 'Thillana Mohanambal'
Legal adviser = 'the opposition'; wore pants and tie
Taped and replayed the actress's outburst
traps: Subbu, not the legal adviser, was the No. 2
The actress's career ended through the tape, not a lawsuit

topics.t: Clippings, a closed department and the MRA visit
topics.h: The author's job was cutting newspapers. Everyone thought he did nothing. Then two hundred foreigners arrived to stage plays.
p: The author's job was to cut out newspaper clippings on many subjects and file them. Because he sat in a cubicle with scissors and paper, others thought he did nothing.
The Story Department of writers and poets was eventually closed, and the legal adviser, part of it, lost his job too.
Gemini Studios was anti-communist; most of its people wore khadi and admired Gandhi. The Boss welcomed the Moral Re-Armament Army (MRA), an international anti-communist group, in 1952.
About two hundred MRA members staged the plays 'Jotham Valley' and 'The Forgotten Factor'. Tamil drama later copied their sunrise and sunset scenes.

ex.q: Why did people think the author did nothing?
st: His work was quiet: cutting and filing newspapers.
He sat alone in a cubicle with scissors.
Others assumed this was not real work.
ex.a: His quiet job of cutting newspaper clippings looked to others like idleness, so they came to him to pour out their troubles.

topics.rl: Research teams in Indian newsrooms still keep 'clippings libraries'. What looked like 'nothing' to Gemini staff is the backbone of good research.

rv.summary: Asokamitran cut and filed newspaper clippings, so others thought he did nothing. The Story Department was closed. Anti-communist Gemini welcomed the MRA in 1952, whose plays influenced Tamil drama.
focus: The MRA visit and its influence
remember: MRA = Moral Re-Armament Army, anti-communist, 1952
Plays: 'Jotham Valley', 'The Forgotten Factor'
Tamil drama copied sunrise and sunset scenes
traps: The MRA was not a business partner
The author's job was not glamorous film work

topics.t: The mystery poet: Stephen Spender
topics.h: An English poet gives a long speech to a Tamil film studio. Nobody understands a word, and nobody knows who he is.
p: An English poet visited Gemini Studios and spoke to the staff. His accent and subject were beyond them; nobody understood him, and why he had come remained a mystery.
Years later the author found out: the visitor was Stephen Spender, the English poet and editor of the magazine 'The Encounter'.
Spender was one of the contributors to 'The God That Failed', essays by former communists: André Gide, Richard Wright, Ignazio Silone, Arthur Koestler, Louis Fischer and Spender himself.
The episode shows the cultural gap between an English poet and Tamil film workers, and the anti-communist mood of the era.

ex.q: Why was the poet's visit a 'mystery'?
st: Tamil film workers could not follow his English or his ideas about poetry.
A poet had no clear link with a studio making Tamil films.
So no one knew who he was or why he came.
ex.a: His speech made no sense to the audience, and his purpose at a Tamil film studio was never clear.

topics.rl: International writers still visit Indian festivals like the Jaipur Literature Festival. Today, translators and subtitles help bridge the gap that left Gemini's staff baffled.

rv.summary: An English poet's talk baffled Gemini's staff. Years later the author learnt he was Stephen Spender, editor of 'The Encounter' and a contributor to 'The God That Failed', essays by ex-communists — showing a cultural gap and the anti-communist mood.
focus: Why the visit was a mystery
remember: Stephen Spender, editor of 'The Encounter'
'The God That Failed': Gide, Wright, Silone, Koestler, Fischer, Spender
Louis Fischer also wrote the source of 'Indigo'
traps: Umberto Eco was not a contributor
The 'god' that failed was communism, not a religion

topics.t: How Asokamitran makes us laugh
topics.h: Asokamitran never tells a joke. He just describes things with a straight face, and that is what makes them funny.
p: Humour, irony and gentle satire on the film industry: hot lights that make actors into monsters, a 'national integration' of make-up men.
Self-deprecating humour: the author laughs at himself, calling his job one that others thought was doing nothing.
Irony and understatement: the legal adviser called 'the opposition'; a lawyer losing his job because poets were sent home.
Mock-heroic description: small matters told in grand language, such as Clive's stables or national integration.
Anecdotal structure: the chapter is a chain of anecdotes; characters like the office boy, Subbu and the legal adviser are drawn almost as caricatures.

ex.q: Identify the device: 'The make-up department was said to have been Robert Clive's stables.'
st: A great historical name is attached to a humble room.
The grand reference makes the ordinary setting look funny.
This is mock-heroic humour mixed with irony.
ex.a: Mock-heroic irony: a lofty historical reference used for an ordinary make-up room.

topics.rl: Indian comic writers like R.K. Laxman, in his cartoons, used the same straight-faced irony to poke fun at offices and officials.

rv.summary: Asokamitran's humour is gentle: irony, exaggeration, self-deprecation, understatement and mock-heroic phrases, in a chain of anecdotes with near-caricature characters, satirising the film world without cruelty.
remember: Mock-heroic: Clive's stables, 'national integration'
Self-deprecating: the 'do-nothing' author
Structure: series of anecdotes
traps: The satire is gentle, not a harsh attack
Self-deprecating humour is about oneself, not others

topics.t: Board exam practice: Poets and Pancakes
topics.h: Subbu, the MRA and Spender: three short-answer favourites. One long answer on humour. Let's lock them in.
p: Think as you read: Pancake is the make-up brand; the office boy was a frustrated would-be star; the author was thought to do nothing because he cut newspapers.
Understanding: humour through irony, exaggeration and self-mockery; Subbu as a many-sided genius (poet, novelist, actor, generous friend); the legal adviser who ended an actress's career.
The poet's visit was a mystery because no one understood him; 'The God That Failed' was a book of essays by ex-communists, including Spender.
Discussion: humour as a tool to criticise gently; the place of poetry and lyrics in Indian films.
Long answer on humour: give at least three examples, such as Clive's stables, 'national integration', the 'opposition' nickname and the do-nothing author.

ex.q: Write a 50-word answer on Subbu as a many-sided genius.
st: He was the Boss's No. 2 and full of ideas for filming.
He was a poet, novelist and gifted actor.
He was cheerful and generous to many dependants.
ex.a: Kothamangalam Subbu, Gemini's No. 2, could suggest many ways to shoot a scene. A poet, novelist (Thillana Mohanambal) and fine actor, he was always cheerful, loyal to the Boss and generous to the many people who depended on him.

topics.rl: Tamil cinema has a long tradition of poet-lyricists, from Kannadasan to Vairamuthu, showing that poetry and film often share a stage.

rv.summary: Board answers cover Pancake, the frustrated office boy, the 'do-nothing' author, Subbu as a many-sided genius, the legal adviser, Spender's mystery visit and 'The God That Failed', and examples of the chapter's humour.
focus: Long answer on humour with examples
remember: Subbu: poet, novelist, actor, planner, generous
Humour examples: crimson monsters, Clive's stables, 'national integration', 'the opposition'
traps: Don't call the office boy young
Give at least three examples in a long answer on humour

topics.t: The interview: an art or an intrusion?
topics.h: Every evening, news channels run interviews with cricketers, ministers and film stars. Yet until the mid-1800s, the interview did not even exist as a form of journalism.
p: Part I: Christopher Silvester's introduction to 'The Penguin Book of Interviews', on the history of interviews and views about them.
Part II: an extract from Mukund Padmanabhan's interview with the Italian writer Umberto Eco, published in The Hindu.
The interview was invented a little over 130 years before Silvester wrote, and has become a commonplace of journalism.
Positive view: at its best the interview is a source of truth and, in practice, an art; the interviewer holds great power and influence.
Negative view: an unwarranted intrusion into private lives that diminishes the celebrities interviewed.

ex.q: Why is the interview described as a 'commonplace of journalism'?
st: Commonplace means ordinary and very common.
Today interviews appear daily in newspapers, TV and online.
So, though it was invented only about 130 years earlier, it is now everywhere.
ex.a: Because interviews have become so common in the media that almost everyone has read or seen one.

topics.rl: From post-match interviews at the IPL to budget-day interviews with the Finance Minister, the interview is a routine part of Indian media today.

rv.summary: Part I, Silvester's introduction to 'The Penguin Book of Interviews', traces the interview's history; Part II is Mukund Padmanabhan's interview with Umberto Eco. Interviews are seen both as a source of truth and art and as an intrusion.
focus: The two parts of the chapter and their sources
Positive and negative views of the interview
remember: Interview invented a little over 130 years before Silvester wrote
Positive: source of truth, an art, great power for the interviewer
Negative: unwarranted intrusion that diminishes celebrities
traps: Don't confuse Silvester (Part I) with Padmanabhan (Part II)
The interview's age does not explain why it became common

topics.t: Writers who dreaded interviewers
topics.h: One of the world's most loved children's writers refused every interviewer who knocked. He had his reasons.
