p: Some primitive cultures believe a photograph steals a person's soul; similarly, V.S. Naipaul felt that some people are wounded by interviews and lose a part of themselves.
Lewis Carroll, author of 'Alice in Wonderland', had a 'defensive dread' of interviewers and never consented to be interviewed; he hated being lionised.
Rudyard Kipling called the interview immoral, a crime, an offence against his person, an assault that deserved punishment, and cowardly and vile.
Kipling's wife wrote in her diary that their day was 'wrecked by two reporters from Boston'.

ex.q: What is the link between the 'photograph steals the soul' belief and Naipaul's view?
st: The belief: a camera takes away part of a person's spirit.
Naipaul: an interview takes away part of the person interviewed.
Both see a loss of self in being recorded.
ex.a: Both suggest that being photographed or interviewed takes away a part of a person's self.

topics.rl: Some Indian sportspeople avoid media before big events. Like Carroll, they feel constant attention takes something away from them.

rv.summary: Many writers dreaded interviews. Naipaul felt people are wounded by them, like the belief that photographs steal the soul. Lewis Carroll hated being lionised and never gave interviews; Kipling called them a crime and an assault.
focus: Writers who disliked interviews and their reasons
remember: Naipaul: people are wounded and lose part of themselves
Lewis Carroll: 'defensive dread', hated being lionised
Kipling: interview is immoral, a crime, an assault; wife's day 'wrecked by two reporters from Boston'
traps: Lewis Carroll never consented to an interview
Kipling did not see the interview as an art

topics.t: Wells, Bellow, Brian and the power of the interviewer
topics.h: Imagine thumbprints pressing on your throat. That is how one Nobel-winning novelist described being interviewed.
p: H.G. Wells called it 'the ordeal of the interview', yet he was interviewed often and later himself interviewed Joseph Stalin.
Saul Bellow agreed to interviews many times but described them as 'thumbprints on his windpipe', a feeling of being choked.
Denis Brian wrote that today we learn most about our contemporaries through interviews.
Theme: interviews are both an art and an intrusion; the interviewer holds great power to shape how the public sees a person.

ex.q: Explain the metaphor 'thumbprints on his windpipe'.
st: The windpipe carries air; pressure on it means choking.
Interviews made Bellow feel suffocated and pressed.
So the metaphor shows extreme discomfort.
ex.a: Interviews made Bellow feel as if he were being choked; they were suffocating and painful.

topics.rl: A single TV interview can change a public figure's image overnight in India. That is the 'power and influence' of the interviewer Silvester describes.

rv.summary: H.G. Wells called interviews an ordeal but interviewed Stalin; Saul Bellow, often interviewed, felt them as 'thumbprints on his windpipe'. Denis Brian valued them as the way we know our contemporaries. Interviewers hold great power.
focus: Views of Wells, Bellow and Brian
remember: Wells: 'the ordeal of the interview'; interviewed Joseph Stalin
Bellow: 'thumbprints on his windpipe' (metaphor)
Denis Brian: we know most about contemporaries through interviews
traps: Bellow did not refuse all interviews
'Thumbprints on his windpipe' is a metaphor, not a simile

topics.t: Who is Umberto Eco?
topics.h: A professor of 'signs' writes a medieval murder mystery that sells millions of copies. Meet Umberto Eco.
p: Umberto Eco: an Italian professor of semiotics, the study of signs and symbols, at the University of Bologna.
His work spans scholarly books on semiotics, literary interpretation and medieval aesthetics, plus essays and novels.
His novel 'The Name of the Rose' (1980), a medieval detective story, sold between 10 and 15 million copies.
He calls himself a university professor who writes novels on Sundays: he sees himself first as an academic.

ex.q: What does Eco mean when he says he writes novels 'on Sundays'?
st: His main identity is academic: a professor of semiotics.
Novels are something he does in his spare time.
So he means novel-writing is a side activity.
ex.a: He sees himself mainly as a scholar; novel-writing is a weekend or spare-time pursuit.

topics.rl: Many Indian professionals write novels on the side: doctors, IAS officers and bankers. Like Eco, their 'Sunday' writing sometimes becomes a bestseller.

rv.summary: Umberto Eco was an Italian professor of semiotics at the University of Bologna who wrote scholarly books, essays and novels. His medieval detective novel 'The Name of the Rose' (1980) sold 10–15 million copies, yet he saw himself mainly as a professor.
remember: Semiotics = study of signs and symbols
'The Name of the Rose', 1980, 10–15 million copies
'A university professor who writes novels on Sundays'
traps: Eco saw himself first as an academic, not a novelist
'The Name of the Rose' is a detective story, not a romance

topics.t: Interstices and a playful style
topics.h: How does one man write scholarly books, essays, a newspaper column and bestselling novels? He uses the gaps.
p: Eco works in 'interstices', the small empty spaces of time between tasks, such as waiting for a lift to arrive.
He says that if all the empty space were removed from the universe's atoms, the universe would be as small as his fist; likewise, our lives are full of empty spaces we can use.
His scholarly writing uses a playful, personal, narrative style, telling the story of his research instead of being dry and formal.
Theme: creativity and the efficient use of time.
Metaphor: 'interstices', literally tiny gaps between things, is used for the small gaps in a day.

ex.q: Give an example of using 'interstices' in a student's day.
st: Find a small gap: the 10-minute bus ride to school.
Use it for a small task: revising formula cards or new words.
Many such gaps add up to hours of work.
ex.a: Revising flashcards during a short bus ride or while waiting for class is using interstices.

topics.rl: Students revising on the Mumbai local or the Delhi Metro are using Eco's interstices. Ten minutes twice a day adds up to over 100 hours in a year.

rv.summary: Eco works in the 'interstices', the small gaps of time such as waiting for a lift; he compares them to the empty space in atoms. His scholarly writing is playful and personal, telling research as a story.
remember: Interstices = small empty spaces of time
Without empty space the universe would be as small as his fist
Theme: efficient use of time
traps: Interstices are small gaps, not long vacations
Eco's academic writing is not dry and formal

topics.t: Why did The Name of the Rose succeed?
topics.h: A difficult novel full of medieval history and theology became a global bestseller. Even its author called this a mystery.
p: Eco thinks the novel's success is a mystery; he says it might not have sold if written ten years earlier or ten years later.
The novel is serious and demanding, a detective story that goes into metaphysics, theology and medieval history, yet it found a mass audience.
Eco suggests readers do not only want easy reading; many enjoy serious, challenging books, and the medieval setting attracted them.
Theme: popularity, scholarship and fiction can meet; a scholar can be a bestselling novelist.
Form: Part I is expository prose packed with quotations; Part II follows a question-answer interview format.

ex.q: How does Eco explain the success of 'The Name of the Rose'?
st: He calls it a mystery that depended on timing.
Readers were drawn by its medieval setting and serious content.
He rejects the idea that readers only want easy books.
ex.a: He says it is a mystery linked to timing; readers enjoyed its serious content and medieval setting, though it was not easy reading.

topics.rl: Indian bestsellers on mythology and history show the same thing Eco noticed: readers will take on serious, layered stories when the setting fascinates them.

rv.summary: Eco calls the success of 'The Name of the Rose' a mystery of timing; readers liked its serious content and medieval setting, showing they do not want only easy books. Part I is expository prose; Part II is a question-answer interview.
focus: Eco's explanation of his novel's success
Forms of Part I and Part II
remember: Ten years earlier or later, it might not have sold
Readers want serious books too
Part I: expository prose with quotations; Part II: question-answer
traps: Eco did not say readers want only easy books
Don't swap the forms of the two parts

topics.t: Understanding the text: The Interview
topics.h: 'Who is lionised today?' Answer that, and you'll see why writers like Carroll ran from reporters.
p: Positive views: art, source of truth, a way to know contemporaries. Negative views: intrusion, diminishing, wounding, a crime. Celebrity writers dislike interviews because they intrude and take something away.
The photograph belief: primitive cultures fear a picture steals the soul; 'thumbprints on his windpipe' means a choking, suffocating feeling.
To be lionised is to be treated as a celebrity. Today film stars, sports stars and influencers are lionised because of media attention.
Eco's interstices explain his output; his academic writing is personal and playful because he tells research as a story.
Eco on his novel's success: a mystery of timing; readers liked its serious content and medieval setting.

ex.q: Who is lionised today, and why?
st: Lionise = treat as a celebrity.
Examples: cricketers, film stars, social media influencers.
Reason: constant media coverage and public admiration.
ex.a: Cricketers, film stars and influencers are lionised today because the media covers them constantly and fans admire them.

topics.rl: When an Indian athlete wins Olympic gold, crowds, interviews and ads follow within hours. That is lionising, and Carroll's 'horror' of it makes more sense.

rv.summary: Writers dislike interviews as intrusive and diminishing; supporters see truth and art. 'Lionised' means treated as a celebrity. Eco's interstices explain his output, his writing tells research as a story, and his novel's success is a mystery of timing.
remember: Lionised = treated as a celebrity
Photograph belief parallels Naipaul's 'wounded' view
Views in Part I are mixed, not all negative
traps: 'Lionised' does not mean attacked or made brave
Not all writers in Part I think interviews are harmful

topics.t: Conducting an interview and exam answers
topics.h: Your school magazine wants an interview with the principal. You have 15 minutes. What do you ask?
p: The interview as journalism: it informs, reveals personality and shapes opinion, but must respect privacy and consent.
Planning an interview: research the person, prepare open questions (what, why, how), start easy, then go deeper, and listen and follow up.
Conducting it: take permission to record, be polite, note exact words, check facts before publishing.
Short answers: views on interviews (positive and negative) and Eco's interstices. Long answer: the interview as a medium, its power, art and risks.

ex.q: Plan three good opening questions for an interview with a local doctor.
st: Begin with an easy, open question.
Move to their work and challenges.
End with advice for students.
ex.a: What made you choose medicine? What is a typical day like at your clinic? What advice would you give students who want to become doctors?

topics.rl: Podcasts by Indian entrepreneurs and sportspeople show interviews at their best: well-researched questions, real listening and respect for the guest.

rv.summary: A good interview is researched and planned with open questions, begins easy, goes deeper, listens and follows up, takes permission to record and checks facts. Exam answers on the interview as a medium should cover both power and risks.
remember: Open questions: what, why, how
Take permission before recording; check facts and quotes
Long answer: power, art and risks
traps: Don't open with intrusive questions
Yes/no questions make dull interviews

topics.t: Sophie's big dreams, Jansie's hard facts
topics.h: Two school-leavers walk home. One plans a boutique and a film career; the other knows the biscuit factory is waiting.
p: Author: A.R. Barton. 'Going Places' is a story of adolescent fantasy set in a working-class English family.
Narration: third person, but it closely follows Sophie's thoughts and daydreams.
Sophie and her friend Jansie are about to leave school. Jansie says they are both 'earmarked for the biscuit factory'.
Sophie dreams of opening a boutique, becoming an actress or a fashion designer, anything glamorous.
Jansie is practical: she reminds Sophie that a boutique needs money and that such jobs need experience.

ex.q: How do Sophie and Jansie differ in their view of the future?
st: Sophie imagines a boutique, acting or fashion design.
Jansie expects work at the biscuit factory.
Jansie points out the need for money and experience.
ex.a: Sophie is a dreamer with unrealistic plans; Jansie is realistic and accepts their limited prospects.

topics.rl: Many Indian teens dream of being influencers or film stars while family finances point to a nearby job. Sophie's tug-of-war between dream and reality is very familiar.

rv.summary: A.R. Barton's story of adolescent fantasy follows Sophie, a working-class girl about to leave school. She dreams of a boutique, acting or fashion design, while her realistic friend Jansie says they are both earmarked for the biscuit factory.
remember: Author: A.R. Barton
Third-person narration following Sophie's thoughts
'Earmarked for the biscuit factory'
traps: The story is not told in the first person
Jansie is realistic, not a dreamer

topics.t: At home: Geoff, Father and a story about Danny Casey
topics.h: Sophie tells her family she met the town's football star. Her father snorts; her brother is unsure. Did it really happen?
p: Home: her father, a big, tired manual worker; her mother, tired and anxious; her elder brother Geoff; her little brother Derek.
Sophie admires Geoff, an apprentice mechanic who travels across the city to work and keeps his life private; she longs to be part of his world.
She tells Geoff she met Danny Casey, the young Irish football star of United, in the arcade.
She says Casey promised to meet her by the canal. Geoff is doubtful, and her father dismisses it as another of her wild stories.

ex.q: Why does Sophie tell the Danny Casey story to Geoff first?
st: She admires Geoff and wants his attention.
Geoff is quiet and private, and she longs to be part of his world.
Sharing a 'secret' about a football star might impress him.
ex.a: Because she admires Geoff and wants to win his attention and be included in his private world.

topics.rl: Fans of cricket stars in India sometimes claim chance meetings that grow in each retelling. Sophie's story works the same way.

rv.summary: At home Sophie's tired parents, private brother Geoff and little Derek surround her. She admires Geoff, an apprentice mechanic, and tells him she met the Irish football star Danny Casey in the arcade; her father dismisses it as a wild story.
remember: Geoff: apprentice mechanic, reserved
Danny Casey: young Irish star of United
Met in the arcade; promised meeting by the canal
traps: Don't swap the arcade (meeting) and the canal (promised meeting)
Geoff does not share his life with Sophie

topics.t: The match, the canal and the broken fantasy
topics.h: At the match, Sophie's family cheers as Danny Casey scores. Later, Sophie waits alone by the canal. Nobody comes.
p: At the United match, Sophie stands with her father and little Derek (Geoff is with his mates); Danny Casey scores a goal, and Sophie feels a private thrill as if he were hers.
Later Sophie walks by the canal and waits on a bench under a solitary elm. Casey never comes.
She goes home sad, but she still clings to the fantasy; her worry is how to keep the truth from others, especially Geoff.
Contrast: dreamy Sophie against realistic Jansie; the canal meeting stands for illusion, a meeting that was never real.

ex.q: What does the canal scene reveal about Sophie?
st: She waits for a meeting that probably never existed.
When Casey does not come, she is sad but does not give up the dream.
This shows how deep her need for fantasy is.
ex.a: It reveals that she lives in illusion; even disappointment does not break her fantasy.

topics.rl: Social media lets fans feel close to stars they have never met. Sophie's canal is an old-fashioned version of waiting for a reply to a fan message.

rv.summary: At the United match Casey scores and Sophie feels a private thrill. She waits by the canal, but Casey never comes. Sad, she still clings to her fantasy and worries about hiding the truth.
focus: The match and the canal scene
What the canal wait reveals about Sophie
remember: Casey scores at the match
Sophie waits by the canal under an elm; Casey never comes
Canal meeting = illusion
traps: Casey never meets Sophie
Sophie does not give up her fantasy

topics.t: The characters of Going Places
topics.h: A dreamer, a gossip, a silent brother and two tired parents. Each one shows a different side of growing up working-class.
p: Sophie: dreamy, romantic and escapist; she longs for glamour and attention and invents stories to escape her dull life.
Jansie: realistic and a bit of a gossip; Sophie fears she will spread the Casey story around the neighbourhood.
Geoff: silent and reserved; he has a world of his own, with friends and places Sophie knows nothing about.
Father: a hard-working manual labourer and keen football fan, sceptical of Sophie's tales. Mother: tired and anxious.

ex.q: Why does Sophie not want Jansie to know about Danny Casey?
st: Jansie is nosy and loves to gossip.
If she knew, the whole neighbourhood would know.
Sophie fears being found out or mocked.
ex.a: Because Jansie gossips; the story, true or not, would spread through the neighbourhood.

topics.rl: Every Indian joint family has a Geoff: an elder brother who says little at dinner but whose approval matters to everyone younger.

rv.summary: Sophie is dreamy and escapist; Jansie is realistic and a gossip; Geoff is silent and reserved; their father is a hard-working, sceptical football fan; their mother is tired and anxious.
focus: Character traits of Sophie and Jansie
Character traits of Geoff and the parents
remember: Sophie – escapist; Jansie – realistic, gossip
Geoff – silent, private world
Father – sceptical football fan; mother – tired, anxious
traps: Jansie is not a dreamer like Sophie
Sophie's father does not support her stories

topics.t: Themes and the irony of the title
topics.h: 'Going places' means heading for success. Sophie isn't going anywhere, and that is exactly the point.
p: Adolescent fantasy and hero worship: Sophie idolises Danny Casey and builds a fantasy around him.
Dreams versus reality, and the limits of class: a poor family's daughter is likely to work at a factory, whatever her dreams.
Communication gaps in the family: Geoff keeps to himself, the father dismisses her, the mother is too tired to listen.
Irony of the title: 'going places' means rising in life, but Sophie's prospects are limited; she goes nowhere except in her dreams.

ex.q: Explain the irony in the title 'Going Places'.
st: The phrase means becoming successful.
Sophie's real future is the biscuit factory.
She 'goes places' only in her imagination.
ex.a: The title promises success, but Sophie's real prospects are limited; she travels only in fantasy.

topics.rl: Hero worship of cricketers in India runs deep. Admiring heroes can inspire, but replacing real plans with fantasy can leave teens like Sophie stranded.

rv.summary: The story explores adolescent fantasy and hero worship, dreams versus reality, the limits of class and family communication gaps. The title is ironic: Sophie 'goes places' only in her dreams.
remember: Hero worship of Danny Casey
Central conflict: dreams versus reality
Irony: limited prospects, travel only in fantasy
traps: The story does not end in success
Don't read the title literally

topics.t: Board exam practice: Going Places
topics.h: 'Fantasy versus reality' is a classic long answer. Know Sophie's world, and the marks follow.
p: Think as you read: Sophie wants a boutique or glamour job; Jansie discourages her because they lack money; Sophie admires Geoff for his grown-up, private world.
Understanding: Sophie's fantasy world centres on Casey; she waits by the canal hoping her daydream is real; the title is ironic.
Discussion: hero worship among teenagers can inspire or mislead; dreams need effort and realism.
Short answers: Sophie (dreamy, escapist) and Geoff (silent, reserved). Long answer: fantasy versus reality, with the boutique, the Casey story, the canal and the ironic title.

ex.q: Write a 50-word answer: Why did Sophie wait by the canal?
st: She claimed Casey promised to meet her there.
She half believes her own fantasy.
Waiting shows her longing for glamour and attention.
ex.a: Sophie had told her family that Danny Casey promised to meet her by the canal. Half believing her own fantasy, she went and waited. Her waiting shows her deep longing for glamour and attention, and her inability to separate dreams from reality.

topics.rl: Career counsellors in Indian schools often say: 'Dream big, but plan step by step.' Sophie had the first part and missed the second.

rv.summary: Board answers on 'Going Places' cover Sophie's dreams and Jansie's realism, Sophie's admiration for Geoff, her fantasy about Casey and the canal, hero worship and the ironic title.
focus: Long answer on fantasy versus reality
remember: Jansie discourages because they lack money and experience
Sophie admires Geoff's grown-up private world
Long answer: boutique, Casey story, canal, ironic title
traps: Don't open a long answer with minor detail
Don't confuse Geoff with Danny Casey

topics.t: Kamala Das and a drive to Cochin
topics.h: A short car ride to the airport. A mother dozing in the seat beside you. In that ordinary moment, Kamala Das finds a lifetime of fear.
p: Poet: Kamala Das, an Indian poet who wrote in English and Malayalam (as Madhavikutty), known for frank, confessional poetry.
Form: a short autobiographical poem written as one long sentence, with no stanza breaks; the flow mirrors a rush of thoughts.
Situation: the poet drives from her parents' home to Cochin airport on a Friday morning.
Her mother sits beside her, dozing with her mouth open.

ex.q: Why might the poet have written the poem as a single sentence?
st: The poem records one continuous stream of thought and feeling.
A single sentence shows feelings flowing without pause.
It matches the short car ride, from home to the airport.
ex.a: The single sentence mirrors an unbroken flow of thoughts and emotions during one journey.

topics.rl: Many Indian students living away from home in Kota, Bengaluru or Delhi know the airport goodbye with a parent. This poem captures the feeling behind it.

rv.summary: Kamala Das's confessional poem, written as one long sentence, records her drive from her parents' home to Cochin airport on a Friday morning, with her sixty-six-year-old mother dozing beside her.
remember: Kamala Das wrote in English and Malayalam (as Madhavikutty)
One long sentence, no stanza breaks
Drive to Cochin airport, Friday morning
traps: She is driving to the airport, not to her parents' home
The poem is not in stanzas

topics.t: A face like a corpse, a mind that turns away
topics.h: Sometimes you notice, all at once, that a parent has grown old. The poet's first instinct is to look away.
p: Looking at her sleeping mother, the poet sees her face ashen like a corpse's and realises with pain that her mother is as old as she looks.
She pushes the thought away and looks outside at young trees sprinting past and merry children spilling out of their homes.
At the airport, after the security check, she looks at her mother again: wan and pale as a late winter's moon.
An old childhood fear returns: the fear of losing her mother, felt now as a familiar ache.

ex.q: Why does the poet look out of the window?
st: The sight of her mother's ashen face is painful.
Outside, the trees and children are full of life.
Looking away helps her escape the thought of ageing and death.
ex.a: To escape the painful thought of her mother's ageing; the lively scene outside is a distraction.

topics.rl: Many of us scroll our phones or change the subject when a hard thought comes up. The poet's glance out of the window is the same human reflex.

rv.summary: Seeing her sleeping mother's ashen, corpse-like face, the poet realises with pain that her mother is old. She looks away at sprinting trees and merry children, but at the airport the pale mother revives her old childhood fear of losing her.
remember: 'Ashen like that of a corpse'
'Pale as a late winter's moon'
'Old familiar ache' = childhood fear of losing her mother
traps: The mother is not dead — the corpse image is a simile
The fear is about losing her mother, not about flying

topics.t: 'See you soon, Amma': love that hides its fear
topics.h: Three simple words: 'See you soon.' Behind them lies everything the poet cannot say.
p: At parting, the poet hides her feelings and says only, 'See you soon, Amma.'
She smiles and smiles and smiles, to reassure her mother and to hide her own fear.
Theme: the ageing of a parent and the fear of separation and death.
Theme: love, helplessness and suppressed emotion; she cannot stop time, so she covers her pain with hope.

ex.q: What do the parting words 'See you soon, Amma' convey?
st: They sound casual and cheerful.
In fact they express hope that her mother will live to meet her again.
They also hide the poet's fear.
ex.a: Hope of meeting again and an attempt to hide fear and reassure her mother.

topics.rl: Indian families often keep goodbyes light, 'Phone kar dena, beta', even when they are worried. The poet's smile is that same brave lightness.

rv.summary: At parting the poet says only 'See you soon, Amma' and smiles again and again, hiding her fear to reassure her mother. The poem's themes are a parent's ageing, fear of separation and death, and suppressed love.
remember: 'See you soon, Amma' = hope of meeting again
'Smile and smile and smile' hides fear
Themes: ageing, fear of loss, love and helplessness
traps: The smile does not show happiness
'See you soon' is a hope, not a fixed promise

topics.t: Youth versus age: similes and images
topics.h: Inside the car: an old woman asleep. Outside: trees racing and children bursting out of homes. Two worlds, one window apart.
p: Theme: the contrast between youth and old age, life and decay.
Similes: the face 'ashen like that of a corpse'; the mother 'pale as a late winter's moon'.
Imagery: young trees sprinting; merry children spilling out of their homes, full of energy and joy.
Personification: the trees are described as sprinting, as if they were runners; in a moving car they seem to race past.

ex.q: Why are the trees said to be 'sprinting'?
st: From a moving car, roadside trees seem to rush backwards.
'Sprinting' gives them life and speed, like young runners.
This energy contrasts with the dozing mother.
ex.a: From the moving car they seem to run past; the word gives them youthful energy that contrasts with the mother's age.

topics.rl: Look out of a Vande Bharat window and the trees seem to race by. The poet uses that everyday effect to say something deep about time.

rv.summary: The poem contrasts youth and age. Similes ('ashen like that of a corpse', 'pale as a late winter's moon') show the mother's age; images of sprinting trees and merry children show youth; the trees are personified.
remember: Simile: 'like' or 'as'
'Young trees sprinting' = personification
Late winter's moon = pale, fading, near its end
traps: 'Pale as a late winter's moon' is a simile, not a metaphor
The winter moon does not suggest vigour

topics.t: Repetition, free verse and the poet's ache
topics.h: 'Smile and smile and smile.' Say it aloud. Does it sound happy, or does it sound like someone trying very hard?
p: Repetition: 'smile and smile and smile' shows the effort of keeping up a brave face; the smile hides pain.
Structure: the contrast between inside the car (age) and outside (youth); enjambment, with lines running on; free verse, with no regular rhyme or metre.
The poet's pain is the realisation that her mother is old and may soon die; the ache is her childhood fear of losing her mother, now returning.
The trees are 'sprinting' because, from a moving car, they appear to rush backwards, and they stand for youth hurrying past.

ex.q: What kind of pain and ache does the poet feel?
st: Pain: realising her mother is truly old.
Ache: an old childhood fear of losing her.
Both come from love and the fear of separation by death.
ex.a: The pain of seeing her mother's age and the ache of her old fear of losing her for ever.

topics.rl: Indian film songs often repeat a line to show feeling. Kamala Das's triple smile works the same way: the repetition is the emotion.

rv.summary: Repetition in 'smile and smile and smile' shows the effort to hide pain. The poem is free verse with enjambment, contrasting the ageing mother inside the car with youth outside; the ache is the poet's old fear of losing her mother.
remember: Free verse: no regular rhyme or metre
Enjambment: sense runs on to the next line
Trees seem to sprint from a moving car
traps: The poem has no regular rhyme scheme
The 'ache' is emotional, not physical

topics.t: Board exam practice: My Mother at Sixty-six
topics.h: Extract-based questions on this poem almost always ask about a simile or the contrast. Let's practise.
p: Merry children: brought in to contrast youth and joy with the mother's old age and to distract the poet from her pain.
Late winter's moon: like the moon at the end of winter, the mother is pale, dim and near the end of her life.
Parting words and smile: hope of meeting again, and a brave mask over her fear.
Extract-based MCQs: identify similes ('ashen like', 'pale as'), the contrast between inside and outside, the poet's feelings; short answers on her fear.

ex.q: Extract (paraphrased): after security, she looks at her mother again, pale like a late winter's moon, and feels the old ache. (a) Device? (b) Feeling?
st: 'Pale as a late winter's moon' uses 'as': a simile.
The 'old familiar ache' is her childhood fear.
Feeling: fear of losing her mother.
ex.a: (a) Simile. (b) Fear and pain at the thought of losing her mother.

topics.rl: CBSE extract questions reward precise terms. Writing 'simile' with the exact words, rather than 'comparison', can earn the full mark.

rv.summary: Board answers explain the merry children as a contrast with age, the late winter's moon as the fading mother, and the parting words and smile as hope masking fear. Extract questions ask for similes, contrasts and feelings.
focus: Extract-based questions on devices and feelings
remember: Merry children = youthful joy against old age
Mood: tender and sad
Smile hides fear and pain
traps: The poet is not happy to leave
Don't read images literally

topics.t: Neruda's invitation: count to twelve
topics.h: What if the whole planet stopped, just for a few seconds, at the same time? A Nobel-winning poet asks us to try.
p: Poet: Pablo Neruda, a Chilean poet and diplomat who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1971.
'Keeping Quiet' was written in Spanish and translated into English by Alastair Reid; it is in free verse.
Opening: the poet asks us to count to twelve and keep still, all over the earth, for once.
In that moment no one would speak in any language, and we would not move our arms.

ex.q: Why does the poet want no one to speak 'in any language'?
st: Languages can divide people into groups.
Silence is shared by everyone in the same way.
So a common silence unites all humanity.
ex.a: Because silence is universal; without language barriers, all people would share one moment together.

topics.rl: India observes two minutes' silence on 30 January, Martyrs' Day. A whole nation pausing together is close to what Neruda imagines.

rv.summary: Pablo Neruda, the Chilean Nobel laureate, wrote 'Keeping Quiet' in Spanish; Alastair Reid translated it. In free verse he asks everyone on earth to count to twelve and keep still, speaking no language, so that silence unites us.
focus: The opening request and its purpose
remember: Pablo Neruda, Chile, Nobel Prize 1971
Translated by Alastair Reid
Count to twelve; no language, no movement
traps: Neruda was Chilean, not Spanish
The poem is free verse, not rhymed

topics.t: A strange, exotic moment of peace
topics.h: No engines. No rush. Fishermen sparing whales. Generals changing into clean clothes. Neruda paints a world on pause.
p: It would be an exotic moment, without rush and without engines; we would all be together in a sudden strangeness.
Fishermen in the cold sea would not harm whales.
The man gathering salt would look at his hurt hands, noticing his own pain for once.
Those who prepare green wars, wars with gas and fire, victories with no survivors, would put on clean clothes and walk with their brothers in the shade, doing nothing.

ex.q: What does the image of the salt gatherer show?
st: He works so hard that he never notices his injuries.
In the quiet moment he looks at his hurt hands.
Stillness lets people notice their own suffering.
ex.a: That constant work makes us ignore our pain; silence lets us see and care for ourselves.

topics.rl: Workers in the salt pans of the Rann of Kutch, the Agariyas, are known to suffer injuries to their hands and feet from salt. Neruda's salt gatherer is real.

rv.summary: The silent moment would be exotic, without rush or engines. Fishermen would spare whales, the salt gatherer would notice his hurt hands, and those who wage green wars and wars of gas and fire would walk with their brothers.
focus: The images of fishermen, salt gatherer and warmongers
remember: Exotic = strange and unusual
Green wars = wars against the environment
'Victory with no survivors' — war destroys all
traps: 'Exotic' here does not mean foreign
The moment has no rush or engines

topics.t: Not death but life: the earth's lesson
topics.h: Does Neruda want us to stop living? No. He wants us to stop rushing, which is very different.
p: The poet says he does not want total inactivity; life is what it is all about, and he wants nothing to do with death.
If we were not so single-minded about keeping our lives moving, a huge silence might end the sadness of never understanding ourselves and of threatening ourselves with death.
The earth can teach us: when everything seems dead in winter, it later proves to be alive in spring.
Ending: the poet counts to twelve, asks us to keep quiet, and leaves.

ex.q: What lesson does the earth teach us?
st: In winter, trees and fields seem dead.
In spring, life returns.
So stillness is not death; it can be a time of renewal.
ex.a: Apparent stillness can hold hidden life; like the earth, silence can renew us.

topics.rl: A field after harvest in Punjab looks dead, but with the next sowing it is green again. Neruda's earth lesson is something every Indian farmer knows.

rv.summary: Neruda says he does not want total inactivity or death; life is what matters. Our single-minded busyness causes the sadness of never understanding ourselves. The earth, which seems dead in winter and revives, teaches us.
focus: What the poet does not mean
remember: 'Life is what it is all about'
Sadness: never understanding ourselves, threatening ourselves with death
What seems dead later proves alive
traps: Keeping quiet is not total inactivity
The earth's lesson is renewal, not that all must die

topics.t: Themes: silence, brotherhood and peace
topics.h: Neruda's poem is short, but it touches war, ecology and the human mind all at once.
p: Silence and introspection: a pause lets us look within and understand ourselves.
Universal brotherhood, peace and non-violence: no language barriers; warmongers walking with their brothers.
Criticism of war, harm to nature and mindless activity: green wars, harming whales, endless rush.
Form: free verse and direct address to the reader with 'let us' and 'we', which includes everyone.

ex.q: How does the poet promote universal brotherhood?
st: Everyone keeps still at once, all over the earth.
No one speaks any language, removing barriers.
Former enemies walk together as brothers.
ex.a: By imagining all humanity sharing one silent moment, without language barriers or war, as brothers.

topics.rl: Yoga and meditation, traditions with roots in India, now practised worldwide, value the same pause and introspection that Neruda praises.

rv.summary: The poem's themes are silence and introspection, universal brotherhood, peace and non-violence, and criticism of war, harm to nature and mindless rush. It uses free verse and direct address with 'let us' and 'we'.
remember: Brotherhood: warmongers walk with brothers
Nature: fishermen spare whales
Direct address: 'let us', 'we'
traps: The poem has no regular rhyme or metre
It criticises rush, not silence

topics.t: Devices and big questions
topics.h: Repeated 'without', fishermen, whales, a salt gatherer: Neruda builds his message image by image.
p: Anaphora and repetition: lines starting the same way ('without rush, without engines') stress the absence of noise and haste.
Imagery: fishermen and whales, the salt gatherer, the warmongers; each shows a different harm we could pause.
Personification of the earth, which can 'teach' us; paradox of life hidden under apparent death.
Counting to twelve and keeping still would help us find peace, introspection and brotherhood. Twelve is often read as the hours on a clock face or the months of a year, a full cycle of time.
The poet does not advocate total inactivity or death: he says life is what it is all about.

ex.q: Explain the paradox in the earth's lesson.
st: A paradox seems self-contradictory but holds a truth.
Things that 'seem dead' are 'alive'.
Truth: rest and stillness hide life and renewal.
ex.a: It seems contradictory that dead things are alive, but in nature dormancy leads to new life; so silence can renew us.

topics.rl: A neem tree sheds its leaves and stands bare, then bursts into fresh green leaves a few weeks later. That is the paradox of the earth that Neruda uses.

rv.summary: Devices include anaphora ('without rush, without engines'), images of different harms, personification of the earth and the paradox of life under apparent death. Counting to twelve suggests a full cycle of time; the poet wants a pause, not death.
remember: Anaphora = repetition at the start of phrases
'The earth can teach us' = personification
Twelve = hours on a clock, months of a year
traps: The earth is personified, not compared in a simile
The poet does not ask for inactivity or death

topics.t: Board exam practice: Keeping Quiet
topics.h: 'What sadness does the poet refer to?' is one of the most-asked short questions on this poem.
p: The sadness: never understanding ourselves and threatening ourselves with death, caused by constant, mindless activity.
Symbol from nature: the earth, which seems dead but later proves to be alive, showing life under apparent stillness.
Lines that best convey the message: the call to count to twelve and keep still, and the line on life being what it is all about.
Extract-based MCQs ask about devices and meanings; short answers should link silence with introspection and peace.

ex.q: Extract (paraphrased): 'If we were not so single-minded about keeping busy, a huge silence might end our sadness.' Which sadness?
st: Read the context: we never understand ourselves.
We also threaten ourselves with death through war and harm.
Silence could break this cycle.
ex.a: The sadness of never understanding ourselves and of threatening ourselves with death.

topics.rl: Exam halls in India go silent before the paper starts. Many toppers say that minute of calm helps them think clearly, a small-scale 'Keeping Quiet'.

rv.summary: Board answers on 'Keeping Quiet' explain the sadness of never understanding ourselves caused by constant busyness, the earth as a symbol of life under stillness, and the call to count to twelve and keep still as the core message.
focus: Extract questions on meanings and devices
remember: Core line: 'Let us count to twelve and keep still'
'A huge silence' = deep pause for reflection
Earth = life beneath apparent death
traps: 'A huge silence' is not permanent silence
Our sadness comes from too much busyness, not too much rest

topics.t: Keats and a joy that lasts for ever
topics.h: A phone's wallpaper fades from your mind in a week. Keats claims some beautiful things never fade. Which ones, and why?
p: Poet: John Keats, an English Romantic poet. These lines are from the opening of his long poem 'Endymion'.
Form: rhyming couplets in iambic pentameter (heroic couplets): pairs of rhyming lines, each with five da-DUM beats.
Opening idea: a thing of beauty is a joy for ever; its loveliness keeps increasing and never passes into nothingness.
It keeps a quiet bower (a shady shelter) for us, and a sleep full of sweet dreams, health and quiet breathing.

ex.q: What does Keats mean by 'a thing of beauty is a joy for ever'?
st: Beautiful things give us joy.
That joy does not end; the memory of beauty stays with us.
In fact its loveliness grows each time we recall it.
ex.a: Beauty gives lasting joy; its memory never fades but grows stronger over time.

topics.rl: Many people in India remember a first sight of the Himalayas or the Taj Mahal for decades. That lasting glow is exactly Keats's claim.

rv.summary: In the opening lines of 'Endymion', John Keats says a thing of beauty is a joy for ever: its loveliness grows and never fades, giving us a quiet bower and peaceful sleep. The lines are heroic couplets.
focus: The opening idea of lasting beauty
remember: John Keats, English Romantic poet; from 'Endymion'
Heroic couplets: rhyming pairs in iambic pentameter (5 beats)
Bower = shady shelter; sleep of sweet dreams, health, quiet breathing
traps: Beauty's loveliness increases — it does not fade
Iambic pentameter has 5 beats, not 10

topics.t: A flowery band against the gloom
topics.h: Life has bad days, bad people and bad news. Keats says we survive by tying ourselves to beauty, one flower at a time.
p: Every morning we weave a flowery band (wreath) that binds us to the earth: beautiful things keep us attached to life.
Beauty helps us in spite of despondence (despair), the inhuman dearth of noble natures (lack of good people), gloomy days and the unhealthy, darkened ways we follow.
Some shape of beauty moves away the pall (dark cloth covering a coffin, here sadness) from our dark spirits.

ex.q: Explain 'some shape of beauty moves away the pall from our dark spirits'.
st: A pall is a dark cloth over a coffin; here, gloom over the mind.
Our spirits are dark with sorrow.
Some beautiful thing lifts this gloom.
ex.a: A beautiful sight lifts the heavy sadness from our troubled minds, like removing a dark cloth.

topics.rl: On a bad day, a monsoon rainbow over Mumbai's Marine Drive or a chai-time sunset can lift the mood. Keats calls this beauty removing the pall.

rv.summary: Every morning we weave a flowery band of beauty that binds us to the earth. Despite despondence, lack of noble people, gloomy days and dark ways, some shape of beauty removes the pall of sorrow from our spirits.
remember: Despondence = hopelessness
Dearth of noble natures = lack of good people
Pall = dark cloth over a coffin, here gloom
traps: 'Dearth' means scarcity, not death
Keats says beauty helps in spite of gloom, not that it fails

topics.t: Keats's list of beautiful things
topics.h: Sun, moon, sheep in shade, daffodils, cool streams, musk roses, heroic tales. Keats's list moves from nature to the human imagination.
p: Nature: the sun, the moon, trees old and young giving shade (a 'shady boon') to simple sheep, daffodils in their green world.
Clear rills (small streams) that make a cooling covert (shelter) against the hot season; the mid-forest brake (thicket) rich with musk-rose blooms.
Human imagination: the grandeur of the dooms (glorious fates) we imagine for the mighty dead, and all lovely tales we have heard or read.
Climax: an endless fountain of immortal drink pouring to us from heaven's brink, beauty as a divine gift.

ex.q: Why is 'grandeur' linked with the 'mighty dead'?
st: The mighty dead are great heroes of the past.
Their lives and deaths were glorious.
We imagine their grand fates, and the stories inspire us.
ex.a: Great people of the past lived and died gloriously; imagining their grand fates gives us a sense of beauty and inspiration.

topics.rl: Tales of heroes like Rani Lakshmibai or Bhagat Singh still move Indian students. Keats counts such inspiring stories of the 'mighty dead' as things of beauty.

rv.summary: Keats lists things of beauty: the sun, moon, trees shading simple sheep, daffodils, cool rills, musk-roses in a forest thicket, the grand fates of the mighty dead and lovely tales — all an endless fountain of immortal drink from heaven.
remember: Rills = small streams; covert = shelter; brake = thicket
Mighty dead: glorious fates (dooms)
Endless fountain of immortal drink from heaven's brink
traps: City buildings are not in Keats's list
The fountain shows beauty is endless, not limited

topics.t: Themes and metaphors of beauty
topics.h: To Keats, beauty is not decoration. It is medicine, rope and fountain all at once.
p: Beauty gives lasting joy and makes life bearable despite pain and disappointment.
Nature's healing power: natural beauty soothes and heals our suffering.
Beauty is a divine gift that binds us to the earth; it pours from heaven's brink.
Metaphors: the 'flowery band' (beauty tying us to life), the 'pall' (gloom), the 'endless fountain of immortal drink' (unending, heavenly beauty).

ex.q: Why does Keats call beauty an 'endless fountain of immortal drink'?
st: A fountain gives water without stopping.
Immortal drink is the drink of the gods, giving eternal life.
Beauty, like that drink, is a heavenly, unending source of joy.
ex.a: Because beauty is an unending, divine source of joy and life, like a fountain of nectar from heaven.

topics.rl: Forest-bathing, nature walks and 'green therapy' are increasingly suggested for stress in Indian cities. Keats said nature heals two hundred years ago.

rv.summary: The poem's themes are lasting joy from beauty, nature's healing power and beauty as a divine gift. Metaphors include the flowery band (beauty tying us to life), the pall (gloom) and the endless fountain of immortal drink.
remember: Flowery band = beauty that binds us to life
Pall = gloom
Immortal drink = nectar; beauty pours from heaven's brink
traps: The pall stands for gloom, not happiness
Beauty is presented as divine, not material

topics.t: Sound and style: alliteration, inversion and couplets
topics.h: Read 'simple sheep' aloud. Feel the soft 's' sounds? Keats chose them on purpose.
p: Nature imagery throughout: sun, moon, trees, sheep, daffodils, rills, musk-roses.
Alliteration: repeated starting consonants, as in 'simple sheep' and 'noble natures'.
Inversion: normal word order reversed for rhythm, as in 'are we wreathing' instead of 'we are wreathing'.
Rhyming couplets and Romantic diction (o'er, 'gainst, boon, bower).

Exam lists: things of beauty (sun, moon, trees, sheep, daffodils, rills, musk-roses, tales, the mighty dead); things that cause suffering (despondence, dearth of noble natures, gloomy days, unhealthy ways).

ex.q: Identify the device: 'Therefore, on every morrow, are we wreathing a flowery band'.
st: Normal order would be 'we are wreathing'.
The verb comes before the subject here.
This reversal is inversion.
ex.a: Inversion (and a metaphor in 'flowery band').

topics.rl: Bollywood lyricists often flip word order to fit a tune. Keats did the same to keep his couplets flowing.

rv.summary: Keats uses nature imagery, alliteration ('simple sheep', 'noble natures'), inversion ('are we wreathing'), rhyming couplets and Romantic diction like o'er and 'gainst. Exams ask for lists of beautiful things and causes of suffering.
remember: Alliteration: repeated starting consonants
Inversion: reversed word order
Rhyming couplets (aabb), not blank verse
traps: Blank verse does not rhyme — this poem does
Don't mix causes of suffering with things of beauty

topics.t: Understanding the poem: band, love of life and the mighty dead
topics.h: Why do people love life even when it hurts? Keats's answer fits in one word: beauty.
p: 'Wreathing a flowery band to bind us to the earth' suggests that every day we gather beautiful experiences that keep us attached to life.
What makes humans love life despite troubles: some shape of beauty that removes the pall of sorrow from our spirits.
'Grandeur' is linked to the 'mighty dead' because great people of the past met glorious fates; imagining them inspires us and is a source of beauty.

ex.q: What makes human beings love life in spite of troubles?
st: Life has despondence, gloomy days and a lack of good people.
Yet some shape of beauty lifts the gloom.
So beauty keeps us attached to life.
ex.a: Beauty, in nature and in stories, lifts our sorrow and makes us love life despite troubles.

topics.rl: Stories of the mighty dead, like the warriors and reformers in NCERT history, are things Indian students 'have heard or read' that inspire them.

rv.summary: The flowery band shows beauty keeps us attached to life; despite troubles, beauty lifts the pall of sorrow so we love life. Grandeur is linked with the mighty dead because their glorious fates inspire us.
focus: Why we love life despite troubles
remember: 'Bind us to the earth' = keep us attached to life
Beauty removes the pall of sorrow
Grandeur = glorious fates of great people of the past
traps: Grandeur is not about large tombs
Beauty is in stories as well as nature

topics.t: Board exam practice: A Thing of Beauty
topics.h: Do beautiful things leave a lasting impression? Keats says yes, and the board exam wants you to prove it.
p: Lasting impression: yes. A thing of beauty is a joy for ever; its memory stays and its loveliness increases.
Image for the bounty of the earth: an endless fountain of immortal drink pouring from heaven's brink.
Extract-based MCQs ask about meaning, devices (metaphor, alliteration, inversion) and the theme of beauty.
Short answers on nature and beauty: link nature's healing power with Keats's claim that beauty is eternal.

ex.q: Extract (paraphrased): beauty's loveliness increases and it will never pass into nothingness. (a) What does this tell us about beauty? (b) Find the opposite of 'nothingness' in the idea.
st: (a) Beauty lasts and grows; it never dies.
(b) The idea opposes nothingness with 'joy for ever'.
So beauty is permanent.
ex.a: (a) Beauty is permanent and its charm increases. (b) Lasting joy, a 'joy for ever'.

topics.rl: Photographers at Kaziranga or the Valley of Flowers say a single frame can stay with viewers for years, a modern proof of Keats's 'joy for ever'.

rv.summary: Board answers stress that beauty makes a lasting impression, the earth's bounty is an endless fountain of immortal drink, and nature heals sorrow. Extract questions ask about meanings and devices like metaphor, alliteration and inversion.
focus: Extract questions on meaning and devices
remember: 'A thing of beauty is a joy for ever'
'Never pass into nothingness' = beauty never dies
Tone: joyful and uplifting
traps: 'Flowery band' is a metaphor, not a simile
Don't misread the double negative in 'never pass into nothingness'

topics.t: Frost's little shed by the highway
topics.h: On every Indian highway there are small stalls selling guavas, corn or jaggery, and most cars speed past. Robert Frost saw the same thing in America.
p: Poet: Robert Frost, an American poet known for poems about rural New England.
Type: a narrative-reflective poem on the plight of the rural poor living beside a busy highway.
Scene: a little old house with a new shed at the edge of the road, where the farmers sell produce to passers-by.
Their hope: a share of city money, so they can live a better life, the kind that city people and the movies promise.

ex.q: What do the people who set up the stand want?
st: They sell produce at the roadside.
They want some city money in their hands.
They hope it will let them live better, like city people.
ex.a: They want to earn some city money to improve their lives and enjoy the comforts city people have.

topics.rl: Roadside stalls on the Mumbai–Pune expressway or NH-44 sell seasonal fruit. For many rural families, those small sales are a key source of cash.

rv.summary: Robert Frost's narrative-reflective poem shows a little old house with a new roadside shed where poor rural folk sell produce, hoping for some city money to live the better life city people enjoy.
focus: What the rural folk hope for
remember: Robert Frost, American poet of rural New England
New shed at the road's edge before an old house
Hope: city money for a better life
traps: The stand is by the roadside, not in a market
Their hope is economic, not fame

topics.t: The polished traffic and its complaint
topics.h: Shiny cars race past, their drivers thinking only of where they are going. If anyone looks at the stand, it is only to grumble.
p: The 'polished traffic' (rich city people in shiny cars) passes with its mind ahead, thinking only of its destination.
If anyone does glance aside, it is only to complain that the crudely painted signs, with N and S turned the wrong way, spoil the landscape.
Goods offered: wild berries in wooden quarts, crook-necked golden squash with silver warts, and even the beauty of the mountain scene.
The poet says the hurt to the scenery is not his complaint; his real complaint is the trusting sorrow of what is left unsaid.

ex.q: Why does the city traffic complain?
st: They notice the stand only for a moment.
They see clumsy signs with letters painted backwards.
They feel these spoil the pretty landscape.
ex.a: They complain that the badly painted signs, with N and S turned wrong, mar the beauty of the scenery.

topics.rl: Travellers often post photos of 'spelling mistakes' on roadside boards. Frost would ask: did you also notice the family behind the board?

rv.summary: The polished traffic of rich city people speeds by with its mind ahead; if anyone looks, it is to complain that the crude signs spoil the view. The poet's real complaint is the trusting, unspoken sorrow of the poor.
focus: The city folk's complaint versus the poet's
remember: Signs with N and S turned wrong
Goods: wild berries in wooden quarts, crook-necked golden squash with silver warts
Poet's complaint: the unsaid sorrow
traps: The poet does not complain about the signs
'Polished' describes the cars, not the road

topics.t: Greedy good-doers and the squeal of brakes
topics.h: News arrives that the rural folk will be 'helped': bought out and moved to villages near a theatre and a store. Frost is not impressed.
p: The poet hears that these 'pitiful kin' are to be bought out and gathered into villages near the theatre and the store, where they will not have to think for themselves.
'Greedy good-doers, beneficent beasts of prey' swarm over their lives, enforcing benefits meant to soothe them and teaching them to sleep all day, destroying their old way of sleeping at night.
The rural folk wait all day for the squeal of brakes. Cars stop only to turn round, to ask the way, or to ask for a gallon of gas.
In despair the poet sometimes wishes to put them out of their pain at once, then wonders, back in a saner mood, how he would feel if someone offered to do that to him.

ex.q: Why does the poet change his mind about putting them out of their pain?
st: At first, their endless disappointment seems unbearable.
Then he imagines someone doing the same to him.
He realises no one would want that; they deserve respect, not pity.
ex.a: Thinking how he himself would feel, he sees that their lives are precious and that such 'mercy' would be cruel.

topics.rl: Development projects in India debate this very question: does moving rural people truly help them, or does it uproot them? Frost asks it in verse.

rv.summary: News says the poor will be bought out and moved near the theatre and store by 'greedy good-doers, beneficent beasts of prey'. They wait in vain for cars that stop only to turn, ask the way or get gas. The poet rejects 'ending their pain'.
focus: The welfare plan and its hypocrisy
remember: 'Greedy good-doers, beneficent beasts of prey'
They teach the folk to sleep all day
Cars stop to turn round, ask the way or ask for gas
traps: Cars do not stop to buy
The poet does not support ending their pain

topics.t: Themes: poverty, hypocrisy and the poet's empathy
topics.h: Frost is angry at three things at once: the rich who ignore, the planners who pretend, and his own helplessness.
p: Rural poverty and the indifference of the urban rich: the polished traffic ignores the stand.
Hypocrisy of welfare planners and agencies: 'greedy good-doers' who claim to help but exploit.
The poet's empathy and helplessness: he feels their pain but cannot change it.
Form: rhyming lines of varied length, giving a conversational, reflective flow.

ex.q: How does the poet show empathy?
st: He notices the unsaid sorrow behind the stand.
He can hardly bear their childish longing in vain.
He imagines himself in their place.
ex.a: By feeling their hidden sorrow, suffering with their disappointment, and imagining himself in their place.

topics.rl: Programmes for farmer welfare in India work best when they listen to farmers. Frost's 'greedy good-doers' are a warning about the opposite.

rv.summary: Frost exposes rural poverty, the indifference of the urban rich and the hypocrisy of welfare planners, while showing his own empathy and helplessness. The poem uses rhyming lines of varied length in a conversational flow.
remember: Polished traffic = indifference of the rich
Greedy good-doers = false welfare
Rhyming lines of varied length
traps: The poem is not free verse
The poet feels empathy, not scorn

topics.t: Devices and the city folk's attitude
topics.h: 'Beneficent beasts of prey.' Two words that should not sit together, and that is the whole point.
p: Oxymoron: 'beneficent beasts of prey' joins kindness with predation to expose fake helpers. Alliteration: 'greedy good-doers', 'beneficent beasts'.
Irony and sarcasm: the 'help' that harms; the 'mercifully gathered in'. Imagery: the little stand, the polished traffic, the squeal of brakes.
City folk ignore the stand (the traffic passes with its mind ahead); if they look, it is only to complain about the badly painted signs that spoil the scene.
The plea of the rural folk: some city money in hand, to see if it will make their lives expand, the life the movies promise and the party in power is said to keep from them.

ex.q: Identify the devices in 'greedy good-doers, beneficent beasts of prey'.
st: 'Greedy good-doers': repeated 'g' sound, alliteration; 'greedy' with 'good' is also contradictory.
'Beneficent beasts': repeated 'b', alliteration.
'Beneficent' + 'beasts of prey': opposites joined, an oxymoron.
ex.a: Alliteration and oxymoron (with sarcasm).

topics.rl: Indian political cartoons often use oxymorons like 'honest corruption'. Frost's phrase does the same job of exposing a contradiction.

rv.summary: Frost uses oxymoron ('beneficent beasts of prey'), alliteration ('greedy good-doers'), sarcasm and vivid imagery. City folk ignore or criticise the stand, while the rural folk plead for city money and the life the movies promise.
remember: Oxymoron: kindness joined with cruelty
Alliteration: repeated starting sounds
Good life said to be kept from them by the party in power
traps: An oxymoron is not a simile
City people do not stop out of sympathy

topics.t: Board exam practice: A Roadside Stand
topics.h: 'What is the childish longing, and why is it in vain?' Learn this answer and you're halfway through the extract questions.
p: Double standards of government and agencies: 'greedy good-doers', 'beneficent beasts of prey', 'enforcing benefits', 'soothe them out of their wits'.
Childish longing: the innocent hope that a passing car will stop and buy; it is in vain because cars stop only to turn round, ask the way or ask for gas.
The poet's pain: he can hardly bear the thought of so much childish longing in vain; the sadness lurks near the open window.
Extract MCQs: identify devices, the meaning of 'polished traffic' or 'mind ahead'; short answers on urban indifference and false welfare.

ex.q: Write a 40-word answer: What is the 'childish longing' and why is it in vain?
st: Define: the simple, innocent hope that cars will stop and buy.
Why in vain: cars stop only for their own needs.
Effect: the hope is never fulfilled.
ex.a: The childish longing is the rural folk's innocent hope that a car will stop to buy their produce. It is in vain, because cars stop only to turn round, ask the way or ask for a gallon of gas.

topics.rl: Highway dhabas thrive when they meet travellers' needs; tiny stalls often struggle. Frost's poem gives a voice to the struggling stall.

rv.summary: Board answers explain the agencies' double standards, the 'childish longing' for buyers that is in vain, the poet's pain at it, and the sadness near the open window, along with urban indifference and false welfare.
focus: Extract questions on images and devices
remember: Childish longing = innocent hope a car will stop to buy
In vain: cars stop only for their own needs
Sadness near the open window = family's hidden despair
traps: 'Childish' is not an insult here
Don't read the window image literally

topics.t: Adrienne Rich and the tigers on the screen
topics.h: A quiet aunt sits stitching. On her cloth, bold yellow tigers leap through a green jungle. Why would a timid woman sew such fearless beasts?
p: Poet: Adrienne Rich, an American poet and feminist.
Form: three quatrains (four-line stanzas) in rhyming couplets, rhyme scheme aabb.
Aunt Jennifer's tigers prance across a screen, the embroidery panel she is stitching.
They are bright topaz denizens of a world of green: golden-yellow inhabitants of a green forest.

ex.q: What does 'bright topaz denizens of a world of green' mean?
st: Topaz is a yellow gemstone: the tigers are bright golden-yellow.
Denizens are inhabitants: the tigers belong there.
A world of green is the jungle.
ex.a: The tigers are bright golden-yellow creatures who live naturally in the green jungle.

topics.rl: Indian women's crafts like phulkari in Punjab or kantha in Bengal have long carried women's stories and dreams in thread, just like Aunt Jennifer's panel.

rv.summary: Adrienne Rich's poem, three quatrains in rhyming couplets (aabb), shows Aunt Jennifer embroidering tigers that prance across a screen: bright topaz denizens of a green jungle world.
remember: Adrienne Rich, American feminist poet
Three quatrains, rhyme scheme aabb
Screen = embroidery panel; topaz = golden-yellow; denizens = inhabitants
traps: The 'screen' is not a cinema or computer screen
The poem is not free verse

topics.t: Fearless tigers, fluttering fingers
topics.h: The tigers pace like knights. Their maker can barely pull a needle. The contrast is the poem's heartbeat.
p: The tigers do not fear the men beneath the tree (hunters); they pace in sleek, chivalric certainty, confident and noble like knights.
Aunt Jennifer's fingers flutter through the wool; she finds even the light ivory needle hard to pull.
The massive weight of Uncle's wedding band sits heavily on her hand: marriage is a burden on her.

ex.q: Why does Aunt Jennifer find the ivory needle hard to pull?
st: An ivory needle is light.
Her fingers are nervous and weak from fear.
The heavy wedding band weighs her down.
ex.a: Because she is nervous and oppressed; the burden of her marriage makes even a light needle feel heavy.

topics.rl: Studies on women's well-being show that stress and fear can show up in the body: shaky hands, tiredness. Rich captures this in 'fluttering fingers'.

rv.summary: The tigers fear no hunters and pace with sleek, chivalric certainty. Aunt Jennifer's fingers flutter and even the light ivory needle is hard to pull, because the massive weight of Uncle's wedding band burdens her.
focus: Meaning of the wedding band's weight
remember: Men beneath the tree = hunters
Chivalric = noble like knights
Massive weight of the wedding band = burden of marriage
traps: The tigers are not afraid
The weight is emotional, not physical

topics.t: Ringed by ordeals, outlived by art
topics.h: The aunt will die. The tigers will not. Rich ends the poem with art outliving its maker.
p: When Aunt Jennifer is dead, her terrified hands will still lie ringed with the ordeals she was mastered by: even death does not free her from her marriage's trials.
The tigers in the panel that she made will go on prancing, proud and unafraid.
Theme: art as escape and self-expression. Through her tigers she expresses the freedom and courage she lacks, and that art outlives the artist.

ex.q: What is the meaning of 'ringed with ordeals she was mastered by'?
st: 'Ringed' recalls the wedding ring.
'Ordeals' are her painful experiences in marriage.
'Mastered by' shows she was dominated and controlled.
ex.a: Her hands remain marked by the hardships of a marriage in which she was dominated, even after death.

topics.rl: Paintings by Amrita Sher-Gil still speak powerfully decades after she died at 28. Art, as Rich says, goes on prancing after the artist is gone.

rv.summary: Even in death Aunt Jennifer's terrified hands will lie ringed with the ordeals that mastered her, but her tigers will go on prancing, proud and unafraid — her art expresses her hidden courage and outlives her.
remember: Ringed = wedding ring, bondage
Mastered by = dominated by
Art outlives the artist
traps: Death does not free her
'Mastered' does not mean she was skilled

topics.t: Oppression, contrast, symbols and irony
topics.h: A ring that weighs a ton, a needle that won't move, and tigers that never stop. Every image in this poem is a symbol.
p: Theme: the oppression of women in a patriarchal marriage; Uncle's wedding band dominates her life.
Contrast: fearless, confident tigers versus a timid, terrified aunt.
Symbols: tigers stand for freedom, courage and strength; the wedding band for bondage and male dominance; the ivory needle for the effort of a woman's self-expression.
Irony: a fearful woman creates fearless creatures; the art she makes has the freedom she never had.

ex.q: Why is it ironic that Aunt Jennifer creates fearless tigers?
st: She herself is terrified and dominated.
Her tigers are proud, free and unafraid.
She gives her art the qualities she lacks.
ex.a: Because a timid, oppressed woman makes creatures full of courage and freedom, qualities she can only express through art.

topics.rl: India's laws on domestic violence (2005) and dowry (1961) aim to protect women. Rich's poem shows the quieter, emotional side of oppression.

rv.summary: The poem shows the oppression of women in patriarchal marriage. Fearless tigers contrast with the timid aunt; the tigers symbolise freedom, the band bondage, the needle the struggle of self-expression. It is ironic that a fearful woman creates fearless beasts.
remember: Tigers = freedom, courage, strength
Wedding band = bondage, male dominance
Irony: a fearful woman creates fearless creatures
traps: The wedding band is not a romantic symbol
Aunt Jennifer is not fearless

topics.t: Colour, sound and close reading
topics.h: 'Prancing, proud.' Hear the p-p? Rich uses sound to make the tigers bold even in the way we say them.
p: Colour imagery: topaz (bright yellow) against the world of green, a vivid, free jungle.
Alliteration: 'prancing, proud' (p), 'fingers fluttering' (f).
'Denizens' shows the tigers belong to and own their world; 'chivalric' gives them knightly grace and confidence.
Her fingers flutter and the needle is hard to pull because of fear and the weight of her oppressive marriage.
The 'massive weight of Uncle's wedding band' suggests the heavy, dominating burden of marriage, not a physical weight.

ex.q: How do 'denizens' and 'chivalric' add to our understanding of the tigers?
st: 'Denizens': they live in and own their jungle world.
'Chivalric': they move like noble, confident knights.
Together: free, proud and certain of themselves.
ex.a: They show the tigers as rightful, confident inhabitants of their world, noble and fearless like knights.

topics.rl: Hindi film titles often use alliteration for punch. Rich's 'prancing, proud' gives her tigers the same punchy confidence.

rv.summary: Rich uses colour imagery (topaz against green), alliteration ('prancing, proud', 'fingers fluttering') and precise words like 'denizens' and 'chivalric' to show the tigers' belonging and confidence, contrasted with the aunt's fear.
remember: Topaz (yellow) and green
Alliteration: 'prancing, proud'; 'fingers fluttering'
Denizens = belonging; chivalric = knightly confidence
traps: The colours are bright, not dull
The poet's background does not explain a device

topics.t: Board exam practice: Aunt Jennifer's Tigers
topics.h: 'Why did Aunt Jennifer create animals so different from herself?' This question appears often. Here's how to answer it.
p: What she is terrified of: her husband and the oppressive marriage that dominates her life.
Tigers prancing after her death: art outlives the artist; her hidden courage survives in her work.
Why animals so unlike herself: to express the freedom and fearlessness she longs for but cannot have; art is her escape.
Extract MCQs on symbols (tigers, band, needle); short answers on oppression of women.

ex.q: Write a 40-word answer: Why did Aunt Jennifer create tigers so unlike herself?
st: She is timid and dominated in her marriage.
She longs for freedom and courage.
Through her art she creates what she cannot be.
ex.a: Aunt Jennifer is timid and oppressed in marriage. Her proud, fearless tigers express the freedom and courage she longs for but cannot have. Art becomes her escape and a quiet protest.

topics.rl: Many self-help groups in Indian villages report that women who take up crafts and earn find new confidence, giving their own 'tigers' a chance to prance.

rv.summary: Board answers explain that Aunt Jennifer fears her husband and marriage, that the tigers prancing after her death show art outliving her, and that she made tigers unlike herself to express the freedom she lacked.
remember: Art = liberating, a silent protest
Needle = struggle to express herself
Key line: 'The massive weight of Uncle's wedding band'
traps: She is not afraid of the tigers
The tigers do not literally come alive

topics.t: Charley and the station with three levels
topics.h: Every official says New York's Grand Central Station has two levels. Charley insists there are three, because he has been to the third.
p: Author: Jack Finney, an American writer of science fiction and fantasy.
Narration: first person, by Charley; the story blends everyday realism with fantasy and time travel.
Charley, aged 31, insists that Grand Central Station in New York has three levels, though railway officials swear it has only two.
One night, working late and in a hurry to get home, he takes a short cut through the station, goes down some stairs and a corridor, gets lost, and finds himself on a third level.

ex.q: Why does the story begin with railway officials denying a third level?
st: It sets up a conflict between official fact and Charley's claim.
The reader is made curious: is he right or imagining?
This uncertainty runs through the whole story.
ex.a: It creates doubt and curiosity: the reader must decide whether Charley's third level is real or imagined.

topics.rl: Big stations like Mumbai's CSMT or New Delhi have endless corridors and stairs. It is easy to imagine getting lost in one, and Finney uses that feeling.

rv.summary: In Jack Finney's first-person fantasy, 31-year-old Charley insists New York's Grand Central has a third level, though officials say it has two. Hurrying home one night, he takes a short cut, gets lost and finds it.
focus: How Charley finds the third level
remember: Author: Jack Finney
Narrator: Charley, 31, first person
Grand Central, New York: officially two levels
traps: Officials do not confirm a third level
The story is first-person, not third-person

topics.t: Stepping into 1894
topics.h: Gas lamps, brass spittoons, derby hats and a steam engine with a funnel chimney. Charley has walked into the past.
p: The third level looks old: flickering gas lights, brass spittoons, people in old-fashioned clothes, derby hats, sideburns and fancy waistcoats, and an old locomotive like a Currier and Ives print.
He sees a newspaper, 'The World', dated 11 June 1894; the paper had not been published for years.
He tries to buy two tickets to Galesburg, Illinois, a peaceful town of that era, for himself and his wife Louisa.
The clerk looks at his modern money, says it is not money, and suspects him of trying to cheat. Charley hurries away.

ex.q: How does Charley realise he is in the past?
st: He notices gas lamps, spittoons and old-fashioned clothes.
He sees the old locomotive.
The newspaper confirms the date: 11 June 1894.
ex.a: From old-fashioned details like gas lights and clothes, and finally from the newspaper dated 11 June 1894.

topics.rl: Heritage trains like the Fairy Queen, one of the world's oldest working steam locomotives, take Indians back in time for a day. Charley's trip is the fantasy version.

rv.summary: The third level has gas lights, spittoons, old clothes and an old locomotive, and a newspaper dated 11 June 1894. Charley tries to buy tickets to peaceful Galesburg, Illinois, but the clerk rejects his modern money as fake.
remember: Newspaper 'The World', 11 June 1894
Two tickets to Galesburg, Illinois, for himself and Louisa
Clerk: modern notes are not money
traps: Don't confuse 11 June 1894 (newspaper) with 18 July 1894 (first-day cover)
Escalators do not belong to the third level

topics.t: Old money, a lost corridor and a psychiatrist's verdict
topics.h: Charley pays a premium for old banknotes, then can never find the corridor again. His psychiatrist friend has a neat explanation.
p: Charley withdraws nearly $300 from the bank and exchanges it for old-style currency, getting less than $200 worth, because old notes cost a premium.
He can never find the corridor to the third level again, though he tries many times.
His psychiatrist friend Sam Weiner calls it a 'waking-dream wish fulfilment': the modern world is full of insecurity, fear, war and worry, and Charley wants to escape.
Sam also says Charley's stamp collecting is a temporary refuge from reality. Charley points out that his grandfather, who started the collection, needed no refuge in his peaceful times.

ex.q: Why did Charley get less than $200 for his $300?
st: Old-style currency is rare.
Dealers charge a premium (extra price) for it.
So $300 bought less than $200 in old notes.
ex.a: Old banknotes are collectors' items sold at a premium, so he got less in face value than he paid.

topics.rl: Coin and note collectors in India pay far more than face value for old notes like early ₹1 notes. Charley faced the same premium.

rv.summary: Charley buys old currency, getting less than $200 for nearly $300, but never finds the corridor again. His psychiatrist friend Sam calls it a waking-dream wish fulfilment and his stamp collecting a refuge; Charley notes his grandfather needed no refuge.
remember: Nearly $300 → less than $200 in old notes (premium)
'Waking-dream wish fulfilment'
Stamp collecting = 'temporary refuge from reality' (Sam)
traps: Charley never found the third level again
The loss was due to the collectors' premium, not a tax

topics.t: The first-day cover: proof from the past
topics.h: An envelope postmarked 18 July 1894 turns up in a stamp album, with a letter from a man who vanished last week. The twist lands like a train.
p: Sam disappears. Later, in his grandfather's stamp collection, Charley finds a first-day cover postmarked 18 July 1894, with a letter from Sam written from Galesburg.
Sam writes that he found the third level, has set up a hay, feed and grain business (his old dream), and urges Charley and Louisa to keep looking.
A first-day cover is an envelope with a new stamp, posted on the first day the stamp is issued; the postmark proves the date.
Twist ending: the first-day cover is evidence that the third level was real, overturning Sam's own theory.
Stamp collecting connects past and present, and the first-day cover becomes the bridge between them.

ex.q: Why is the first-day cover important to the story?
st: Its postmark proves the date: 18 July 1894.
The letter inside is from Sam, who had vanished.
So it proves Sam reached 1894 through the third level.
ex.a: It is dated proof from 1894 that Sam reached the past, so the third level was real.

topics.rl: India Post issues first-day covers with special cancellations whenever a new stamp comes out. Philatelists value them because the date is certain.

rv.summary: Sam disappears; later Charley finds in his grandfather's collection a first-day cover postmarked 18 July 1894 with Sam's letter from Galesburg, where he runs a hay, feed and grain business. This twist suggests the third level was real.
focus: The first-day cover and its evidence
remember: Postmark: 18 July 1894
First-day cover = envelope posted on a stamp's first day of issue
Sam: hay, feed and grain business; 'keep looking'
traps: The cover does not prove it was only a dream
The letter was from Sam, not the grandfather

topics.t: Charley, Louisa and Sam
topics.h: The dreamer, the supportive wife, and the expert who explains it all away and then vanishes into 1894.
p: Charley: imaginative and anxious, longing for a simpler, peaceful past.
Louisa: Charley's wife; at first she is worried and asks him to stop looking, but after Sam's letter they both search for the third level every weekend.
Sam Weiner: the psychiatrist who rationalises Charley's experience yet himself escapes into the past.
Devices: first-person narration makes the fantasy feel personal; irony, as the psychiatrist escapes; Grand Central is compared to a tree pushing out new corridors and staircases like roots.

ex.q: What is ironic about Sam Weiner?
st: He calls Charley's third level a wish fulfilment.
He treats it as a mental escape.
Then he himself escapes to 1894 through it.
ex.a: The psychiatrist who dismissed the third level as a fantasy is the one who actually uses it to escape.

topics.rl: Delhi's metro keeps adding new interchange tunnels and exits. Finney's image of a station growing like a tree with roots feels very real today.

rv.summary: Charley is imaginative and anxious, longing for the past; Louisa worries at first but later joins the search; Sam, the sceptical psychiatrist, ironically escapes. First-person narration and the image of the station as a spreading tree support the fantasy.
remember: Charley – imaginative; Louisa – supportive wife
Sam doubts the third level, then uses it
Grand Central like a tree spreading roots
traps: Louisa did not oppose Charley completely
Sam's escape is ironic because he dismissed it

topics.t: Themes: escape, time and nostalgia
topics.h: Fear, war, worry: Charley's modern world feels heavy. Galesburg, 1894, feels light. Who wouldn't want a door between them?
p: Escapism: Charley wants to escape modern insecurity, war and worry.
Fantasy versus reality: the story keeps us guessing; the corridor, the newspaper and the first-day cover blur the line.
Intersection of time and space: one place (Grand Central) opens onto another time (1894).
