Nostalgia: a longing for a peaceful past: big lawns, long summer evenings, people sitting out under trees in Galesburg.
Was the third level a medium of escape? Yes: it was Charley's way out of a stressful present, and later Sam's.

ex.q: Was the third level a medium of escape for Charley?
st: Sam says he is escaping insecurity, fear and war.
Charley wants to go to peaceful 1894 Galesburg.
So the third level is his door out of the stressful present.
ex.a: Yes. It offered an escape from modern insecurity and worry into a peaceful, simpler past.

topics.rl: Weekend getaways to hill stations like Shimla or Munnar are a modern Indian form of escape. Finney's third level is escape with a time machine attached.

rv.summary: The story explores escapism from modern insecurity, the blur between fantasy and reality, the intersection of time and space, and nostalgia for a peaceful past like 1894 Galesburg. The third level was an escape for Charley and Sam.
focus: Meaning of intersection of time and space
remember: Escape from insecurity, fear, war and worry
Nostalgia = longing for the past
Both Charley and Sam seek escape
traps: Charley was not happy with modern life
'Intersection of time and space' is not a train junction

topics.t: Board exam practice: The Third Level
topics.h: Did Charley really time-travel, or just dream? The board exam wants you to argue it either way, with evidence.
p: Sam's letter suggests the third level was real: it is postmarked 1894, written by Sam, who had vanished.
Intersection of time and space: the third level links a present place to a past time; the story blurs the boundary.
Can the past be relived? In reality, only in memory, through hobbies like stamp collecting, or nostalgia; in the story, through fantasy.
Short answers on Charley's experience (the third level, the newspaper, the clerk); long answer on escapism (causes, the third level, Sam, the first-day cover).

ex.q: Write a 50-word answer: What does Sam's letter suggest about the third level?
st: The letter is in a first-day cover postmarked 18 July 1894.
Sam, a sceptic, writes that he found it and lives in Galesburg.
This suggests the third level was real.
ex.a: Sam's letter, found in a first-day cover postmarked 18 July 1894, says he found the third level and now runs a business in Galesburg. Coming from a sceptical psychiatrist, it strongly suggests the third level was real, not just Charley's wish fulfilment.

topics.rl: Museums like the Rail Museum in New Delhi let visitors 'step into the past' for an afternoon. That is as close as most of us get to Charley's third level.

rv.summary: Board answers explain that Sam's 1894-postmarked letter suggests the third level was real, that the story shows an intersection of time and space, and that in real life the past is relived through memory, hobbies and nostalgia.
remember: Strongest evidence: Sam's letter postmarked 18 July 1894
Key detail of Charley's trip: newspaper of 11 June 1894
End an escapism answer with the first-day cover
traps: Don't end a long answer with irrelevant detail
The past cannot literally be relived in real life

topics.t: Kalki's king and a tiger prophecy
topics.h: A ten-day-old baby sits up and lectures the royal astrologers. From that moment, you know this story is a satire.
p: Author: Kalki, the pen name of R. Krishnamurthy, a Tamil writer and journalist known for satire.
Type: a satire on the vanity of rulers and on the destruction of wildlife.
Hero: Maharaja Sir Jilani Jung Jung Bahadur of Pratibandapuram, known as the Tiger King.
At his birth the astrologers foretold that he would one day die because of a tiger.
The ten-day-old prince miraculously spoke and warned that tigers should beware: a deliberately absurd, exaggerated moment.

ex.q: Why does the author include the talking ten-day-old prince?
st: A baby cannot really speak at ten days.
The absurd miracle mocks the grand myths built around royals.
It sets a humorous, satirical tone.
ex.a: To exaggerate and mock royal legends, setting up the story's satire.

topics.rl: Wildlife officials in India say many tigers were lost to royal hunts in the princely era. Kalki's satire hits a real target.

rv.summary: Kalki's satire 'The Tiger King' mocks royal vanity and the destruction of wildlife. At the birth of the Maharaja of Pratibandapuram, astrologers foretold death by a tiger, and the ten-day-old prince absurdly spoke a warning to tigers.
remember: Kalki = R. Krishnamurthy
Maharaja Sir Jilani Jung Jung Bahadur of Pratibandapuram
Prophecy: death because of a tiger
traps: The story mocks rulers; it does not praise them
The talking baby is deliberate exaggeration

topics.t: The vow of a hundred tigers
topics.h: Told that a tiger may kill him, the king decides to kill tigers first, a hundred of them.
p: The prince was raised the 'English' way: an English nurse (nanny) and an English tutor. At twenty he became king.
He killed his first tiger and vowed to kill a hundred. The chief astrologer warned him: he might kill ninety-nine, but he must be careful with the hundredth.
To keep all the tigers for himself, he banned tiger hunting by anyone else in his state.

ex.q: Why did the Maharaja ban tiger hunting by others?
st: He had vowed to kill a hundred tigers himself.
Others hunting would reduce the number left for him.
So he made tiger hunting his own monopoly.
ex.a: To keep all the tigers for himself so he could complete his vow of a hundred kills.

topics.rl: Today India's Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, bans tiger hunting for everyone, kings included. Kalki's Maharaja banned it only so he could hunt alone.

rv.summary: Raised by an English nurse and tutor, the prince became king at twenty, killed his first tiger and vowed to kill a hundred. The astrologer warned him about the hundredth, and he banned all others from hunting tigers.
focus: Why hunting was banned for others
remember: King at 20
Vow: 100 tigers
Warning: beware the hundredth tiger
traps: The ban was not for conservation
The warning was about the hundredth tiger, not the first

topics.t: Diamonds for a duchess, brides for tigers
topics.h: To keep his tigers, the king risks his throne. To keep his throne, he buys diamonds. To find more tigers, he chooses a wife.
p: A high-ranking British officer wanted to hunt a tiger in the state. The king refused, and risked losing his throne.
He saved his kingdom by sending about fifty costly diamond rings to the officer's wife, who chose one or two but kept them all.
Within ten years he had killed seventy tigers, and tigers vanished from his state.
He then married a girl from a state with many tigers, and killed tigers there on each visit to his father-in-law.

ex.q: What does the Maharaja's choice of bride reveal about him?
st: He chooses her for her state's tiger population.
Marriage becomes a tool for his vow.
His obsession rules even his personal life.
ex.a: That his obsession with killing tigers is so great that even his marriage is chosen to serve it.

topics.rl: Bribery to stay in power is an old target of satire. Kalki's fifty diamond rings make the point through comic exaggeration.

rv.summary: Refusing a British officer a tiger hunt, the king risked his throne and saved it by sending about fifty diamond rings to the officer's wife, who kept them all. After seventy tigers in ten years, he married a girl from a tiger-rich state.
remember: About 50 diamond rings; wife kept all
70 tigers in ten years
Bride from a state with many tigers
traps: The rings were a bribe, not gifts for his bride
Don't confuse 70 (in ten years) with 99 or 100

topics.t: The hundredth tiger takes its revenge
topics.h: Ninety-nine down. The last tiger is an old one from a park, and the king's bullet misses. The real hundredth tiger is made of wood.
p: After ninety-nine tigers, none were left. The worried dewan secretly brought an old tiger from the People's Park in Madras and let it loose.
The king's bullet missed. The tiger fainted from shock; the hunters found it alive and killed it secretly, without telling the king.
For his son's third birthday, the king bought a cheap wooden toy tiger, crudely carved. A sliver from it pierced his right hand.
The infection spread; he died during the operation. The hundredth tiger had taken its revenge.

ex.q: How is the prophecy fulfilled?
st: The king believes he has killed his hundredth tiger, but it was actually killed by hunters.
The real 'hundredth' tiger is the wooden toy.
A sliver from it causes the infection that kills him.
ex.a: The wooden toy tiger, effectively the hundredth, wounds him and leads to his death, as the astrologer foretold.

topics.rl: Doctors in India warn that even a small wooden splinter can cause a serious infection if ignored. Kalki uses this tiny cause for a huge, ironic end.

rv.summary: With no tigers left, the dewan released an old tiger from Madras. The king's shot missed; the hunters killed it secretly. Later a sliver from a cheap wooden toy tiger, bought for his son, infected his hand and he died in surgery.
remember: Old tiger from the People's Park, Madras
Bullet missed; tiger fainted; hunters killed it
Toy for son's third birthday; sliver in right hand; died during the operation
traps: The king did not really kill the hundredth tiger
A real tiger did not kill the king

topics.t: The Maharaja, the dewan and the astrologer
topics.h: A vain king, a frightened but clever minister, and an astrologer who gets the last laugh.
p: The Maharaja: vain, stubborn and proud of his power; he risks his throne, bribes officials and wipes out tigers for his vow.
The dewan: fearful of the king but cunning; he smuggles in an old tiger to save his own job.
The chief astrologer: prophetic; his warning about the hundredth tiger comes true.
Theme: satire on royalty, arrogance and the abuse of power.

ex.q: How does the dewan show both fear and cunning?
st: He fears losing his job if no tiger is found.
He secretly brings an old tiger from Madras.
This saves him and fools the king.
ex.a: Afraid of the king's anger, he cleverly arranges a fake hunt with an old park tiger.

topics.rl: Political satire in India, from R.K. Laxman's cartoons to modern sketches, pokes fun at the vanity of the powerful, the same target as Kalki's.

rv.summary: The Maharaja is vain, stubborn and abuses his power; the dewan is fearful but cunning; the chief astrologer's prophecy comes true. The story satirises royal arrogance.
remember: Maharaja – vain, stubborn
Dewan – fearful, cunning
Astrologer – prophetic
traps: The Maharaja is not humble or kind
The dewan acted from fear, not love of tigers

topics.t: Irony, fate, wildlife and humour
topics.h: The man who killed ninety-nine real tigers dies because of a wooden one. Irony doesn't get sharper than that.
p: Irony of fate and the inevitability of destiny: the king tries to defeat the prophecy, but it is fulfilled in an unexpected way.
Destruction of wildlife: one man's vanity wipes out tigers from his state and beyond; the story indirectly argues for conservation.
Satire, irony and dramatic irony: readers know the 'hundredth' tiger was killed by hunters while the king celebrates.
Humour and exaggeration (a talking baby, fifty rings, a bride chosen for tigers), with suspense around the hundredth tiger.

ex.q: Explain the dramatic irony in the hunt of the old tiger.
st: Dramatic irony: the reader knows something a character does not.
We know the tiger fainted and was killed by the hunters.
The king believes he killed it, and that his danger is over.
ex.a: Readers know the king missed and the hunters killed the tiger, while he believes his vow is complete and he is safe.

topics.rl: Project Tiger, launched in India in 1973, helped tiger numbers recover. Kalki's satire shows the kind of thinking that brought tigers to the edge.

rv.summary: The story shows the irony of fate: the king who killed ninety-nine tigers dies because of a toy. Dramatic irony, exaggeration, suspense and humour expose vanity and the destruction of wildlife.
focus: Irony of fate and dramatic irony
remember: Central irony: a wooden toy kills the Tiger King
Dramatic irony: readers know the hunters killed the tiger
Destiny cannot be escaped
traps: The king does not escape the prophecy
Exaggeration is for humour, not realism

topics.t: Board exam practice: The Tiger King
topics.h: Vow, rings, toy tiger: three short answers. Irony and satire: one long answer. Let's lock them in.
p: Irony builds suspense: we wait for the hundredth tiger, sure it will be dangerous, and the danger comes from a toy.
Satire on those in power: vanity, bribery (the rings), selfish bans, and a ruler who thinks he can defeat fate.
Wildlife: the story shows how hunting for pride wiped out tigers; it supports conservation by showing the cost.
The vow leads to death: the obsession with a hundred tigers leads to the toy that kills him.
Short answers on the vow, the rings and the toy tiger; long answer on irony and satire.

ex.q: Write a 50-word answer: How does the Maharaja's vow lead to his death?
st: The vow: kill a hundred tigers to defeat the prophecy.
The 99th and the fake 100th leave him confident.
The wooden toy becomes the real hundredth tiger; its sliver kills him.
ex.a: To defeat the prophecy, the Maharaja vowed to kill a hundred tigers. Believing he had killed the hundredth, he relaxed. But the wooden toy tiger he bought for his son became the true hundredth; its sliver caused a fatal infection.

topics.rl: Satire like Kalki's appears in Indian newspapers' editorial cartoons every day. Learning to spot it in literature helps you spot it in life.

rv.summary: Board answers explain how irony builds suspense, how Kalki satirises those in power, the story's comment on wildlife, and how the vow of a hundred tigers leads to death through the wooden toy.
focus: Long answer on irony and satire
remember: Rings = bribe to save the throne
Opening line for irony: the Tiger King dies because of a wooden tiger
Vanity wiped out the tigers
traps: Don't open a long answer with trivia
The story supports conservation; it does not praise hunting

topics.ch: Vistas: Journey to the End of the Earth
topics.t: From Madras to the bottom of the world
topics.h: A writer from Madras boards a Russian research ship and sails to the coldest, driest, windiest place on Earth.
p: Author: Tishani Doshi, an Indian poet, journalist and dancer from Madras (Chennai).
Form: a travel account of her visit to Antarctica with the 'Students on Ice' programme.
The journey: from Madras, crossing nine time zones, six checkpoints, three bodies of water and three ecospheres.
The voyage is aboard the Russian research vessel 'Akademik Shokalskiy'.
Antarctica: the coldest, driest and windiest continent, holding about 90 per cent of the Earth's ice.

ex.q: Why does the author list time zones, checkpoints, waters and ecospheres?
st: The numbers show how long and complex the journey was.
They build a sense of distance from home.
They prepare us for the strangeness of Antarctica.
ex.a: To show the vast distance and variety covered, stressing that Antarctica is truly at the end of the Earth.

topics.rl: India runs research stations in Antarctica, Maitri and Bharati, where Indian scientists study ice, weather and climate.

rv.summary: Tishani Doshi's travel account describes her voyage from Madras to Antarctica with Students on Ice aboard the Russian ship Akademik Shokalskiy, crossing nine time zones. Antarctica is the coldest, driest, windiest continent, with 90% of Earth's ice.
remember: Tishani Doshi of Madras
Akademik Shokalskiy, Russian research vessel
9 time zones, 6 checkpoints, 3 bodies of water, 3 ecospheres; 90% of Earth's ice
traps: She did not travel alone on a yacht
Don't confuse 9 time zones with 6 checkpoints

topics.ch: Vistas: Journey to the End of the Earth
topics.t: Gondwana and the Earth's memory in ice
topics.h: Six hundred and fifty million years ago, India and Antarctica were neighbours in one giant landmass.
p: About 650 million years ago, a giant southern supercontinent, Gondwana, existed, centred roughly around present-day Antarctica.
Gondwana broke up, and the continents, including India, drifted to their present positions.
Antarctica's ice preserves a record of the Earth's past: layers of ice trap air and carbon from ancient times.
So Antarctica is key to understanding the Earth's past, present and future.

ex.q: Why is Antarctica the place to understand the Earth's past?
st: It was once the centre of Gondwana.
Its ice layers trap records of ancient air and climate.
These records help scientists read history and predict change.
ex.a: Its ice holds a record of ancient climate and it was the heart of Gondwana, so it tells the Earth's history.

topics.rl: India was part of Gondwana too. Geologists find similar rocks and fossils, like Glossopteris plants, in India and Antarctica.

rv.summary: About 650 million years ago the supercontinent Gondwana, centred around Antarctica, included India; it broke up and the continents drifted apart. Antarctica's ice layers trap ancient air and carbon, recording Earth's history.
focus: How Antarctic ice records the past
remember: Gondwana: about 650 million years ago, centred near Antarctica
It broke up; continents including India drifted
Ice traps ancient air and carbon
traps: Gondwana was not an Indian kingdom or a ship
It was centred near the Antarctic, not the Arctic

topics.ch: Vistas: Journey to the End of the Earth
topics.t: Melting ice, carbon and the tiny plants that feed an ocean
topics.h: The smallest living things in the Southern Ocean hold up the whole food chain, including the whales.
p: If the West Antarctic ice sheet melted, sea levels would rise dramatically, threatening coastal lands.
Rising carbon dioxide levels, global warming and the thinning of the ozone layer threaten the planet.
Phytoplankton, the 'grasses of the sea', are single-celled plants that use sunlight to make food by photosynthesis; they nourish and sustain the entire Southern Ocean food chain.
Lesson: small changes can have big effects. Take care of the small things, and the big things will fall into place.

ex.q: Why are phytoplankton important?
st: They are tiny plants that make food by photosynthesis.
Krill and fish feed on them; bigger animals feed on those.
If they decline, the whole food chain suffers.
ex.a: They are the base of the Southern Ocean food chain; damage to them affects every animal above them.

topics.rl: Coastal cities like Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata are among those studied for sea-level-rise risk. Antarctic ice matters to India directly.

rv.summary: Melting of the West Antarctic ice sheet would raise sea levels; rising carbon dioxide, warming and ozone loss threaten the planet. Phytoplankton, single-celled plants and 'grasses of the sea', feed the Southern Ocean, showing that small changes matter.
remember: Phytoplankton: single-celled plants, photosynthesis, base of the food chain
Threats: CO₂, global warming, ozone thinning
Care for small things; big things will fall into place
traps: Phytoplankton are plants, not large animals
Small changes do matter

topics.ch: Vistas: Journey to the End of the Earth
topics.t: Students on Ice: hope for the planet
topics.h: Take teenagers to the end of the Earth, show them melting glaciers, and they come home as the planet's defenders.
p: 'Students on Ice' is a programme led by Canadian Geoff Green that takes high school students to Antarctica.
Its aim is to give young people an experience that inspires them to understand and protect the planet.
Students see the effects of climate change first-hand: retreating glaciers and collapsing ice shelves.
Theme: young people are the future policy-makers; their early understanding can save the planet.

ex.q: Why does Geoff Green take school students, not adults?
st: Young people are the future policy-makers.
They are at an age to absorb, learn and act.
Seeing climate change first-hand inspires them for life.
ex.a: Because students will be tomorrow's decision-makers, and an early, first-hand experience can inspire them to protect the planet.

topics.rl: Indian teens like the young climate activists who speak at school assemblies and global summits show what Geoff Green's idea can achieve.

rv.summary: Canadian Geoff Green's Students on Ice takes high school students to Antarctica so they see climate change first-hand and are inspired to protect the planet, since they are the future policy-makers.
remember: Geoff Green, Canada
High school students
Future policy-makers inspired by first-hand experience
traps: Don't confuse Geoff Green with Geoff in 'Going Places'
The aim is inspiration, not commerce or sport

topics.ch: Vistas: Journey to the End of the Earth
topics.t: Board exam practice: Journey to the End of the Earth
topics.h: Gondwana and phytoplankton are favourite short answers. Climate change is the classic long answer.
p: Theme: climate change and environmental conservation, seen in melting ice, carbon and ozone.
Antarctica explains past, present and future: Gondwana and ice records (past), visible warming (present), sea-level risk (future).
Students on Ice gives hope: it inspires the young, the future policy-makers.
Phytoplankton and small changes: tiny plants sustain an ocean; small actions matter.
Short answers on Gondwana and phytoplankton; long answer on climate change and our responsibility.

ex.q: Write a 50-word answer: Why is Antarctica the place to understand the Earth's past, present and future?
st: Past: Gondwana and ancient air in ice layers.
Present: visible signs of warming, melting ice.
Future: ice-sheet melt and sea-level rise.
ex.a: Antarctica was the heart of Gondwana, and its ice preserves records of ancient climate. Today it shows the effects of warming clearly, and its melting ice sheets could raise sea levels. So it holds the Earth's past, present and future.

topics.rl: India's National Action Plan on Climate Change includes missions on solar energy and sustainable habitats, big steps built on many small ones.

rv.summary: Board answers on this chapter cover climate change and conservation, how Antarctica explains the Earth's past, present and future, Gondwana, phytoplankton and the hope given by Students on Ice.
focus: Long answer on climate change and responsibility
remember: Past: Gondwana, ice records; present: melting ice; future: sea-level rise
Lesson: small changes can have big effects
traps: Don't fill a long answer with trivia
Ancient trapped air is a past record, not a present sign

topics.t: Dr Sadao's house by the sea
topics.h: War between Japan and America. A Japanese surgeon trained in America. One misty evening, the war washes up on his beach.
p: Author: Pearl S. Buck, an American writer who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1938.
Setting: Japan during the Second World War, when Japan and the USA were enemies.
Dr Sadao Hoki, a skilled Japanese surgeon trained in America, lives in a house on the Japanese coast with his wife Hana.
His father had valued education and Japan's future. Sadao met Hana in America, and they married in Japan with their families' approval.

ex.q: Why is it significant that Sadao was trained in America?
st: He learnt his surgical skill in America.
Japan and America are now at war.
So he owes his skill to the country of the 'enemy'.
ex.a: He owes his medical skill to America, the enemy nation, which deepens the dilemma he will face.

topics.rl: Many Indian doctors train abroad and serve at home, at AIIMS or district hospitals. Medicine crosses borders even when politics divides them.

rv.summary: Pearl S. Buck's story is set in wartime Japan. Dr Sadao Hoki, a Japanese surgeon trained in America, lives by the coast with his wife Hana, whom he met in America; his father valued education and Japan's future.
remember: Pearl S. Buck, Nobel Prize 1938
Setting: Japan in the Second World War
Sadao trained in America; met Hana there
traps: The story is set in wartime, not peace
Sadao trained in America, not Japan

topics.t: A wounded enemy on the shore
topics.h: Through the mist, Sadao and Hana see a body on the rocks. The cap says 'U.S. Navy'. What would you do?
p: In the evening mist, Sadao and Hana find a wounded white man washed up on the shore; his cap reads 'U.S. Navy'.
He is an escaped American prisoner of war with a gunshot wound.
Sadao and Hana are torn between patriotism (hand him over) and humanity (save his life). They take him into their house.
The servants disapprove and refuse to help; later they leave the house together.

ex.q: Why are Sadao and Hana torn about what to do?
st: As patriots, they should hand over an enemy.
As human beings, and Sadao as a doctor, they should save a dying man.
Helping him also puts them at risk.
ex.a: Their duty to their country clashes with their humanity and Sadao's medical duty, and helping him is dangerous.

topics.rl: Doctors in conflict zones, like those with the International Committee of the Red Cross, are trained to treat every wounded person, friend or foe.

rv.summary: Sadao and Hana find a wounded escaped American prisoner of war on the shore, his cap reading 'U.S. Navy'. Torn between patriotism and humanity, they take him in; the disapproving servants refuse to help and later leave.
remember: Cap: 'U.S. Navy'; gunshot wound
Dilemma: patriotism versus humanity
Servants refuse and finally leave
traps: The servants did not support Sadao
They took him in from humanity, not because of Sadao's training

topics.t: The operation and the General
topics.h: Sadao removes the bullet, then confesses everything to the General, who promises to have the man quietly killed. Then he forgets.
p: Sadao operates and removes the bullet; Hana, after the maid Yumi refuses, washes the man and later feeds him herself.
Sadao is called to treat the ailing General and confesses that he is hiding the American.
The General promises to send his private assassins to kill the man silently and remove the body, so Sadao would not be blamed.
But the General forgets, absorbed in his own health; he needs Sadao for his own operation.

ex.q: Why did the General forget to send the assassins?
st: He was ill and worried about his own operation.
He was self-centred and absorbed in his health.
So the matter of the American slipped from his mind.
ex.a: He was so absorbed in his own illness and needs that he forgot about the American.

topics.rl: Hospitals in India follow strict medical ethics: a doctor's first duty is the patient's life. Sadao follows that rule even in war.

rv.summary: Sadao removes the bullet; Hana washes and feeds the man when Yumi refuses. Called to the ailing General, Sadao confesses; the General promises assassins but, absorbed in his own health, forgets.
remember: Yumi refused to wash him; Hana did it
General promised private assassins
General needed Sadao for his own operation
traps: Yumi did not help
The assassins did not come because the General forgot

topics.t: A boat, a flashlight and an escape
topics.h: No assassins arrive. Sadao makes his own plan: a boat, food, water and a flashlight.
p: When no assassins come, Sadao helps the American escape by boat to a nearby island, with food, water, clothes and a flashlight for signalling if he needs help.
The American gets away safely. Sadao wonders why he could not simply kill him.
This is how Sadao finally solves his problem: he follows his conscience as a doctor and a human being, while protecting his family from discovery.

ex.q: How did Sadao finally solve his problem?
st: The General's plan failed, so the man was still there.
Sadao could not kill a patient he had saved.
He arranged a boat, food and a flashlight so the American could escape.
ex.a: He helped the American escape secretly by boat, saving both the man's life and his own family from trouble.

topics.rl: The Geneva Conventions protect wounded soldiers and prisoners of war. Sadao's choice reflects that spirit even when people around him want the enemy dead.

rv.summary: When no assassins come, Sadao helps the American escape by boat to a nearby island with food, water, clothes and a flashlight for signalling. The man escapes safely, and Sadao wonders why he could not kill him.
remember: Boat, food, water, clothes, flashlight
First stop: a nearby island
Sadao wondered why he could not kill him
traps: Sadao did not kill the American
The flashlight was for signalling, not reading maps

topics.t: Sadao, Hana, the General and the title's irony
topics.h: Who is 'the enemy'? The wounded American, the self-centred General, or hatred itself?
p: Dr Sadao: a dedicated surgeon torn between nationalism and humanity; his professional ethics win.
Hana: compassionate and supportive; she washes and feeds the enemy herself when the servants refuse.
The General: self-centred and pragmatic; he offers murder and then forgets because of his own health.
Devices: third-person narration; irony (the General forgets); the title's irony about who 'the enemy' really is.

ex.q: Explain the irony of the title 'The Enemy'.
st: The American is officially the enemy.
Yet Sadao and Hana treat him with humanity.
The real enemy may be hatred, prejudice and war itself.
ex.a: The 'enemy' by nationality is saved by kindness, suggesting the true enemy is hatred and war, not a person.

topics.rl: In real life too, labels like 'enemy' often fade when one human being faces another in need.

rv.summary: Sadao is a dedicated surgeon torn between nationalism and humanity; Hana is compassionate and supportive; the General is self-centred. The third-person story uses irony, and the title asks who the real enemy is.
remember: Sadao – ethical, torn; Hana – compassionate; General – self-centred
Third-person narration
Real enemy = hatred and war
traps: Hana did not refuse to touch the American
The story is not first-person

topics.t: Themes: humanity, medical ethics and compassion in war
topics.h: A doctor's oath does not ask for a passport. Sadao proves it in the middle of a war.
p: Humanity above patriotism and prejudice: Sadao and Hana save a man whom their country calls the enemy.
Professional ethics: a doctor's first duty is to save life; Sadao cannot let a patient die.
Hatred in war versus individual compassion: the servants and the General reflect wartime hatred; Sadao and Hana show personal kindness.

ex.q: How do professional ethics guide Sadao?
st: As a surgeon, his duty is to save life.
He operates on the American even though it is risky.
He cannot kill the man he has healed.
ex.a: His duty as a doctor to save life outweighs national hatred; he heals the man and later helps him escape.

topics.rl: Under the Geneva Conventions, medical teams in war must care for all wounded people without discrimination, the very principle Sadao follows.

rv.summary: The story places humanity above patriotism and prejudice, shows a doctor's ethic of saving life, and contrasts wartime hatred (servants, General) with personal compassion (Sadao, Hana).
remember: A doctor's first duty is to save life
Servants and General = wartime hatred
Message: compassion rises above enmity
traps: The story does not glorify hatred in war
Don't place Sadao and Hana among the hateful characters

topics.t: Board exam practice: The Enemy
topics.h: 'Sadao's dilemma' is the classic long answer from Vistas. Know its two sides, and the marks follow.
p: Sadao's dilemma: duty to his country (hand over the enemy) versus duty as a doctor (save a dying man).
Why the servants left: they believed sheltering an enemy was wrong and dangerous. The General: self-centred, cares only for his own health.
Short answers on Sadao (dedicated, ethical, torn) and Hana (compassionate, supportive).
Long answer on humanity versus patriotism: the discovery, the operation, the General's failed plan, the escape, and the message.

ex.q: Write a 50-word answer: What was Sadao's dilemma?
st: As a patriot, he should hand over an enemy prisoner.
As a doctor, he must save the dying man.
Helping him risked his family's safety.
ex.a: Sadao had to choose between patriotism and humanity. As a loyal Japanese he should hand over the escaped American prisoner, but as a doctor he could not let a wounded man die. Helping him also endangered his family.

topics.rl: Films and stories often show soldiers or doctors helping a wounded rival. The board exam often asks students to connect such ideas to 'The Enemy'.

rv.summary: Board answers explain Sadao's dilemma between country and medical duty, why the servants left, the General's self-centredness, Hana's compassion and how Sadao resolved the problem by saving the man and helping him escape.
focus: Long answer on humanity versus patriotism
remember: Dilemma: duty to country versus duty as a doctor
Hana washed and fed the American
Conclusion: humanity triumphs over hatred
traps: Don't end a long answer with a minor fact
Sadao did not hand the man over

topics.ch: Vistas: On the Face of It
topics.t: A burnt face meets a tin leg
topics.h: A bitter boy climbs a wall into what he thinks is an empty garden. An old man with a tin leg says, 'Come in.'
p: Author: Susan Hill, an English novelist and playwright. 'On the Face of It' is a one-act play in two scenes.
Characters: Derry, a boy of about fourteen; Mr Lamb, an old man; and Derry's mother.
Derry climbs into Mr Lamb's garden thinking it empty. Mr Lamb welcomes him instead of scolding him.
One side of Derry's face was burnt by acid; he is bitter, defensive and withdrawn.
Mr Lamb has a tin leg, lost in a war; children mock him as 'Lamey-Lamb', but he does not mind.

ex.q: How do Derry and Mr Lamb first react to each other?
st: Derry is startled and defensive; he expects disgust.
Mr Lamb is calm and welcoming; he doesn't comment on the face first.
Their contrast sets up the play.
ex.a: Derry is suspicious and defensive, while Mr Lamb is warm and accepting, which disarms him.

topics.rl: Acid attack survivors in India, like those at Agra's Sheroes Hangout café, show the courage Derry must learn: facing the world without hiding.

rv.summary: Susan Hill's one-act play in two scenes brings together Derry, a bitter fourteen-year-old with an acid-burnt face, and Mr Lamb, an old man with a tin leg lost in war, who welcomes him into his garden.
remember: Susan Hill; one-act play, two scenes
Derry: about 14, face burnt by acid
Mr Lamb: tin leg from a war; called 'Lamey-Lamb'
traps: Mr Lamb is welcoming, not angry
Don't swap Derry's injury with Mr Lamb's

topics.ch: Vistas: On the Face of It
topics.t: Crab apples, bees and a picture that fell
topics.h: Mr Lamb thinks weeds are flowers too. That one idea starts to change how Derry sees himself.
p: The garden: crab apples for making jelly, bees and their honey, weeds and flowers growing together.
Mr Lamb's philosophy: all things in nature are equal (a weed is a flower too); people fear what is different.
Derry recalls overhearing his mother say that only a mother could love a face like his, which hurt him deeply.
Mr Lamb tells of a man who shut himself away for fear of the world and was killed anyway, when a picture fell off his wall.
Derry, touched, promises to come back to help pick the crab apples.

ex.q: What is the point of Mr Lamb's story about the man and the picture?
st: The man hid indoors to stay safe.
He died at home anyway, when a picture fell on him.
So hiding from life does not protect you; it only wastes life.
ex.a: That shutting yourself away out of fear doesn't keep you safe; you might as well live fully.

topics.rl: Indian kitchens turn fruit into jams and murabbas the way Mr Lamb turns crab apples into jelly: making something sweet from something sour.

rv.summary: In the garden of crab apples and bees, Mr Lamb says weeds and flowers are equal and people fear difference. Derry recalls his mother's hurtful remark; Mr Lamb's story of a man killed by a falling picture shows hiding is useless. Derry promises to return.
focus: The story of the man and the picture
remember: Crab apples for jelly
'Only a mother could love such a face'
Man hid indoors; killed by a falling picture
traps: Mr Lamb does not think weeds are worthless
Don't confuse the falling picture with Mr Lamb's fall from the ladder

topics.ch: Vistas: On the Face of It
topics.t: Scene 2: going back, and finding loss
topics.h: Derry's mother says no. For the first time, Derry says, 'I'm going.' He gets there too late.
p: At home, Derry's mother forbids him to go back to Mr Lamb, distrusting the old man.
Derry insists: he wants to go out and see the world and things; he will not stay shut away.
He returns to the garden to find Mr Lamb has fallen from the ladder while picking crab apples, and has died. Derry weeps.

ex.q: Why is Derry's decision to go back so important?
st: Earlier he hid from people and the world.
Now he defies his mother to go out.
This shows Mr Lamb's influence has changed him.
ex.a: It shows he has begun to overcome his bitterness and fear, choosing to face the world as Mr Lamb taught.

topics.rl: Peer support groups in Indian schools help students who feel 'different' to step out. Derry's step out of the house is that same turning point.

rv.summary: Derry's mother forbids him to see Mr Lamb, but Derry insists on going out to see the world. He returns to find Mr Lamb has fallen from the ladder while picking crab apples and died, and he weeps.
remember: Mother forbids the visit
Derry wants to see the world
Mr Lamb fell from the ladder picking crab apples
traps: Mr Lamb is not waiting for Derry at the end
Derry's return shows change, not rebellion for its own sake

topics.ch: Vistas: On the Face of It
topics.t: Derry, Mr Lamb, and living with difference
topics.h: One is young and bitter; one is old and cheerful. Both carry a visible difference, and both are lonely.
p: Derry: bitter, insecure and defensive at first, but he learns hope and courage from Mr Lamb.
Mr Lamb: wise and cheerful, but lonely; he accepts his tin leg and others' teasing, and keeps his gate open to all.
Theme: disability, loneliness and acceptance. Both are isolated by how others see them; acceptance begins within.

ex.q: How does Mr Lamb handle his disability differently from Derry?
st: Derry hides and feels bitter about his face.
Mr Lamb accepts his tin leg and laughs at teasing.
He keeps his gate open and lives fully.
ex.a: Mr Lamb accepts his disability cheerfully and stays open to life, while Derry hides in bitterness.

topics.rl: The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, in India aims at dignity and inclusion. Mr Lamb's attitude shows what inner acceptance looks like.

rv.summary: Derry begins bitter and defensive but learns hope from Mr Lamb, who is wise and cheerful yet lonely and accepts his disability. Both are isolated by how others see them; acceptance begins within.
remember: Derry – bitter, insecure, then hopeful
Mr Lamb – wise, cheerful, lonely; open gate
Both lonely and 'different'
traps: Derry does not stay the same
Mr Lamb is not bitter about teasing

topics.ch: Vistas: On the Face of It
topics.t: Friendship, appearance and the play's ending
topics.h: 'On the face of it' means 'as it seems at first'. The title is a pun, and the play is about looking beneath faces.
p: Friendship across ages: a boy and an old man find understanding; a positive attitude to life is passed from one to the other.
Appearance versus reality: 'on the face of it' means as things first appear; a scarred face or a tin leg hides a whole person beneath.
Form: a one-act play built on dialogue; irony of the ending, as Derry returns, changed and ready to live, only to find Mr Lamb has died.

ex.q: Why is the ending ironic?
st: Mr Lamb taught Derry to stop fearing and start living.
Derry comes back, ready to help and be a friend.
But Mr Lamb, who was full of life, has died in an ordinary accident.
ex.a: Just when Derry has learnt to live and returns as a friend, Mr Lamb, the teacher of that lesson, is gone.

topics.rl: Inter-generational programmes where students spend time with senior citizens are growing in Indian cities. Derry and Mr Lamb show why they work.

rv.summary: The play shows friendship across ages and appearance versus reality; its pun title means 'as it seems at first'. Built on dialogue, it ends ironically: Derry returns changed just as Mr Lamb dies.
focus: Meaning and pun of the title
remember: 'On the face of it' = as it seems at first
Main tool: dialogue
Irony: Mr Lamb dies just as Derry returns
traps: The play is not a novel
We should not judge people by appearance

topics.ch: Vistas: On the Face of It
topics.t: Board exam practice: On the Face of It
topics.h: 'What draws Derry to Mr Lamb?' and 'Will Derry return to his old self?' are favourite board questions.
p: What draws Derry: Mr Lamb treats him normally, doesn't pity or stare, and talks sense about fear and difference.
Mr Lamb's loneliness: open gate, few visitors, talking to bees, children mocking him.
Will Derry return to his old self? Unlikely; he has learnt to face the world, and he weeps for a friend he chose to return to.
Aptness of the title: appearance versus reality; both characters are more than what they look like.
Long answer: attitudes to disability: Derry's bitterness, Mr Lamb's acceptance, society's fear of difference.

ex.q: Write a 50-word answer: What draws Derry towards Mr Lamb?
st: Mr Lamb does not stare at or pity his face.
He speaks to him as an equal and shares wisdom.
He gives Derry a new way to see himself.
ex.a: Mr Lamb treats Derry normally, without staring or pity. He talks to him as an equal, shares his view that all things are equal and that hiding is useless. This acceptance and wisdom draw the lonely, bitter boy towards him.

topics.rl: Board examiners reward answers that use evidence. Quote small details, the open gate, the bees, the weeds, to support every point.

rv.summary: Board answers explain that Mr Lamb's acceptance draws Derry, that the open gate shows Mr Lamb's loneliness, that Derry is unlikely to return to his old self, why the title is apt and how people react to disability.
focus: Long answer on attitudes to disability
remember: Draw: acceptance without pity or fear
Change shown by defying his mother
Society fears what is different
traps: Don't use a detail from before the change to show Derry has changed
Disability is not a punishment

topics.t: Two childhoods, two continents
topics.h: One girl in America, one in Tamil Nadu, decades and oceans apart, yet their childhood memories echo each other.
p: The chapter has two autobiographical episodes by women from marginalised communities.
Part 1 is by Zitkala-Sa (Gertrude Simmons Bonnin), a Native American writer. Part 2 is by Bama, a Tamil Dalit writer, from her autobiography 'Karukku'.
Zitkala-Sa recalls her first day at a missionary boarding school for Native American children.
Strict rules: bells rang for everything, the children marched, and meals followed a fixed routine; she felt embarrassed and closely watched in unfamiliar clothes.

ex.q: Why are the two accounts placed together?
st: Both are true stories by women from marginalised groups.
Both describe painful childhood experiences of discrimination.
Together they show oppression is not limited to one culture.
ex.a: Because both show how marginalised children faced discrimination, and how they responded, across very different cultures.

topics.rl: NCERT pairs these two stories to help students see that injustice can look different in different places but feels similar to those who suffer it.

rv.summary: The chapter pairs two autobiographical accounts by women from marginalised communities: Zitkala-Sa, a Native American, on her first day at a strict missionary boarding school, and Bama, a Tamil Dalit writer, from 'Karukku'.
focus: The two authors and their backgrounds
remember: Zitkala-Sa = Gertrude Simmons Bonnin, Native American
Bama, Tamil Dalit writer, 'Karukku'
School life ruled by bells and strict rules
traps: The writers are from different countries
Don't mix up which part each wrote

topics.t: The cutting of her long hair
topics.h: Her friend whispers a warning: they are going to cut our hair. For Zitkala-Sa, that is worse than any punishment.
p: Her friend Judewin, who knew a little English, warned that the school authorities would cut their long, heavy hair.
In her culture, shingled hair was worn by cowards and short hair by mourners; long hair was a mark of pride.
She decided to resist: she crept upstairs and hid under a bed in a large, dimly lit room.
She was found, dragged out kicking and scratching, tied to a chair, and her long hair was cut. She felt like one of many little animals driven by a herder.
She lost her spirit; no one came to comfort her as her mother would have.

ex.q: Why was the cutting of her hair so painful for Zitkala-Sa?
st: In her culture long hair meant pride and dignity.
Shingled hair marked cowards; short hair marked mourners.
Cutting it by force insulted her identity.
ex.a: Because it stripped her of her cultural identity and dignity, branding her, in her people's eyes, as a coward or mourner.

topics.rl: In many Indian communities, hair also carries meaning, in rituals, vows and identity. That helps us feel why the forced haircut was such a deep wound.

rv.summary: Warned by Judewin that their long hair would be cut, Zitkala-Sa hid under a bed, since in her culture short hair marked mourners and shingled hair cowards. She was dragged out, tied to a chair and shorn, and felt like a herded animal.
focus: Meaning of long hair in her culture
remember: Judewin warned her
Shingled hair – cowards; short hair – mourners
Tied to a chair; felt like an animal driven by a herder
traps: She did not cut her hair willingly
No one came to comfort her

topics.t: Bama and the packet of vadai
topics.h: A little girl laughs at an old man carrying a snack by its string. Her brother's explanation changes her life.
p: Bama, in the third grade, takes her time walking home, watching the sights of the street: performers, shops, festivals and the threshing floor.
She sees an elder of her community carrying a small packet of vadai by its string, without touching it, and handing it to the landlord.

She finds it funny at first. Her elder brother, Annan, explains that it is because of untouchability: people of so-called upper castes believe they would be polluted by the touch of people from her community.
Annan tells her that because of the community they are born into, they are denied honour and dignity, but that education can win them respect; she must study hard.
Bama takes his words to heart, studies hard and stands first in her class.

ex.q: How does Bama's understanding change after Annan's explanation?
st: At first she sees only a comic way of carrying a packet.
Annan explains it is caused by untouchability.
She now sees the humiliation behind it and resolves to study.
ex.a: She moves from amusement to painful awareness of caste discrimination, and resolves to win respect through education.

topics.rl: The Constitution of India abolishes untouchability (Article 17) and makes its practice an offence. Bama's story shows why this protection matters.

rv.summary: In the third grade, Bama saw an elder of her community carry a packet of vadai by its string to the landlord. She found it funny until her brother Annan explained untouchability and urged her to study hard; she stood first in her class.
remember: Bama in the third grade
Packet held by the string to avoid 'polluting' it
Annan: education wins respect; Bama stood first
traps: Bama did not understand at once — she first found it funny
Annan, not a teacher, explained it

topics.t: Themes: identity, caste and the power of education
topics.h: Two girls, two kinds of oppression, and two forms of resistance: one who fights, one who studies.
p: Cultural oppression and loss of identity: Zitkala-Sa's long hair, language and freedom are taken away by the school.
Casteism and untouchability: Bama sees an elder humiliated by caste practice.
Resistance and the power of education: Zitkala-Sa resists by hiding and struggling; Bama resists by studying and excelling.
Style: first-person narration, vivid sensory detail (the bells, the cold scissors, the street sights), and a parallel drawn between two cultures.

ex.q: How do the two narrators resist oppression differently?
st: Zitkala-Sa resists physically: she hides, kicks and struggles.
Bama resists through education: she studies and stands first.
Both refuse to accept injustice quietly.
ex.a: Zitkala-Sa resists openly and physically, while Bama resists through education; both refuse to accept their oppression.

topics.rl: Dr B.R. Ambedkar, chief architect of the Indian Constitution, urged people to 'educate, agitate, organise'. Bama's choice reflects the first of those words.

rv.summary: The accounts show cultural oppression and loss of identity, casteism and untouchability, and resistance — Zitkala-Sa by struggling, Bama by education — told in first person with vivid sensory detail.
remember: Zitkala-Sa: physical resistance
Bama: resistance through education
Both use first-person narration
traps: Don't swap the two forms of resistance
The haircut is about identity, not just school discipline

topics.t: Board exam practice: Memories of Childhood
topics.h: 'What is common to the two accounts?' is almost certain to appear. Here is a clean answer frame.
p: Common features: both are autobiographical, by women from marginalised communities; both describe childhood discrimination; both show resistance.
Responses: Zitkala-Sa fights physically and loses her hair but not her will to resist; Bama channels her pain into education.
Bama's growing understanding: from amusement, to Annan's explanation, to anger, to a resolve to study.
Short answers on each part; long answer on resistance and identity, comparing both narrators.

ex.q: Write a 50-word answer: What is common to the two accounts?
st: Both are true stories by women from marginalised groups.
Both show discrimination in childhood.
Both narrators resist in their own way.
ex.a: Both are autobiographical accounts by women from marginalised communities. Each describes childhood discrimination, cultural in Zitkala-Sa's case and caste-based in Bama's, and each shows resistance: Zitkala-Sa by struggling, Bama by studying hard to win respect.

topics.rl: Many first-generation learners in India today, the first in their families to reach college, echo Bama's belief that education opens closed doors.

rv.summary: Board answers compare the two accounts: both are by marginalised women, show childhood discrimination and resistance. Zitkala-Sa fought physically; Bama moved from amusement to awareness to resolve and studied hard.
focus: Common features of the two accounts
Long answer on resistance and identity
remember: Bama's growth: amusement → awareness → resolve
Part 1 key event: forced haircut
Shared message: dignity is worth fighting for
traps: Don't end a long answer with a minor fact
Don't mix details of the two parts

qa.q: Who wrote 'The Last Lesson'?
qa.a: Alphonse Daudet
qa.e: 'The Last Lesson' is by the French writer Alphonse Daudet.

qa.q: The historical background of 'The Last Lesson' is the
qa.a: Franco-Prussian War of 1870–71
qa.e: Prussia defeated France in 1870–71 and took Alsace and Lorraine; the story is set in that period.

qa.q: Which districts did Prussia take from France, as shown in the story?
qa.a: Alsace and Lorraine
qa.e: The order from Berlin applies to the schools of Alsace and Lorraine, the districts annexed by Prussia.

qa.q: From whose point of view is the story narrated?
qa.a: Franz, a schoolboy
qa.e: Franz tells the story in the first person.

qa.q: Why was Franz in great dread of going to school that morning?
qa.a: He had not learnt his participles
qa.e: M. Hamel had said he would question them on participles, and Franz did not know them.

qa.q: What tempted Franz to spend the day outdoors?
qa.a: The warm day, birds and drilling soldiers
qa.e: The bright weather, chirping birds and soldiers drilling behind the sawmill attracted him.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Franz's opening fear of the participle test is important to the story.
Reason (R): It shows his careless attitude, which contrasts with his later regret.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both are true, and the contrast between carelessness and remorse is exactly why the opening matters.

qa.q: Case: A student skips practice, plans to bunk class on a sunny day, but then goes in. Which part of 'The Last Lesson' does this mirror?
qa.a: Franz resisting the outdoors and hurrying to school
qa.e: Like Franz, the student is tempted but finally goes to school.

qa.q: Why was there a crowd in front of the bulletin board?
qa.a: New orders had been put up there
qa.e: For two years all bad news, like lost battles and orders, came from the bulletin board, so people gathered to read the latest.

qa.q: What did Franz count on to reach his desk without being seen?
qa.a: The usual bustle of the class
qa.e: Normally the noise was so great that he could slip in unnoticed.

qa.q: How did M. Hamel react when Franz came in late?
qa.a: He kindly asked him to take his seat
qa.e: Instead of scolding, he said gently that they were starting without him.

qa.q: When did M. Hamel normally wear his green coat and silk cap?
qa.a: On inspection and prize days
qa.e: These were his special clothes, worn only on inspection and prize days.

qa.q: What did old Hauser bring with him to the class?
qa.a: An old primer, thumbed at the edges
qa.e: He held his old primer open on his knees with his spectacles across it.

qa.q: Why were the village elders sitting in the classroom?
qa.a: To pay respect and share the last lesson
qa.e: They came to thank their master for forty years of service and to show respect to the country that was no longer theirs.

qa.q: What did the silence in the classroom most clearly suggest to the reader?
qa.a: Something serious had happened
qa.e: An unusual silence builds suspense and hints at bad news.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The crowd at the bulletin board made Franz uneasy.
Reason (R): M. Hamel had taught in the village for forty years.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both are true, but Hamel's forty years of teaching do not explain why the crowd at the board worried Franz.

qa.q: What order had come from Berlin?
qa.a: Only German to be taught in Alsace and Lorraine
qa.e: The order said that only German would be taught in the schools of Alsace and Lorraine.

qa.q: When was the new German master to arrive?
qa.a: The next day
qa.e: M. Hamel says the new master comes tomorrow, so this was the very last lesson.

qa.q: Which of these did Franz NOT regret in the story?
qa.a: Learning his German lessons
qa.e: His regrets were about wasting time on play and not learning French; German lessons are not among them.

qa.q: Why did M. Hamel not scold Franz for failing to recite the participles?
qa.a: He felt everyone shared the blame
qa.e: He says Franz is not the only one; all of them have put off learning, and he blames parents and himself too.

qa.q: According to M. Hamel, what was the great trouble with Alsace?
qa.a: It put off learning till tomorrow
qa.e: He says Alsace always believed there was plenty of time and delayed learning.

qa.q: How did M. Hamel admit his own fault?
qa.a: He sent pupils to water his flowers
qa.e: He admits sending children to water his flowers and giving holidays when he went fishing.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Many children in the village had not learnt French properly.
Reason (R): Their parents preferred to send them to work on farms or in mills.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; M. Hamel says parents chose a little extra money over schooling, which explains the poor learning.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Franz was happy to hear there would be no more French lessons.
Reason (R): He had always disliked his French grammar books.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: Franz was shocked and sad. R is true, since he once found the books a nuisance.

qa.q: How did M. Hamel describe the French language?
qa.a: The most beautiful, clearest and most logical
qa.e: He called it the most beautiful language in the world, the clearest and the most logical.

qa.q: In M. Hamel's words, language for an enslaved people is like
qa.a: the key to their prison
qa.e: Holding on to one's language is like holding the key to one's prison.

qa.q: What did the new copies on the desks say?
qa.a: France, Alsace
qa.e: M. Hamel gave new copies with 'France, Alsace' in round hand; they looked like little flags.

qa.q: What did Franz wonder about the pigeons on the roof?
qa.a: Whether they would be made to sing in German
qa.e: His remark shows how absurd and total the imposition of German felt.

qa.q: Why did Franz understand the grammar lesson so easily that day?
qa.a: He listened with full attention and feeling
qa.e: Knowing it was the last lesson, he listened closely and found everything clear.

qa.q: What did 'Vive La France!' written on the board express?
qa.a: Long live France
qa.e: 'Vive La France!' means 'Long live France', a final cry of patriotism.

qa.q: Why did M. Hamel write on the board instead of speaking at the end?
qa.a: He was too overcome with emotion
qa.e: He tried to speak, choked, and wrote the words instead.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The pigeon remark adds a touch of irony to the story.
Reason (R): The church clock struck twelve at the end of the lesson.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both are true, but the clock striking twelve does not explain the irony of the pigeon remark.

qa.q: How many years had M. Hamel taught at the school?
qa.a: Forty years
qa.e: The story speaks of his forty years of faithful service.

qa.q: Which word best describes M. Hamel at the end of the story?
qa.a: Patriotic
qa.e: His praise of French and his final words 'Vive La France!' show his love for his country.

qa.q: What change do we see in Franz by the end?
qa.a: From careless to remorseful and keen to learn
qa.e: The order makes him regret wasted time and value his lessons.

qa.q: Why did the villagers regret their past?
qa.a: They had not learnt their language when they could
qa.e: Their presence shows sorrow at not having gone to school more.

qa.q: 'Linguistic chauvinism' in the story is best shown by
qa.a: the order to teach only German
qa.e: Imposing a conqueror's language on a defeated people is linguistic chauvinism.

qa.q: Why is a mother tongue so important, according to the story?
qa.a: It keeps a people's identity alive
qa.e: Language binds a people to their culture and identity; losing it is losing freedom.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): M. Hamel was a strict teacher.
Reason (R): He blamed only the students for their poor learning.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true; he was strict. R is false, because he blamed parents and himself too.

qa.q: Case: In a novel, a conquering king orders that only his own language may be taught in the schools of a defeated land, and bans the people's language. Which idea from the story does this reflect?
qa.a: Linguistic chauvinism
qa.e: Forcing the conqueror's language on a people and banning theirs is linguistic chauvinism, just like the order from Berlin.

qa.q: Which theme is shown by 'I'll learn it tomorrow'?
qa.a: Procrastination
qa.e: Putting off learning till tomorrow is procrastination.

qa.q: The story is ironic mainly because
qa.a: the last lesson becomes the best one
qa.e: Franz learns most eagerly in the lesson that is his last, which is the central irony.

qa.q: In the story, the bulletin board mainly symbolises
qa.a: a source of bad news
qa.e: For two years it had brought only bad news: lost battles, the draft and orders.

qa.q: Which narrative technique does Daudet use?
qa.a: First-person narration
qa.e: Franz narrates his own experience using 'I'.

qa.q: Which line best creates pathos at the end?
qa.a: M. Hamel choking and unable to speak
qa.e: The teacher's broken voice and silent writing move the reader deeply.

qa.q: How is the theme of patriotism shown?
qa.a: Hamel's praise of French and his last words
qa.e: His love for the language and final cry show patriotism.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The use of first-person narration makes the story emotionally powerful.
Reason (R): Readers see the changing feelings of Franz from the inside.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; seeing events through Franz's eyes makes his remorse and sadness personal.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The story suggests that people often value things only when they are about to lose them.
Reason (R): Franz had always loved his French lessons.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true; R is false, because Franz used to find his lessons boring.

qa.q: 'In great dread of' means
qa.a: very much afraid of
qa.e: Dread is great fear; Franz feared being questioned.

qa.q: 'I had counted on the bustle' — 'counted on' means
qa.a: relied on
qa.e: To count on is to depend or rely on something.

qa.q: 'Thumbing the pages' of a primer means
qa.a: turning the pages with the thumb
qa.e: Old Hauser's primer was worn at the edges from turning its pages.

qa.q: The word 'tycoon' comes from
qa.a: Japanese
qa.e: It comes from Japanese 'taikun', meaning great lord.

qa.q: The word 'zero' comes, through Italian, from
qa.a: Arabic
qa.e: Zero comes from Arabic 'sifr' through Italian; the concept of zero was developed in India, but the English word traces to Arabic.

qa.q: Which sentence uses the past perfect correctly?
qa.a: The bell had rung before Franz arrived.
qa.e: Past perfect is had + past participle: had rung; it shows the earlier action.

qa.q: In 'we've all a great deal to reproach ourselves with', 'reproach' means
qa.a: blame
qa.e: To reproach is to criticise or blame someone, here oneself.

qa.q: Choose the correct meaning of 'bustle' in 'the great bustle of the class'.
qa.a: noisy busy activity
qa.e: Here bustle means the busy noise of desks and voices.

qa.q: What had Franz expected to happen when he reached school late?
qa.a: A scolding from M. Hamel
qa.e: He feared a scolding and the ruler, which is why M. Hamel's kindness surprised him.

qa.q: What was the main change the order from Berlin caused in the school?
qa.a: French would no longer be taught
qa.e: German replaced French as the only language taught.

qa.q: Which detail best supports the answer 'the villagers regretted not learning French'?
qa.a: They sat on the back benches with primers
qa.e: Their silent presence in class shows their regret and respect.

qa.q: What do the pigeons' cooing and Franz's question about them suggest?
qa.a: Imposing a language is unnatural and absurd
qa.e: Franz imagines that even birds must change their song, which shows the absurdity of the order.

qa.q: Which is the best opening line for a long answer on 'importance of mother tongue'?
qa.a: A mother tongue carries a people's identity and freedom.
qa.e: A long answer should begin with a clear thesis linked to the question.

qa.q: A discussion question asks if pride in language can go too far. The term for this is
qa.a: linguistic chauvinism
qa.e: Excessive pride that leads to imposing one's language is linguistic chauvinism.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Franz's feelings toward M. Hamel changed during the lesson.
Reason (R): He forgot all his past troubles with the teacher once he knew M. Hamel was leaving.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; the thought of Hamel leaving made Franz forget the ruler and his crankiness, which explains the change.

qa.q: Case: A student writes, 'M. Hamel was only strict.' What is missing from this character sketch?
qa.a: His devotion, patriotism and kindness
qa.e: A balanced sketch adds that he was devoted, patriotic and gentle on the last day.

qa.q: 'Lost Spring' is taken from a book by
qa.a: Anees Jung
qa.e: Anees Jung wrote 'Lost Spring: Stories of Stolen Childhood'.

qa.q: What is the form of 'Lost Spring'?
qa.a: Reportage on child labour
qa.e: It reports on real children trapped in poverty and labour.

qa.q: Why did Saheb's family leave Dhaka?
qa.a: Storms swept away their fields and homes
qa.e: Saheb recalls his mother telling him that, many years ago, storms swept away their fields and homes.

qa.q: Where does Saheb live?
qa.a: Seemapuri, on the outskirts of Delhi
qa.e: Seemapuri is on the periphery of Delhi.

qa.q: What are the houses in Seemapuri made of?
qa.a: Mud with roofs of tin and tarpaulin
qa.e: They are mud structures roofed with tin and tarpaulin.

qa.q: For the elders of Seemapuri, ragpicking is
qa.a: a means of survival
qa.e: Elders depend on it to survive; only children find wonder in it.

qa.q: Why do children in Seemapuri find garbage 'wrapped in wonder'?
qa.a: They might find a coin or note
qa.e: Finding a rupee or even a ten-rupee note keeps their hope alive.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Lost Spring is written as a reportage.
Reason (R): The author reports on real people she met, like Saheb and Mukesh.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; reportage is a first-hand report of real people and events, which R describes.

qa.q: What reason is often given for children walking barefoot?
qa.a: It is a tradition
qa.e: People say it is a tradition, though the author feels it hides poverty.

qa.q: What does the author think the 'tradition' of walking barefoot really hides?
qa.a: A perpetual state of poverty
qa.e: She wonders if the tradition is just an excuse for constant poverty.

qa.q: Why is Saheb's full name ironic?
qa.a: It means lord of the universe; he owns nothing
qa.e: A boy who owns nothing is called 'lord of the universe'.

qa.q: Why was the author embarrassed when Saheb asked 'Is your school ready?'
qa.a: She had made a promise she did not mean
qa.e: She had spoken half in jest, and he took it seriously.

qa.q: How much did Saheb earn at the tea stall?
qa.a: 800 rupees and all his meals
qa.e: He was paid 800 rupees and all his meals.

qa.q: What does the steel canister symbolise?
qa.a: Saheb's loss of freedom
qa.e: The canister belongs to his employer, so it shows he now works for someone else.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Saheb is no longer his own master.
Reason (R): The steel canister belongs to the man who owns the tea shop.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; the canister shows he now serves an employer, which explains the loss of independence.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): At the tea stall Saheb earns a fixed wage and gets meals.
Reason (R): Saheb looks more carefree at the tea stall than as a ragpicker.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: R is false: his carefree look is gone. A is true; he gets 800 rupees and meals.

qa.q: Firozabad is famous for its
qa.a: glass bangles
qa.e: Firozabad is the centre of India's glass-bangle industry.

qa.q: About how many children work in the Firozabad bangle industry, as per the text?
qa.a: About 20,000
qa.e: The text mentions about 20,000 children.

qa.q: What is the main hazard faced by the child workers?
qa.a: Losing their eyesight
qa.e: Dark rooms and furnaces damage their eyes; many lose their eyesight before adulthood.

qa.q: Why does child labour continue in Firozabad though it is illegal?
qa.a: Poverty and generations of family tradition
qa.e: Families have made bangles for generations and are trapped in poverty.

qa.q: What is Savita doing when the author sees her?
qa.a: Soldering pieces of glass
qa.e: She sits beside an elderly woman soldering bits of glass.

qa.q: What do bangles symbolise for an Indian married woman, according to the text?
qa.a: Suhaag, or auspiciousness
qa.e: Bangles are a symbol of a married woman's suhaag.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Many bangle workers lose their eyesight before they become adults.
Reason (R): They work in dingy cells without air and light, near hot furnaces.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; the dark, hot conditions cause the damage.

qa.q: Case: A shopper buys a dozen colourful glass bangles for a wedding. Which idea from 'Lost Spring' would make her think twice?
qa.a: Child makers often lose their eyesight
qa.e: The hidden cost of the bangles is the health and childhood of child workers.

qa.q: What did the elderly woman say about her life?
qa.a: She had never had one full meal
qa.e: Despite a lifetime of bangle making she had not enjoyed a full meal.

qa.q: The 'vicious circle' in Firozabad includes all of these EXCEPT
qa.a: teachers
qa.e: The circle is of sahukars, middlemen, policemen, keepers of the law, bureaucrats and politicians.

qa.q: Who are 'sahukars'?
qa.a: Moneylenders
qa.e: Sahukars are moneylenders who keep workers in debt.

qa.q: Why can't the bangle workers organise themselves?
qa.a: Fear of the police and no cooperative
qa.e: If they organise they fear the police; there is no leader or cooperative.

qa.q: What does Mukesh dream of becoming?
qa.a: A motor mechanic
qa.e: Mukesh wants to be a motor mechanic and learn to drive a car.

qa.q: Why is Mukesh's dream significant in the chapter?
qa.a: It breaks away from inherited bangle making
qa.e: He chooses his own path instead of the family tradition, which gives hope.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The bangle workers stay poor generation after generation.
Reason (R): They are caught in a vicious circle of moneylenders, middlemen, police and politicians.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; the exploitation by this circle keeps them poor.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The workers of Firozabad have formed a strong cooperative.
Reason (R): A cooperative could help them avoid middlemen.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: there is no cooperative. R is true in general, and that is why its absence matters.

qa.q: In the title 'Lost Spring', 'spring' stands for
qa.a: childhood
qa.e: Spring, the season of fresh growth, symbolises childhood.

qa.q: What does 'karam' mean as used by Mukesh's grandmother?
qa.a: Destiny or fate
qa.e: She calls her husband's blindness, caused by polishing glass, his karam, his destiny.

qa.q: Which is NOT a theme of 'Lost Spring'?
qa.a: Time travel
qa.e: Time travel belongs to 'The Third Level', not 'Lost Spring'.

qa.q: Which character best represents hope in 'Lost Spring'?
qa.a: Mukesh
qa.e: Mukesh dreams of becoming a motor mechanic, showing hope.

qa.q: How does the burden of tradition harm the bangle makers?
qa.a: It makes them accept poverty as fate
qa.e: Believing their life is destiny, they do not try to change it.

qa.q: A good short answer on Saheb would mention
qa.a: his ragpicking and later loss of freedom
qa.e: Key points about Saheb: ragpicking in Seemapuri and the tea-stall job that cost him his freedom.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The title 'Lost Spring' is apt.
Reason (R): Children in the chapter lose their childhood to poverty and labour.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; the loss of childhood is exactly what makes the title fitting.

qa.q: Case: A debate team says 'Poverty is the only cause of child labour.' Which point from the chapter challenges their claim?
qa.a: Tradition and exploiters also keep them working
qa.e: The chapter shows tradition and the vicious circle of exploiters also keep children working.

qa.q: Which feature marks 'Lost Spring' as reportage?
qa.a: First-hand observation of real people
qa.e: The author met and describes real children and their words.

qa.q: Which is an example of irony in the chapter?
qa.a: Bright bangles made in dark, grim cells
qa.e: Bright symbols of joy made by people living joyless lives is ironic.

qa.q: What is Saheb looking for in the garbage?
qa.a: Coins or money
qa.e: He hopes to find a rupee or even a ten-rupee note.

qa.q: What is the best answer to 'Why do the bangle workers not organise?'
qa.a: They fear the police and have no cooperative
qa.e: Fear of police action and lack of leadership keep them from uniting.

qa.q: Which step by society would most directly address the problem in Firozabad?
qa.a: Strictly enforcing child-labour laws
qa.e: Enforcing the law and providing schooling keeps children out of furnaces.

qa.q: Why does the author use dialogue such as 'Is your school ready?'
qa.a: To make the account real and moving
qa.e: Dialogue brings real voices into reportage and moves the reader.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Saheb's ragpicking life in Seemapuri is shown with vivid imagery.
Reason (R): Saheb's family came from Dhaka in Bangladesh.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both are true, but where the family came from does not explain the vivid imagery.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Ending child labour needs laws backed by schools, cooperatives and public awareness.
Reason (R): The government alone can end child labour.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: R is false; the chapter suggests society also has a role. A is true.

qa.q: Who wrote 'Deep Water'?
qa.a: William O. Douglas
qa.e: William O. Douglas, a US Supreme Court judge, wrote it.

qa.q: 'Deep Water' is taken from
qa.a: Of Men and Mountains
qa.e: It is an extract from Douglas's autobiography 'Of Men and Mountains'.

qa.q: What kind of writing is 'Deep Water'?
qa.a: An autobiographical account
qa.e: Douglas describes his own experience in the first person.

qa.q: Where did Douglas first develop a fear of water?
qa.a: On a beach in California
qa.e: At three or four, waves on a California beach knocked him down and swept over him.

qa.q: Why did Douglas's mother warn him about the Yakima River?
qa.a: It was treacherous and dangerous
qa.e: She kept warning him that the river was treacherous; the pool was safer.

qa.q: How old was Douglas when he decided to learn swimming at the YMCA?
qa.a: Ten or eleven
qa.e: He was ten or eleven; three or four was his age at the beach.

qa.q: How deep was the deep end of the YMCA pool?
qa.a: About nine feet
qa.e: The deep end was about nine feet; the shallow end about three.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Douglas already had a fear of water before the YMCA incident.
Reason (R): As a small child he had been knocked down by waves on a California beach.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; the beach experience is where the fear began.

qa.q: Who threw Douglas into the deep end of the pool?
qa.a: A big boy of about eighteen
qa.e: A 'big bruiser of a boy', about eighteen, tossed him in.

qa.q: What did Douglas plan to do when he hit the bottom?
qa.a: Jump up, come to the surface and paddle
qa.e: He planned to spring up from the bottom, lie flat on the surface and paddle to the edge.

qa.q: 'Those nine feet were more like ninety.' What does this suggest?
qa.a: His terror made the depth feel endless
qa.e: Fear exaggerated the distance in his mind.

qa.q: How many times did Douglas go down?
qa.a: Three times
qa.e: He rose and sank three times before he blacked out.

qa.q: What did Douglas experience when he tried to scream?
qa.a: No sound came out
qa.e: His voice failed in his panic.

qa.q: How did Douglas feel just before he blacked out?
qa.a: Calm and peaceful
qa.e: When he stopped struggling, he felt peace and drowsiness.

qa.q: Where did Douglas find himself when he came to?
qa.a: Beside the pool, vomiting
qa.e: He woke up lying on his stomach beside the pool, vomiting.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Douglas's legs felt paralysed during the drowning.
Reason (R): The YMCA pool was about nine feet deep at the deep end.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both are true, but the depth of the pool is not why his legs felt paralysed; terror was.

qa.q: What happened to Douglas whenever he went into water after the incident?
qa.a: His legs froze with terror
qa.e: The fear returned each time, and his legs would freeze.

qa.q: In which river did Douglas's legs freeze with terror when he went wading?
qa.a: Tieton
qa.e: He says terror gripped him whenever he waded in the Tieton or the Bumping River.

qa.q: What was Douglas doing in the Tieton and the Bumping River when the old terror returned?
qa.a: Wading
qa.e: Whenever he waded in the Tieton or the Bumping River, his legs froze and terror gripped him.

qa.q: Why did Douglas resolve to conquer his fear?
qa.a: It was ruining his enjoyment of life
qa.e: The fear robbed him of the joys of outdoor life he loved.

qa.q: What was the instructor's equipment made of?
qa.a: A belt, a rope, a pulley and a cable
qa.e: The belt was tied to a rope running through a pulley on an overhead cable.

qa.q: Why did the instructor use the rope and pulley?
qa.a: To keep Douglas safe while he learnt
qa.e: The rope let the instructor hold him up, so Douglas could practise without drowning.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Douglas hired an instructor to learn swimming.
Reason (R): He had already become an expert swimmer on his own.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true; R is false, since he still could not swim and was full of fear.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The fear of water affected Douglas for years.
Reason (R): It stopped him from enjoying canoeing, bathing and fishing.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; R shows how deeply and how long the fear affected him.

qa.q: What was the first step in the instructor's training?
qa.a: Putting his face under water to exhale
qa.e: He began with breathing: face down to exhale, nose up to inhale.

qa.q: 'Piece by piece he built a swimmer' means that the instructor
qa.a: taught one skill at a time
qa.e: He taught breathing, kicking and strokes separately, then joined them.

qa.q: What remained even after the training?
qa.a: Traces of terror when swimming alone
qa.e: Vestiges of the old terror returned when he was alone in the pool.

qa.q: Where is Lake Wentworth?
qa.a: New Hampshire
qa.e: Douglas swam at Lake Wentworth in New Hampshire.

qa.q: How far did Douglas swim across Lake Wentworth?
qa.a: Two miles
qa.e: He dived off a dock and swam two miles across the lake.

qa.q: What did Douglas do at Warm Lake to show the fear was gone?
qa.a: Swam across and back, shouting with joy
qa.e: Swimming across and back alone, he shouted with joy at his victory.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Douglas went to Warm Lake even after his training was over.
Reason (R): He wanted to be sure that the last traces of fear were gone.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; the test at Warm Lake was to make sure he was free of terror.

qa.q: Case: A student afraid of public speaking first reads aloud alone, then to a friend, then to a class, and finally at assembly. Which part of 'Deep Water' is this like?
qa.a: Building a swimmer piece by piece
qa.e: Both conquer fear in gradual stages, like the instructor's method.

qa.q: Whose words does Douglas quote: 'All we have to fear is fear itself'?
qa.a: Franklin D. Roosevelt
qa.e: He quotes US President Franklin D. Roosevelt.

qa.q: According to Douglas, where does terror lie?
qa.a: In the fear of death
qa.e: He felt peace in near-death; the terror was in fearing death.

qa.q: What is the central message of 'Deep Water'?
qa.a: Fear can be beaten with will and effort
qa.e: Douglas shows determination and practice can defeat fear.

qa.q: What did Douglas gain after conquering his fear?
qa.a: Freedom to enjoy rivers and lakes
qa.e: He could again enjoy canoeing, fishing and lakes.

qa.q: What effect did the near-death experience have on Douglas's will to live?
qa.a: It became much stronger
qa.e: He says the will to live grows in intensity.

qa.q: Which word best describes Douglas's approach to his fear?
qa.a: Determined
qa.e: He kept training for months and tested himself alone.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Douglas felt that the fear of water was worse than water itself.
Reason (R): He agreed with Roosevelt that all we have to fear is fear itself.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; the quote expresses exactly that fear is the real enemy.

qa.q:
