Assertion (A): Douglas found that terror lasts until the very moment of death.
Reason (R): Near death he felt calm and peaceful.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: he felt peace near death. R is true and contradicts A.

qa.q: What does Douglas call the YMCA incident?
qa.a: A misadventure
qa.e: He calls being thrown into the deep end his 'misadventure'.

qa.q: 'Flailed' in the drowning scene means
qa.a: moved the arms wildly
qa.e: To flail is to wave arms or legs wildly and helplessly.

qa.q: 'Vestiges of the old terror' means
qa.a: small traces of the old fear
qa.e: Vestiges are small remaining parts.

qa.q: 'Residual doubt' in the text refers to
qa.a: doubt that still remained
qa.e: Residual means remaining; some doubt about his freedom from fear remained.

qa.q: What literary quality makes the drowning scene gripping?
qa.a: Vivid sensory detail and suspense
qa.e: Details of sight, breath and body plus repeated sinking create suspense.

qa.q: What is the tone of 'Deep Water'?
qa.a: Reflective
qa.e: The adult Douglas thoughtfully looks back on his experience.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The narrative contrasts helplessness with triumph.
Reason (R): Douglas later became a judge of the US Supreme Court.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both are true, but his later career does not explain the contrast within the narrative.

qa.q: Extract (paraphrased): Rising, he opened his eyes and saw only water glowing yellow all around him. This line mainly creates
qa.a: a sense of being trapped
qa.e: Seeing only water conveys being trapped below the surface.

qa.q: Why was Douglas determined to get over his fear?
qa.a: It robbed him of the joys of outdoor life
qa.e: His fear kept him from canoeing, fishing and bathing in rivers he loved.

qa.q: Which phrase sums up the instructor's method best?
qa.a: Piece by piece he built a swimmer
qa.e: The instructor broke swimming into parts and built it up gradually.

qa.q: Why did Douglas not stop after the instructor's training ended?
qa.a: He still felt traces of terror
qa.e: Vestiges of fear remained, so he kept testing himself.

qa.q: How did Douglas finally know his fear was gone?
qa.a: He swam across Warm Lake and back alone
qa.e: Swimming alone across and back at Warm Lake proved it.

qa.q: Which is the best opening sentence for a long answer on courage in 'Deep Water'?
qa.a: Courage is facing fear, not lacking it.
qa.e: A long answer should open with a clear thesis on the theme.

qa.q: What does the near-death experience teach Douglas about death?
qa.a: Death has peace; the terror is in fearing it
qa.e: He felt peace and calm; he says the terror lies in the fear of death.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Douglas had to test himself in lakes afterwards.
Reason (R): The instructor's training was enough by itself to remove all of Douglas's fear.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: R is false: traces of fear remained. A is true; he tested himself at Lake Wentworth and Warm Lake.

qa.q: Case: A girl who fell off a bicycle avoids cycling for years, then practises daily with her brother holding the seat until she rides alone. Which value from 'Deep Water' does she show?
qa.a: Determination to overcome fear
qa.e: Like Douglas, she faces her fear with steady practice and help.

qa.q: Who wrote 'The Rattrap'?
qa.a: Selma Lagerlöf
qa.e: Selma Lagerlöf, the Swedish Nobel laureate, wrote it.

qa.q: In which year did Selma Lagerlöf win the Nobel Prize in Literature?
qa.e: She won in 1909, the first woman to receive it in literature.

qa.q: Where is 'The Rattrap' set?
qa.a: Värmland, Sweden
qa.e: It is set in the iron-mining region of Värmland in Sweden.

qa.q: How did the peddler keep body and soul together?
qa.a: By selling traps, begging and petty theft
qa.e: His trade was poor, so he also begged and stole.

qa.q: According to the peddler, what is the 'bait' in the world's rattrap?
qa.a: Riches and joys of life
qa.e: Riches, joys, shelter, food and clothing are the bait.

qa.q: Why did the peddler enjoy his rattrap idea?
qa.a: He liked to think of others being trapped
qa.e: It amused him to think of people who were caught.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The peddler saw the world as a rattrap.
Reason (R): He believed the world's riches tempted people and then trapped them.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; R explains what he meant by A.

qa.q: Case: A man takes a loan to buy a flashy car, then works day and night to repay it. Which idea from 'The Rattrap' fits?
qa.a: Material things are baits that trap us
qa.e: The car is bait, and the debt is the trap.

qa.q: Why was the crofter so happy to see the peddler?
qa.a: He was lonely and wanted company
qa.e: He had no wife or child, so a visitor was a welcome change.

qa.q: How did the crofter earn his thirty kronor?
qa.a: By selling his cow's milk
qa.e: His cow's milk was sold at the creamery.

qa.q: What was the game the crofter played with the peddler?
qa.a: Mjölis
qa.e: They played mjölis, a card game.

qa.q: Why did the crofter show the money to the peddler?
qa.a: To prove his claim, as the peddler doubted it
qa.e: The peddler seemed doubtful, so the crofter showed the notes proudly.

qa.q: How did the peddler steal the money?
qa.a: He came back, broke a pane and took it
qa.e: He returned after they parted, smashed a pane and took the notes.

qa.q: Why did the peddler leave the main road after the theft?
qa.a: To avoid being caught
qa.e: He felt it was unsafe to stay on the highway with stolen money.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The peddler felt trapped in the forest.
Reason (R): He had taken the bait of the thirty kronor.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; he sees himself as a rat that took the bait and is now caught.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The crofter was suspicious of the peddler.
Reason (R): He lived alone and longed for company.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: the crofter trusted him fully. R is true and explains his trust.

qa.q: Where did the peddler take shelter after getting lost?
qa.a: In a forge at the Ramsjö ironworks
qa.e: He found the Ramsjö ironworks and was allowed to rest in the forge.

qa.q: Who did the ironmaster think the peddler was?
qa.a: Captain von Stahle, an old comrade
qa.e: He believed him to be an old regimental comrade, Captain von Stahle.

qa.q: Why did the peddler not correct the ironmaster's mistake at once?
qa.a: He hoped to gain some money from it
qa.e: He thought the ironmaster might give him a few kronor out of pity for an old comrade.

qa.q: Why did the peddler say going to the manor was like the 'lion's den'?
qa.a: He feared being caught with stolen money
qa.e: With the stolen kronor on him, a house full of people was dangerous.

qa.q: Who finally persuaded the peddler to come to the manor house?
qa.a: Edla Willmansson
qa.e: Edla's gentle manner won his trust.

qa.q: When did the ironmaster realise his mistake?
qa.a: Next day, in daylight, after he was cleaned up
qa.e: In daylight, bathed and shaved, the peddler clearly was not the captain.

qa.q: Which trait of the ironmaster is shown by his quick mistake and quick anger?
qa.a: Impulsiveness
qa.e: He jumps to a conclusion and then to anger and threats.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The ironmaster welcomed the peddler warmly at first.
Reason (R): The story is set in the iron-mining region of Värmland.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both are true, but the setting does not explain the ironmaster's warmth; the mistaken identity does.

qa.q: Why did Edla insist that the peddler stay?
qa.a: They had promised him Christmas cheer
qa.e: She felt he should enjoy one day of peace as promised.

qa.q: What did the peddler leave for Edla?
qa.a: A rattrap with the money and a letter
qa.e: He left a rattrap containing the crofter's thirty kronor and a letter.

qa.q: What did the peddler ask Edla to do with the money?
qa.a: Return it to the old crofter
qa.e: He asked her to return the stolen money to the crofter.

qa.q: How did the peddler sign his letter?
qa.a: Captain von Stahle
qa.e: He signed as Captain von Stahle, showing his new self-respect.

qa.q: What changed the peddler?
qa.a: Edla's kindness and respect
qa.e: Being treated like a captain awakened his goodness.

qa.q: Which word best describes Edla?
qa.a: Compassionate
qa.e: She shows kindness and understanding to a stranger.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The peddler returned the stolen money.
Reason (R): Edla's kindness awakened his conscience.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; her goodness explains why he made amends.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Edla believed the peddler deserved one day of peace at Christmas.
Reason (R): Edla wanted the peddler to leave as soon as the truth came out.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: R is false: she insisted he stay. A is true and is why she did so.

qa.q: What does the rattrap symbolise in the story?
qa.a: The temptations of the material world
qa.e: Riches and joys act as bait that trap people.

qa.q: The rattrap image running through the whole story is an example of
qa.a: an extended metaphor
qa.e: A metaphor developed throughout a work is an extended metaphor.

qa.q: What is the central irony of the story?
qa.a: A tramp mistaken for a captain becomes honourable
qa.e: Treated like a captain, the peddler behaves like one.

qa.q: Which theme does Edla mainly represent?
qa.a: The redeeming power of kindness
qa.e: Her compassion transforms the peddler.

qa.q: How does the story show loneliness?
qa.a: Through the crofter and the friendless peddler
qa.e: The crofter lives alone; the peddler wanders without friends.

qa.q: Why is the Christmas setting important?
qa.a: It suits a story of goodwill and redemption
qa.e: Christmas, a season of kindness, matches the theme of redemption.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The peddler escapes from the 'rattrap' at the end.
Reason (R): He resists greed and returns the stolen money.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; giving up the bait is how he gets free.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The story is entirely gloomy with no humour.
Reason (R): Lagerlöf shows the ironmaster's confusion with a light touch.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: there is gentle humour. R is true.

qa.q: 'To keep body and soul together' means
qa.a: to manage to stay alive
qa.e: It means earning just enough to survive.

qa.q: 'Unwonted joy' means
qa.a: unusual joy
qa.e: 'Unwonted' means not usual; it is not the same as 'unwanted'.

qa.q: A 'ragamuffin' is
qa.a: a person in ragged, dirty clothes
qa.e: It describes someone shabby and ragged, like the peddler.

qa.q: Which word does NOT describe weary movement?
qa.a: sprint
qa.e: Sprint means run fast; the others describe slow, tired movement.

qa.q: What is an anvil?
qa.a: An iron block on which metal is hammered
qa.e: Smiths hammer hot metal on an anvil.

qa.q: In 'The ironmaster himself came to the forge', 'himself' is used for
qa.a: emphasis
qa.e: Removing 'himself' leaves a complete sentence, so it is emphatic.

qa.q: Choose the correct sentence.
qa.a: The peddler hurt himself on the fence.
qa.e: The reflexive form for 'he' is 'himself'; 'hisself' is non-standard.

qa.q: 'Nodded a haughty consent' means
qa.a: agreed in a proud manner
qa.e: Haughty means proud and superior; consent means agreement.

qa.q: Where did the peddler get the idea that the world is a rattrap?
qa.a: While thinking about his own rattraps
qa.e: The idea came to him while he was thinking of his traps.

qa.q: Why was the crofter so talkative with the peddler?
qa.a: He was lonely and glad of company
qa.e: Living alone, he was happy to have someone to talk to.

qa.q: Why did the peddler finally accept the invitation?
qa.a: Edla's kind and gentle manner
qa.e: Edla's compassion made him trust them.

qa.q: How did the peddler repay the crofter's hospitality?
qa.a: By stealing his savings
qa.e: He took advantage of the crofter's trust and stole his thirty kronor.

qa.q: Which pair of words best contrasts the ironmaster and Edla?
qa.a: Impulsive vs compassionate
qa.e: He is impulsive and proud; she is compassionate and observant.

qa.q: A long answer on 'kindness in The Rattrap' must include
qa.a: Edla's influence on the peddler
qa.e: Edla's kindness is the turning point of the story.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The peddler said the ironmaster too might one day be caught in the rattrap.
Reason (R): He believed everyone in the world is tempted by bait.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; his rattrap philosophy applies to everyone, which explains his warning.

qa.q: Case: A shopkeeper catches a hungry boy stealing bread and, instead of calling the police, gives him a meal and a job. Which character's approach does this mirror?
qa.a: Edla
qa.e: Like Edla, the shopkeeper reforms through kindness, not punishment.

qa.q: 'Indigo' is taken from a book by
qa.a: Louis Fischer
qa.e: Louis Fischer wrote 'The Life of Mahatma Gandhi', from which 'Indigo' is taken.

qa.q: Louis Fischer was
qa.a: an American journalist
qa.e: Fischer was an American journalist and writer.

qa.q: In which year did the Champaran movement take place?
qa.e: Gandhi went to Champaran in 1917.

qa.q: Where did Rajkumar Shukla first meet Gandhi?
qa.a: At the Lucknow Congress session
qa.e: He met Gandhi at the annual Congress session at Lucknow in December 1916.

qa.q: Which word best describes Rajkumar Shukla?
qa.a: Resolute
qa.e: He kept following Gandhi until he agreed; he was determined.

qa.q: How did Fischer come to know the story of Champaran in such detail?
qa.a: Gandhi told it to him at Sevagram
qa.e: Gandhi narrated it to Fischer in 1942 at his Sevagram ashram.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Gandhi finally agreed to go to Champaran.
Reason (R): Rajkumar Shukla kept following him from place to place.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; Shukla's persistence is what made Gandhi agree.

qa.q: Case: A villager writes to the district office every week for six months until a hand pump is installed. Whose quality from 'Indigo' does he share?
qa.a: Rajkumar Shukla's persistence
qa.e: Repeated, determined effort mirrors Shukla.

qa.q: Why did Rajendra Prasad's servants not allow Gandhi to draw water from the well?
qa.a: They feared he was an untouchable
qa.e: Taking him for a poor peasant, they feared their master's water might be polluted by an 'untouchable'.

qa.q: Who received Gandhi at Muzaffarpur station at midnight?
qa.a: Professor J.B. Kripalani and students
qa.e: Kripalani came with a large body of students.

qa.q: Under the tinkathia system, what share of their land did peasants have to grow indigo on?
qa.a: 15 per cent
qa.e: They grew indigo on 15 per cent, that is 3 parts in 20, of their holdings.

qa.q: If a sharecropper held 20 bighas, how many bighas came under indigo by tinkathia?
qa.e: 15 per cent of 20 = 3. That is the 'three in twenty' of tinkathia.

qa.q: Why did indigo lose its value for the landlords?
qa.a: Germany developed synthetic indigo
qa.e: Cheap synthetic indigo from Germany made natural indigo unprofitable.

qa.q: What did the secretary of the landlords' association tell Gandhi?
qa.a: He could give no information to an outsider
qa.e: He called Gandhi an outsider and refused information.

qa.q: What did the commissioner of Tirhut division advise Gandhi?
qa.a: To leave Tirhut at once
qa.e: He bullied Gandhi and advised him to leave Tirhut forthwith.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The landlords' demand for compensation exploited the peasants.
Reason (R): The landlords already knew that indigo had lost its value because of synthetic indigo.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; knowing indigo was worthless, they still extracted money, which is exploitation.

qa.q: Motihari was
qa.a: the capital of Champaran
qa.e: Gandhi went to Motihari, the capital of Champaran district.

qa.q: What was Gandhi ordered to do by the official notice?
qa.a: Leave Champaran at once
qa.e: He was served a notice to quit Champaran immediately.

qa.q: How did Gandhi respond to the notice?
qa.a: He signed it and wrote he would disobey
qa.e: He openly said he would disobey, accepting the consequences.

qa.q: In court, Gandhi said he was obeying
qa.a: the voice of conscience
qa.e: He spoke of 'the higher law of our being, the voice of conscience'.

qa.q: Why were the officials at Motihari 'powerless'?
qa.a: Thousands of peasants had gathered peacefully
qa.e: The huge, spontaneous peaceful gathering left officials unable to act.

qa.q: What finally happened to the case against Gandhi?
qa.a: The Lieutenant-Governor had it dropped
qa.e: The Lieutenant-Governor ordered the case to be dropped.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The Champaran episode is called the first civil disobedience in modern India.
Reason (R): Gandhi openly broke an unjust order and was ready to accept the penalty.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; open, non-violent defiance with acceptance of punishment is civil disobedience.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Gandhi believed he had broken the order in obedience to his conscience.
Reason (R): Gandhi pleaded not guilty at Motihari.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: R is false: he pleaded guilty. A is true; that was his reason.

qa.q: What percentage of refund did Gandhi first ask for?
qa.a: 50 per cent
qa.e: He asked for 50 per cent; the planters offered 25.

qa.q: What refund did Gandhi finally accept?
qa.a: 25 per cent
qa.e: He accepted the planters' offer of 25 per cent.

qa.q: A peasant had paid ₹400 as compensation. Under the settlement, how much would be refunded?
qa.e: 25 per cent of ₹400 = ₹100.

qa.q: Why did Gandhi say the amount of the refund was not important?
qa.a: The landlords had to give up money and prestige
qa.e: Their surrender of money also meant a surrender of prestige.

qa.q: What happened to the planters' estates within a few years?
qa.a: They were abandoned and went to the peasants
qa.e: The British planters abandoned their estates, which reverted to the peasants.

qa.q: What did the settlement teach the peasants?
qa.a: They had rights and could stand up for them
qa.e: They learnt they had rights and defenders.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Gandhi accepted only 25 per cent refund.
Reason (R): He believed the landlords' surrender of prestige mattered more than the amount.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; R is Gandhi's reason for accepting 25 per cent.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The 25 per cent settlement weakened the peasants' position.
Reason (R): The planters soon abandoned their estates in Champaran.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: the settlement strengthened the peasants. R is true.

qa.q: In how many villages did Gandhi open primary schools?
qa.a: Six
qa.e: Primary schools were opened in six villages.

qa.q: Which medicines did the volunteer doctor use?
qa.a: Castor oil, quinine and sulphur ointment
qa.e: Only three medicines were available: castor oil, quinine and sulphur ointment.

qa.q: Who taught the villagers personal cleanliness and sanitation?
qa.a: Kasturba
qa.e: Kasturba taught cleanliness and community sanitation.

qa.q: Who among these was NOT a teacher in the Champaran schools?
qa.a: C.F. Andrews
qa.e: Andrews was not kept on; the others volunteered as teachers.

qa.q: Why did Gandhi refuse C.F. Andrews's help?
qa.a: To teach the Indians self-reliance
qa.e: Relying on an Englishman would show weakness; Indians had to rely on themselves.

qa.q: What does Gandhi's social work in Champaran show?
qa.a: He worked for the people's overall welfare
qa.e: He cared about education, health and sanitation, not just politics.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Gandhi opened schools in Champaran villages.
Reason (R): Gandhi met Rajkumar Shukla at the Lucknow Congress session.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both are true, but meeting Shukla does not explain why Gandhi opened schools.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Andrews was an Englishman who had become Gandhi's devoted follower.
Reason (R): Gandhi wanted C.F. Andrews to stay and lead the fight.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: R is false: Gandhi refused his help. A is true.

qa.q: According to Gandhi, what was the real relief for the peasants?
qa.a: Freedom from fear
qa.e: He said they should stop going to courts; relief lay in freeing them from fear.

qa.q: Which is a key feature of civil disobedience?
qa.a: Accepting the penalty for breaking an unjust law
qa.e: Gandhi openly disobeyed and accepted punishment.

qa.q: What did Gandhi mean by 'The British could not order me about in my own country'?
qa.a: Indians need not obey unjust foreign orders
qa.e: It expresses the right to defy unjust foreign authority.

qa.q: Why did Gandhi criticise the lawyers at first?
qa.a: They charged poor peasants heavy fees
qa.e: He chided them for collecting big fees from sharecroppers.

qa.q: Which present-day action best reflects Gandhi's idea of protest?
qa.a: A peaceful sit-in, accepting arrest
qa.e: Civil disobedience is non-violent and accepts consequences.

qa.q: The Champaran movement gave peasants
qa.a: courage and awareness of their rights
qa.e: They learnt they had rights and could defend them.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Gandhi told the lawyers to stop going to the law courts.
Reason (R): He felt the peasants' real need was to be free from fear.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; R gives his reason.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Civil disobedience allows violence when the law is unjust.
Reason (R): Gandhi's method was strictly non-violent.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: civil disobedience is non-violent. R is true.

qa.q: Why is the Champaran episode called a turning point in Gandhi's life?
qa.a: He first openly defied British rule in India
qa.e: Gandhi said it was when he declared the British could not order him about in his own country.

qa.q: What impact did the Champaran movement have on the peasants?
qa.a: They lost their fear and gained their rights
qa.e: They learnt courage; indigo sharecropping soon ended.

qa.q: Which detail best shows Shukla's persistence?
qa.a: He followed Gandhi to Cawnpore and Ahmedabad
qa.e: Repeatedly following Gandhi shows persistence.

qa.q: In a short answer on the tinkathia system, which point is essential?
qa.a: Indigo on 15 per cent of land, given as rent
qa.e: That is the definition of tinkathia.

qa.q: Which example best supports a long answer on self-reliance?
qa.a: Gandhi refusing C.F. Andrews's help
qa.e: He wanted Indians to rely on themselves, not on an Englishman.

qa.q: Why did Gandhi accept a 25 per cent refund? Choose the best exam answer.
qa.a: The planters' loss of prestige mattered more
qa.e: Gandhi said the amount was less important than the surrender of prestige.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The lawyers decided to follow Gandhi to jail if needed.
Reason (R): Motihari was the capital of Champaran.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both are true, but Motihari being the capital does not explain the lawyers' decision.

qa.q: Case: A student writes, 'The Champaran movement was only about money.' Which point corrects this?
qa.a: It was about freeing peasants from fear
qa.e: The deeper aim was courage and self-reliance.

qa.q: Who wrote 'Poets and Pancakes'?
qa.a: Asokamitran
qa.e: Asokamitran wrote it about his years at Gemini Studios.

qa.q: 'Poets and Pancakes' is an extract from
qa.a: My Years with Boss
qa.e: It is taken from Asokamitran's 'My Years with Boss'.

qa.q: What was 'Pancake'?
qa.a: A brand of make-up material
qa.e: Pancake was the make-up brand bought by the truckload.

qa.q: Who was 'the Boss' of Gemini Studios?
qa.a: S.S. Vasan
qa.e: S.S. Vasan founded Gemini Studios and is called the Boss.

qa.q: Where was the make-up department located?
qa.a: In a building said to be Robert Clive's stables
qa.e: It was upstairs in a building believed to have been Robert Clive's stables.

qa.q: Why was the make-up room compared to a torture chamber?
qa.a: Its hot, glaring lights and mirrors
qa.e: Incandescent lights and mirrors made it unbearably hot.

qa.q: In which city was Gemini Studios?
qa.a: Madras
qa.e: Gemini Studios was in Madras, now Chennai.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The make-up at Gemini turned decent-looking actors into 'crimson-hued monsters'.
Reason (R): Asokamitran uses humorous exaggeration in the memoir.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; the monster image is an example of his humorous exaggeration.

qa.q: Why does the author call the make-up department an example of 'national integration'?
qa.a: Its staff came from many regions of India
qa.e: People from Bengal, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra and Tamil Nadu, plus an Anglo-Burmese, worked there.

qa.q: Who made up the crowd players?
qa.a: The office boy
qa.e: The strict hierarchy left crowd players to the office boy.

qa.q: How old was the 'office boy'?
qa.a: In his early forties
qa.e: He was not a boy but a man in his early forties.

qa.q: Why had the office boy joined Gemini Studios?
qa.a: Hoping to become a star or a writer
qa.e: He wanted to be a star actor, top screenwriter, director or lyricist.

qa.q: Whom did the office boy blame for his failure?
qa.a: Kothamangalam Subbu
qa.e: He directed his anger at Subbu, the No. 2 at Gemini.

qa.q: What does the strict hierarchy in the make-up room show?
qa.a: Rank decided who did whose make-up
qa.e: The chief did main actors, assistants did lesser players, the office boy did the crowd.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The office boy was frustrated.
Reason (R): He had hoped to become a star or a writer but remained an office boy.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; his unfulfilled dreams explain his frustration.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The author describes Gemini's make-up department as an example of national integration.
Reason (R): The make-up department had staff from only Tamil Nadu.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: R is false: staff came from many regions. A is true.

qa.q: Who was the No. 2 at Gemini Studios?
qa.a: Kothamangalam Subbu
qa.e: Subbu was second in command, a loyal aide of the Boss.

qa.q: Which quality of Subbu made him valuable to film-makers?
qa.a: He could suggest many ways to shoot a scene
qa.e: He could offer several ways a scene could be shot, which helped producers.

qa.q: Which novel did Subbu write?
qa.a: Thillana Mohanambal
qa.e: Subbu wrote 'Thillana Mohanambal'.

qa.q: How did Subbu treat the many people who depended on him?
qa.a: Generously; he supported many
qa.e: He had a large house where many dependants lived; he was generous.

qa.q: What was the legal adviser's nickname?
qa.a: The opposition
qa.e: Others called him 'the opposition'.

qa.q: How did the legal adviser stand out in appearance?
qa.a: He wore pants, a tie and sometimes a coat
qa.e: Everyone else wore khadi; he alone wore Western clothes.

qa.q: How did the legal adviser end the actress's career?
qa.a: He played back a tape of her angry outburst
qa.e: She was stunned to hear herself and her career ended.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The legal adviser was ironically called 'the opposition'.
Reason (R): Instead of helping, his actions sometimes harmed the studio, as with the actress.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; R explains the irony of the nickname.

qa.q: What was Asokamitran's job at Gemini Studios?
qa.a: Cutting and filing newspaper clippings
qa.e: He cut out newspaper clippings and stored them in files.

qa.q: Why did others think the author did nothing?
qa.a: His quiet job looked like idling
qa.e: Cutting paper in a cubicle did not look like real work.

qa.q: What happened to the Story Department?
qa.a: It was closed down
qa.e: The Boss wound up the Story Department.

qa.q: What does MRA stand for?
qa.a: Moral Re-Armament Army
qa.e: MRA is the Moral Re-Armament Army.

qa.q: Why did the Boss welcome the MRA?
qa.a: Like the studio, it was anti-communist
qa.e: The MRA was an anti-communist movement, matching Gemini's outlook.

qa.q: Which plays did the MRA stage in Madras?
qa.a: Jotham Valley and The Forgotten Factor
qa.e: The MRA performed 'Jotham Valley' and 'The Forgotten Factor'.

qa.q: What did Tamil drama copy from the MRA plays?
qa.a: Their sunrise and sunset scenes
qa.e: For years Tamil plays had sunrise and sunset scenes in the MRA manner.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Gemini Studios welcomed the MRA in 1952.
Reason (R): Both the studio and the MRA were opposed to communism.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; the shared anti-communism explains the welcome.

qa.q: Why did the English poet's speech puzzle the Gemini staff?
qa.a: His accent and ideas were beyond them
qa.e: His accent and subject were beyond the Tamil film workers.

qa.q: Who was the mystery English poet?
qa.a: Stephen Spender
qa.e: Years later the author found it was Stephen Spender.

qa.q: Which magazine did Spender edit?
qa.a: The Encounter
qa.e: Spender was editor of 'The Encounter'.

qa.q: 'The God That Failed' was a collection of essays by
qa.a: former communists
qa.e: The 'god' that failed them was communism.

qa.q: Which of these was NOT a contributor to 'The God That Failed'?
qa.a: Umberto Eco
qa.e: Eco is from 'The Interview'; the others were contributors.

qa.q: Which contributor to 'The God That Failed' also appears as an author in Flamingo?
qa.a: Louis Fischer
qa.e: Louis Fischer wrote 'The Life of Mahatma Gandhi', the source of 'Indigo'.

qa.q: What does the poet's visit show about the era?
qa.a: A cultural gap and the anti-communist mood
qa.e: An English poet was a stranger to Tamil film workers; his link to anti-communism fitted the mood.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The author later understood the poet's visit.
Reason (R): He found that Stephen Spender had contributed to the anti-communist book 'The God That Failed'.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; knowing Spender's anti-communist link explained why he had come.

qa.q: Which best describes the tone of 'Poets and Pancakes'?
qa.a: Gently humorous and ironic
qa.e: The memoir uses gentle humour and irony throughout.

qa.q: 'Self-deprecating humour' means
qa.a: joking about oneself
qa.e: The author laughs at his own job and position.

qa.q: Calling a mixed group of make-up men 'national integration' is an example of
qa.a: mock-heroic humour
qa.e: A grand ideal applied to a small matter is mock-heroic.

qa.q: How is the chapter structured?
qa.a: As a series of anecdotes
qa.e: It moves from one anecdote to another about studio life.

qa.q: The office boy and the legal adviser are presented almost as
qa.a: caricatures
qa.e: Their traits are exaggerated for comic effect.

qa.q: Which line is an example of understatement?
qa.a: People thought the author did nothing
qa.e: He plays down his own work with a quiet, ironic remark.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Asokamitran's humour is never cruel.
Reason (R): Gemini Studios bought Pancake make-up by the truckload.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both are true, but the make-up purchases do not explain why his humour is gentle.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The chapter is a harsh attack on Gemini Studios.
Reason (R): Asokamitran uses gentle satire about the film world.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: the satire is gentle and affectionate. R is true.

qa.q: What is the best short answer to 'Who was the office boy?'
qa.a: A frustrated forty-year-old doing crowd make-up
qa.e: He was in his early forties, made up crowd players and was frustrated in his ambitions.

qa.q: Which example best shows humour in the chapter?
qa.a: Make-up turning actors into crimson monsters
qa.e: The exaggerated description of make-up is comic.

qa.q: Why was Subbu called a many-sided genius?
qa.a: He was a poet, novelist, actor and planner
qa.e: His talents spanned poetry, a novel, acting and film planning.

qa.q: What was 'The God That Failed' about?
qa.a: Ex-communists' disillusionment with communism
qa.e: Six writers described how communism failed them.

qa.q: A discussion question asks about humour as a tool. Which point fits best?
qa.a: Humour can criticise without hurting
qa.e: Gentle humour lets the author point out flaws kindly.

qa.q: What happened to the actress after the legal adviser played back her outburst?
qa.a: She was stunned, and her career ended
qa.e: Hearing herself, she was struck dumb; her career ended.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The author realised who the English poet was years later.
Reason (R): He came across Spender's name as editor of 'The Encounter'.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; finding Spender's name revealed the visitor's identity.

qa.q: Case: A student says 'Poetry has no place in films.' Which point from the chapter counters this?
qa.a: Gemini employed poets like Subbu
qa.e: Poets and writers were central to the studio's work.

qa.q: Part I of 'The Interview' is taken from
qa.a: Silvester's introduction to an anthology
qa.e: It is from Christopher Silvester's introduction to 'The Penguin Book of Interviews'.

qa.q: Who interviewed Umberto Eco in Part II?
qa.a: Mukund Padmanabhan
qa.e: Mukund Padmanabhan interviewed Eco for The Hindu.

qa.q: According to Silvester, when was the interview invented?
qa.a: A little over 130 years before he wrote
qa.e: He says the interview was invented a little over 130 years ago.

qa.q: Which is a positive view of the interview?
qa.a: It is a source of truth and an art
qa.e: At its highest the interview is a source of truth, and in practice an art.

qa.q: Why do some people see the interview as an intrusion?
qa.a: It pries into celebrities' private lives
qa.e: Critics feel it invades privacy and diminishes those interviewed.

qa.q: The interviewer, according to the positive view, holds
qa.a: great power and influence
qa.e: The interviewer occupies a position of unprecedented power and influence.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The interview has become a commonplace of journalism.
Reason (R): It was invented only a little over 130 years ago.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both statements are true, but R gives the interview's age, not why it became common.

qa.q: Case: A TV channel camps outside an actor's home to ask about his divorce. Which view of interviews does this support?
qa.a: It is an intrusion into private life
qa.e: Prying into personal matters is exactly the 'intrusion' view.

qa.q: Some primitive cultures believe that a photograph
qa.a: steals a person's soul
qa.e: The belief is that taking a picture takes away the soul.

qa.q: Which writer felt that people are 'wounded' by interviews?
qa.a: V.S. Naipaul
qa.e: Naipaul felt some people are wounded and lose a part of themselves.

qa.q: How did Lewis Carroll feel about interviewers?
qa.a: He had a defensive dread of them
qa.e: He had a defensive dread and never agreed to be interviewed.

qa.q: Why did Lewis Carroll avoid interviewers?
qa.a: He hated being lionised
qa.e: His horror of being lionised made him repel interviewers.

qa.q: What did Kipling call the interview?
qa.a: Immoral, a crime and an assault
qa.e: Kipling called it immoral, a crime, an assault deserving punishment.

qa.q: Kipling's wife wrote that their day had been wrecked by
qa.a: two reporters from Boston
qa.e: Her diary says their day was wrecked by two reporters from Boston.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Kipling refused to be interviewed.
Reason (R): He considered the interview a crime, an assault on a person.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; his view of the interview as an assault explains his refusal.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Lewis Carroll had a horror of being lionised.
Reason (R): Lewis Carroll gave many interviews late in life.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: R is false: he never consented to be interviewed. A is true.

qa.q: What did H.G. Wells call the interview?
qa.a: An ordeal
qa.e: He spoke of 'the ordeal of the interview'.

qa.q: Whom did H.G. Wells later interview?
qa.a: Joseph Stalin
qa.e: Despite calling it an ordeal, he interviewed Stalin.

qa.q: What does 'thumbprints on his windpipe' suggest?
qa.a: Interviews felt choking and painful
qa.e: Pressure on the windpipe means suffocation, a strong metaphor of discomfort.

qa.q: Who wrote that we know most about our contemporaries through interviews?
qa.a: Denis Brian
qa.e: Denis Brian made this point in favour of interviews.

qa.q: Which figure of speech is 'thumbprints on his windpipe'?
qa.a: Metaphor
qa.e: It is an implied comparison without 'like' or 'as', so it is a metaphor.

qa.q: Why is H.G. Wells's attitude ironic?
qa.a: He disliked interviews yet interviewed Stalin
qa.e: Calling it an ordeal but conducting one himself is ironic.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The interviewer holds great power and influence.
Reason (R): Interviews shape how the public sees famous people.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; shaping public image is the source of that power.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Saul Bellow refused every request for an interview.
Reason (R): He described interviews as thumbprints on his windpipe.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: he consented several times. R is true.

qa.q: Umberto Eco was a professor of
qa.a: semiotics
qa.e: He was a professor of semiotics, the study of signs.

qa.q: Semiotics is the study of
qa.a: signs and symbols
qa.e: Semiotics studies how signs and symbols make meaning.

qa.q: At which university did Eco teach?
qa.a: University of Bologna
qa.e: He was a professor at the University of Bologna in Italy.

qa.q: 'The Name of the Rose' is
qa.a: a medieval detective novel
qa.e: It is a detective story set in the Middle Ages.

qa.q: In which year was 'The Name of the Rose' published?
qa.e: It came out in 1980.

qa.q: How many copies did 'The Name of the Rose' sell?
qa.a: Between 10 and 15 million
qa.e: Between 10 and 15 million copies were sold.

qa.q: Eco calls himself
qa.a: a professor who writes novels on Sundays
qa.e: He sees himself first as a professor; novels are a Sunday activity.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Eco considered himself primarily an academic.
Reason (R): He called himself a university professor who writes novels on Sundays.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; his self-description explains A.

qa.q: What does Eco mean by 'interstices'?
qa.a: Small empty spaces of time
qa.e: He uses gaps in his day, such as waiting for a lift.

qa.q: Which example does Eco give of an interstice?
qa.a: Waiting for a lift to arrive
qa.e: Waiting for a lift is a small gap he uses productively.

qa.q: What would happen to the universe, according to Eco's analogy, if all empty space were removed?
qa.a: It would be as small as his fist
qa.e: Without empty space, the universe would be the size of his fist.

qa.q: How is Eco's scholarly writing different from typical academic writing?
qa.a: It is playful, personal and narrative
qa.e: He tells the story of his research in a personal way.

qa.q: The theme linked with 'interstices' is
qa.a: efficient use of time
qa.e: Eco's productivity comes from using small gaps in time.

qa.q: A student uses a 12-minute bus ride every day of a 365-day year to learn new words. How many hours is that in total?

Assertion (A): Eco was able to produce a large amount of work.
Reason (R): He made use of interstices, the small gaps in his day.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; using interstices explains his productivity.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): 'Interstices' in the interview is used as a metaphor.
Reason (R): The word literally means small gaps between things, and Eco applies it to time.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; extending a word for physical gaps to gaps in time is metaphor.

qa.q: How did Eco describe the success of his novel?
qa.a: As a mystery
qa.e: He said why it worked at that time was a mystery.

qa.q: What role did timing play, according to Eco?
qa.a: Ten years earlier or later, it may have failed
qa.e: He believed the moment of publication mattered.

qa.q: Which feature of the novel do readers seem to have liked?
qa.a: Its medieval setting and serious content
qa.e: It is a serious book set in medieval times, and readers liked that.

qa.q: What does the novel's success suggest about readers?
qa.a: They do not want only easy reading
qa.e: Eco suggests readers welcome challenging books.

qa.q: What does Eco's own career suggest about scholarship and popular fiction?
qa.a: A scholar can also write a bestselling novel
qa.e: Eco was a professor of semiotics whose demanding medieval novel sold millions, so scholarship, popularity and fiction can meet.

qa.q: What is the form of Part II of the chapter?
qa.a: A question-answer interview
qa.e: Part II is the interview between Padmanabhan and Eco.

qa.q: Part I of the chapter is best described as
qa.a: expository prose with quotations
qa.e: Silvester explains the interview's history using many quotations.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The success of 'The Name of the Rose' surprised Eco.
Reason (R): Eco taught at the University of Bologna.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both are true, but where Eco taught does not explain his surprise at the novel's success.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): 'The Name of the Rose' sold between 10 and 15 million copies.
Reason (R): Eco believed readers want only light, easy books.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: R is false: Eco thought readers also want serious books. A is true.

qa.q: Why do many celebrity writers despise being interviewed?
qa.a: They feel it intrudes and diminishes them
qa.e: Interviews feel like an invasion of privacy that takes a part of them.

qa.q: 'Lionised' means
qa.a: treated as a celebrity
qa.e: To lionise is to treat someone as very important or famous.

qa.q: Which group is most commonly lionised in India today?
qa.a: Cricketers and film stars
qa.e: Media attention makes them celebrities.

qa.q: Why is Eco's academic writing personal and playful?
qa.a: He tells the story of his research
qa.e: He found that scholarly writing can follow the narrative of a search.

qa.q: Which phrase best paraphrases Eco's answer about his novel's success?
qa.a: It is a mystery linked to its timing
qa.e: He said if written ten years earlier or later it might not have sold.

qa.q: The belief about photographs is mentioned to explain
qa.a: how interviews may take something from us
qa.e: It parallels Naipaul's view that interviews take away part of a person.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Eco's scholarly works have a narrative quality.
Reason (R): He believes research can be told as the story of a search.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; R explains A.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): All writers in Part I agree that interviews are harmful.
Reason (R): Denis Brian valued interviews as a way of knowing contemporaries.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: views are mixed, and Brian is positive. R is true.

qa.q: Which is the best opening question for an interview?
qa.a: What inspired you to choose this career?
qa.e: An open, friendly question builds comfort and invites a full answer.

qa.q: An open question is one that
qa.a: invites a detailed answer
qa.e: Open questions start with what, why or how and invite explanation.

qa.q: Before publishing an interview, the interviewer should
qa.a: check facts and quotes
qa.e: Accuracy and honesty matter in journalism.

qa.q: Which practice respects the interviewee's privacy?
qa.a: Taking permission before recording
qa.e: Consent is basic to ethical interviewing.

qa.q: A long answer on 'the interview as a medium' should include
qa.a: both its power and its risks
qa.e: A balanced answer covers both positive and negative views.

qa.q: Which is a short-answer point about Eco?
qa.a: He works in the interstices of time
qa.e: Using small gaps of time is a key point about Eco.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A good interviewer listens carefully and asks follow-up questions.
Reason (R): Christopher Silvester introduced The Penguin Book of Interviews.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both are true, but Silvester's book does not explain why listening and follow-ups matter.

qa.q: Case: A student reporter asks a sports star only yes/no questions and gets a dull interview. What should she change?
qa.a: Ask open what, why and how questions
qa.e: Open questions invite fuller, more interesting answers.

qa.q: Who wrote 'Going Places'?
qa.a: A.R. Barton
qa.e: A.R. Barton wrote 'Going Places'.

qa.q: From whose point of view is the story mainly told?
qa.a: Sophie's, in the third person
qa.e: A third-person narrator follows Sophie's thoughts.

qa.q: Where are Sophie and Jansie likely to work after school?
qa.a: The biscuit factory
qa.e: Jansie says they are earmarked for the biscuit factory.

qa.q: Which is NOT one of Sophie's dreams?
qa.a: Becoming a doctor
qa.e: Sophie dreams of glamorous careers: boutique, acting, fashion.

qa.q: What does Jansie say Sophie would need to open a boutique?
qa.a: Money
qa.e: Jansie reminds her that a boutique needs money.

qa.q: Which word best describes Jansie?
qa.a: Realistic
qa.e: She accepts their prospects and points out practical problems.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Jansie discourages Sophie's plans.
Reason (R): She knows their families cannot afford such dreams and that the factory awaits them.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; Jansie's realistic view explains why she discourages Sophie.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The narrator of 'Going Places' closely follows Sophie's thoughts.
Reason (R): The story is narrated by Sophie in the first person.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: R is false: it is a third-person narration. A is true.

qa.q: What does Geoff do for a living?
qa.a: He is an apprentice mechanic
qa.e: Geoff is training as a mechanic.

qa.q: Why does Sophie admire Geoff?
qa.a: He is grown-up, with a world of his own
qa.e: She longs to be included in his private world.

qa.q: Who is Danny Casey?
qa.a: A young Irish football star
qa.e: He is the young Irish player in the United team.

qa.q: Where does Sophie claim she met Danny Casey?
qa.a: In the arcade
qa.e: She says she met him in the arcade.

qa.q: How does Sophie's father react to her story?
qa.a: He dismisses it as one of her wild stories
qa.e: He is sceptical and does not believe her.

qa.q: Where, according to Sophie, did Casey promise to meet her?
qa.a: By the canal
qa.e: She says he promised to meet her by the canal.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Sophie's father does not believe her story about Danny Casey.
Reason (R): Sophie often makes up wild stories.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; her habit of fantasy explains his disbelief.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Geoff tells Sophie everything about his life.
Reason (R): Sophie longs to be included in Geoff's world.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: Geoff is reserved and private. R is true.

qa.q: What happens during the United match the family watches?
qa.a: Danny Casey scores a goal
qa.e: Casey scores, and Sophie feels a private thrill.

qa.q: Where does Sophie wait for Danny Casey?
qa.a: By the canal, near a tree
qa.e: She waits alone by the canal.

qa.q: Does Danny Casey come to meet Sophie?
qa.a: No, he never comes
qa.e: Casey does not come; the meeting was a fantasy.

qa.q: How does Sophie feel as she goes home?
qa.a: Sad, but she still clings to the dream
qa.e: She is sad but holds on to the fantasy.

qa.q: What does the canal meeting symbolise?
qa.a: Illusion and fantasy
qa.e: It is a meeting that exists only in her mind.

qa.q: Which contrast does the author build through the two girls?
qa.a: Dreamer versus realist
qa.e: Sophie dreams; Jansie is practical.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Sophie keeps her disappointment secret.
Reason (R): She fears that others will discover her story was untrue.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; fear of being found out explains her secrecy.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Sophie waits by the canal for Danny Casey.
Reason (R): Danny Casey meets Sophie and gives her his autograph.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: R is false: Casey never comes. A is true.

qa.q: Which trait best describes Sophie?
qa.a: Escapist
qa.e: She escapes her dull life through fantasy.

qa.q: Why is Sophie wary of Jansie?
qa.a: Jansie might gossip about her
qa.e: Jansie is nosy and would spread the story.

qa.q: How is Geoff described?
qa.a: Silent and reserved, with his own world
qa.e: He keeps his life private.

qa.q: What is Sophie's father's attitude to her stories?
qa.a: Sceptical and dismissive
qa.e: He does not believe her and calls her stories wild.

qa.q: Which detail shows Sophie's father is a football fan?
qa.a: He watches United and admires Casey
qa.e: He follows United and is excited by Casey's play.

qa.q: How is Sophie's mother shown?
qa.a: Tired and anxious
qa.e: She is worn out by work and worried.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Sophie longs to be included in Geoff's world.
Reason (R): Derek is Sophie's younger brother.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both are true, but Derek's place in the family does not explain her longing for Geoff's world.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Jansie is a dreamer like Sophie.
Reason (R): Jansie expects to work at the biscuit factory.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: Jansie is realistic. R is true.

qa.q: Why is the title 'Going Places' ironic?
qa.a: Sophie's real prospects are very limited
qa.e: The title suggests success, but she is headed for the factory.

qa.q: Which theme does Sophie's attitude to Danny Casey show?
qa.a: Hero worship
qa.e: She idolises him and builds fantasies around him.

qa.q: How does class limit Sophie?
qa.a: Her family cannot fund her glamorous dreams
qa.e: Without money or connections, her dreams cannot come true.

qa.q: Which is an example of a communication gap in the family?
qa.a: Geoff rarely shares his life with Sophie
qa.e: Geoff's silence keeps Sophie outside his world.

qa.q: What is the central conflict of 'Going Places'?
qa.a: Dreams versus reality
qa.e: Sophie's fantasies clash with her real situation.

qa.q: Sophie's fantasy mainly helps her to
qa.a: escape a dull, limited life
qa.e: Fantasy is her escape from a monotonous life.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The title 'Going Places' is ironic.
Reason (R): Sophie 'goes places' only in her imagination.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; R explains the irony.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Sophie clings to her fantasy even after Casey fails to come.
Reason (R): The story celebrates Sophie's success at the end.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: R is false: there is no success. A is true.

qa.q: Why does Jansie discourage Sophie's dreams?
qa.a: They lack money and experience
qa.e: Jansie points out that a boutique needs money and the jobs need experience.

qa.q: What does Sophie's fantasy world centre on?
qa.a: Danny Casey and glamour
qa.e: Her daydreams revolve around Casey and glamorous jobs.

qa.q: Which is the best opening for a long answer on fantasy versus reality?
qa.a: Sophie is torn between dreams and reality.
qa.e: A thesis sentence should state the contrast directly.

qa.q: Which point best answers 'Is hero worship harmful?' using the story?
qa.a: It can trap teens in fantasy, as with Sophie
qa.e: Sophie's hero worship keeps her from facing reality.

qa.q: In a short answer on Geoff, the key point is
qa.a: he is reserved and has a private world
qa.e: Geoff's silence and private life are central.

qa.q: In an answer on Sophie and Geoff, what explains her admiration for him?
qa.a: He seems grown-up, with a life of his own
qa.e: She longs to share his independent world.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Sophie's dreams are unlikely to come true.
Reason (R): Her family is working-class and she is earmarked for the biscuit factory.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; her circumstances explain why her dreams are unrealistic.

qa.q: Case: A Class 12 student spends hours imagining fame but skips practice and planning. Which character is she like?
qa.a: Sophie
qa.e: Like Sophie, she dreams without effort or realism.

qa.q: Who wrote 'My Mother at Sixty-six'?
qa.a: Kamala Das
qa.e: Kamala Das wrote this autobiographical poem.

qa.q: Besides English, Kamala Das also wrote in
qa.a: Malayalam
qa.e: She wrote in Malayalam under the name Madhavikutty.

qa.q: Where is the poet driving to?
qa.a: Cochin airport
qa.e: She drives from her parents' home to Cochin.

qa.q: On which day does the journey take place?
qa.a: Friday
qa.e: The poem mentions a Friday morning.

qa.q: What is the mother doing during the drive?
qa.a: Dozing with her mouth open
qa.e: She is asleep beside the poet, mouth open.

qa.q: What is unusual about the poem's structure?
qa.a: It is one sentence with no stanzas
qa.e: The whole poem is one long sentence without stanza breaks.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The poem has no stanza breaks.
Reason (R): It flows as one continuous sentence of thought.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; the continuous flow explains the lack of breaks.

qa.q: Kamala Das's poetry is often called 'confessional' because
qa.a: it frankly reveals personal feelings
qa.e: Confessional poetry openly shares private emotions and experiences.

qa.q: What does the poet realise when she looks at her sleeping mother?
qa.a: Her mother is as old as she looks
qa.e: She realises with pain that her mother has really grown old.

qa.q: What does 'ashen' suggest about the mother's face?
qa.a: It is pale and lifeless
qa.e: Ashen means grey and pale, like ash, suggesting lifelessness.

qa.q: Why does the poet compare her mother's face to a corpse's?
qa.a: It looks pale and death-like
qa.e: The comparison shows how lifeless and old the face looks; it does not mean she is dead.

qa.q: After the security check, the poet sees her mother as
qa.a: pale as a late winter's moon
qa.e: She is wan and pale, like a fading winter moon.

qa.q: What returns to the poet at the airport?
qa.a: Her childhood fear of losing her mother
qa.e: The old familiar ache is her childhood fear of losing her mother.

qa.q: Why does the poet 'put that thought away'?
qa.a: Her mother's age is too painful to face
qa.e: She avoids the painful thought by looking outside.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The poet turns to look at the trees and children outside.
Reason (R): She wants to escape the painful thought of her mother's ageing.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; R explains why she looks outside.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The poet sees her mother as healthy and young at the airport.
Reason (R): She compares her mother to a late winter's moon.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: she sees her mother as pale and wan. R is true.

qa.q: What does the poet say to her mother at parting?
qa.a: See you soon, Amma
qa.e: Her only words are 'See you soon, Amma'.

qa.q: Why does the poet smile again and again?
qa.a: To hide her fear and reassure her mother
qa.e: The smile masks her pain and comforts her mother.

qa.q: The phrase 'See you soon' expresses
qa.a: hope of meeting again
qa.e: It carries her hope that she will see her mother again.

qa.q: Which theme is central to the poem?
qa.a: Fear of losing an ageing parent
qa.e: The poet fears her mother's death.

qa.q: What does 'all I said was' suggest?
qa.a: She held back much more than she said
qa.e: It shows suppressed emotion: many feelings, few words.

qa.q: The poet's feeling as she parts from her mother is mainly
qa.a: helplessness mixed with love
qa.e: She loves her mother but cannot stop her ageing.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The poet hides her feelings at the airport.
Reason (R): She does not want to upset her ageing mother.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; she hides her fear to protect her mother from worry.

qa.q: Case: A son waves cheerfully at his elderly father at the railway station, though he is worried about his health. Which line from the poem matches?
qa.a: smile and smile and smile
qa.e: Like the poet, he hides worry behind a reassuring smile.

qa.q: Which figure of speech is 'pale as a late winter's moon'?
qa.a: Simile
qa.e: It uses 'as' to compare, so it is a simile.

qa.q: 'Her face ashen like that of a corpse' is a
qa.a: simile
qa.e: It uses 'like' to compare the face to a corpse.

qa.q: Which figure of speech is 'young trees sprinting'?
qa.a: Personification
qa.e: Trees are given the human action of sprinting.

qa.q: What do the 'merry children spilling out of their homes' represent?
qa.a: Youth, energy and joy
qa.e: They contrast with the ageing mother.

qa.q: Why is a 'late winter's moon' a fitting image for the mother?
qa.a: It is pale and fading, like old age
qa.e: A late winter's moon is dim and pale, nearing its end, like the mother's life.

qa.q: What contrast is central to the poem's imagery?
qa.a: Youth outside versus age inside
qa.e: Lively trees and children outside contrast with the ageing mother inside.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The image of sprinting trees is an example of personification.
Reason (R): The poet is driving to Cochin airport.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both are true, but the destination does not explain why the image is personification.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Winter is often linked with the last stage of life.
Reason (R): The 'late winter's moon' suggests vigour and youth.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: R is false: it suggests paleness and decline. A is true.

qa.q: What does the repetition in 'smile and smile and smile' suggest?
qa.a: A forced effort to hide pain
qa.e: Repeated smiling shows she is trying hard to seem cheerful.

qa.q: The poem is written in
qa.a: free verse
qa.e: It has no regular rhyme or metre.

qa.q: Enjambment means
qa.a: a sentence running on past a line's end
qa.e: In enjambment the sense continues into the next line.

qa.q: What is the poet's 'familiar ache'?
qa.a: Her childhood fear of losing her mother
qa.e: It is an old fear she has had since childhood.

qa.q: Why does the poet say the trees are 'sprinting'?
qa.a: They seem to rush past the moving car
qa.e: Seen from a moving car, trees appear to race backwards, full of energy.

qa.q: What is the main contrast in the poem?
qa.a: The ageing mother inside versus youth outside
qa.e: The poem sets age against youth.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The poet feels pain on seeing her mother's face.
Reason (R): She realises her mother has grown old and may not live long.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; R explains her pain.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The poem uses a regular rhyme scheme.
Reason (R): Kamala Das writes in free verse.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: there is no regular rhyme scheme. R is true.

qa.q: Why does the poet bring in the image of merry children?
qa.a: To set youthful joy against old age
qa.e: The children's energy sharpens the contrast with old age.

qa.q: The mother is compared to a late winter's moon because she looks
qa.a: pale and fading
qa.e: A late winter's moon is dim and pale, like old age.

qa.q: What do the parting words 'See you soon, Amma' signify?
qa.a: Hope and a brave hiding of fear
qa.e: They express hope while concealing fear.

qa.q: In an extract question, 'the old familiar ache' refers to
qa.a: her childhood fear of losing her mother
qa.e: It is the fear she has felt since childhood.

qa.q: Which pair best describes the poem's mood?
qa.a: Tender and sad
qa.e: The poem is gentle, loving and sorrowful.

qa.q: Which line best shows the poet suppressing her emotions?
qa.a: All she says is 'See you soon, Amma'
qa.e: She says little and hides her fear.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The poet compares her mother to a late winter's moon.
Reason (R): Like such a moon, her mother looks pale and close to her end.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; R explains the comparison.

qa.q: Case: In a short answer, a student writes that the poet is happy to leave her mother. What has the student missed?
qa.a: Her fear and pain beneath the smile
qa.e: The smile hides fear and pain; the poet is not happy.

qa.q: Who wrote 'Keeping Quiet'?
qa.a: Pablo Neruda
qa.e: Pablo Neruda, the Chilean poet, wrote it.

qa.q: Pablo Neruda was from
qa.a: Chile
qa.e: He was a Chilean poet who wrote in Spanish.

qa.q: In which year did Neruda win the Nobel Prize in Literature?
qa.e: He won the Nobel Prize in 1971.

qa.q: Who translated 'Keeping Quiet' into English?
qa.a: Alastair Reid
qa.e: Alastair Reid translated it from Spanish.

qa.q: What does the poet ask us to count up to?
qa.a: Twelve
qa.e: We are asked to count to twelve and keep still.

qa.q: Why does the poet ask people not to speak in any language?
qa.a: So that silence can unite all people
qa.e: Silence is common to all and removes the barriers of language.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The poet wants everyone on earth to keep still at the same time.
Reason (R): A shared moment of silence can unite people across all divisions.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; R explains why the stillness must be shared by all.

qa.q: The poem 'Keeping Quiet' is written in
qa.a: free verse
qa.e: It has no fixed rhyme or metre.

qa.q: Why is the moment of silence called 'exotic'?
qa.a: It would be strange and unusual for us
qa.e: We are so used to rush and noise that stillness would feel strange.

qa.q: What would fishermen do in the quiet moment?
qa.a: Not harm the whales
qa.e: They would stop harming the whales.

qa.q: What would the man gathering salt do?
qa.a: Look at his hurt hands
qa.e: He would pause and notice his own pain.

qa.q: What are 'green wars'?
qa.a: Wars against the environment
qa.e: Green wars harm nature and the environment.

qa.q: 'Victory with no survivors' suggests that
qa.a: war destroys everyone, even the winners
qa.e: If no one survives, there is no real victory.

qa.q: What would warmongers do during the stillness?
qa.a: Walk in clean clothes with their brothers
qa.e: They would give up war and walk peacefully together.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The poet imagines the salt gatherer looking at his hurt hands.
Reason (R): In the rush of daily work, people ignore their own suffering.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; the pause allows him to see pain he usually ignores.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Neruda calls the quiet moment one without rush, without engines.
Reason (R): The quiet moment would be full of rush and engines.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: R is false: there would be no rush or engines. A is true.

qa.q: Does the poet advocate total inactivity?
qa.a: No, he says life is what it is all about
qa.e: He clearly says his wish should not be confused with total inactivity.

qa.q: What makes us sad, according to the poet?
qa.a: Never understanding ourselves
qa.e: Our sadness is never understanding ourselves and threatening ourselves with death.

qa.q: 'Single-minded about keeping our lives moving' means
qa.a: obsessed with constant activity
qa.e: We are fixed on being busy all the time.

qa.q: What does the earth teach us, according to the poem?
qa.a: What seems dead may later prove alive
qa.e: As in the seasons, apparent death leads to new life.

qa.q: How does the poem end?
qa.a: The poet counts to twelve and leaves
qa.e: He asks us to keep quiet, and he goes.

qa.q: The 'huge silence' would help us to
qa.a: end our sadness and understand ourselves
qa.e: Silence gives us a chance for self-understanding.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The poet wants nothing to do with death.
Reason (R): He says his idea should not be confused with total inactivity.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; R clarifies that his stillness is about life, not death.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The poet wants people to stop all activity forever.
Reason (R): He uses the earth's example of life returning after apparent death.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: he rejects total inactivity. R is true.

qa.q: Which theme is central to 'Keeping Quiet'?
qa.a: Introspection and peace
qa.e: The poem calls for silence to look within and live in peace.

qa.q: How does the poem show concern for nature?
qa.a: Fishermen would not harm whales
qa.e: Sparing the whales shows care for nature.

qa.q: Which image shows universal brotherhood?
qa.a: Warmongers walking with brothers
qa.e: Enemies walking together as brothers shows brotherhood.

qa.q: What does the poet criticise?
qa.a: War, harm to nature and mindless rush
qa.e: He criticises war, destruction of nature and constant activity.

qa.q: The use of 'let us' and 'we' in the poem is an example of
qa.a: direct address to the reader
qa.e: The poet speaks directly to readers and includes himself.

qa.q: Why is introspection important in the poem?
qa.a: It helps us understand ourselves
qa.e: Silence lets us look within and end the sadness of not knowing ourselves.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The poem promotes peace and non-violence.
Reason (R): The poem was translated from Spanish by Alastair Reid.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both are true, but the translation does not explain the poem's message of peace.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): 'Keeping Quiet' is written in free verse with direct address.
Reason (R): The poem uses a regular rhyme and metre.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: R is false: there is no regular rhyme. A is true.

qa.q: 'Without rush, without engines' is an example of
qa.a: anaphora
qa.e: Repeating 'without' at the start of phrases is anaphora.

qa.q: 'Perhaps the earth can teach us' uses
qa.a: personification
qa.e: The earth is given the human ability to teach.

qa.q: Which line contains a paradox?
qa.a: What seems dead later proves alive
qa.e: Dead things proving alive is a seeming contradiction with a truth.

qa.q: What will counting to twelve and keeping still help us achieve?
qa.a: Peace, introspection and brotherhood
qa.e: The pause brings peace, self-reflection and unity.

qa.q: Why is 'twelve' a fitting number for the count?
qa.a: It suggests a full cycle of time
qa.e: Twelve is commonly read as the hours on a clock or months of a year.

qa.q: Does the poet ask for death or inactivity?
qa.a: No; he wants a pause for reflection
qa.e: He wants no truck with death; life is what matters.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The poet uses the earth as an example.
Reason (R): The earth seems dead in winter but comes alive later, just as silence can renew us.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; R explains why the earth is a fitting example.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The poet uses a simile to describe the earth.
Reason (R): The earth is personified as a teacher.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: there is no simile here; it is personification. R is true.

qa.q: Which 'sadness' does the poet refer to?
qa.a: Never understanding ourselves
qa.e: It is the sadness of not knowing ourselves and threatening ourselves with death.

qa.q: Which symbol from nature shows life under apparent stillness?
qa.a: The earth
qa.e: The earth seems dead yet comes alive.

qa.q: Which line best conveys the poet's main message?
qa.a: Let us count to twelve and keep still
qa.e: The call to pause and be still is the core message.

qa.q: What causes our sadness, according to the poem?
qa.a: Being single-minded about keeping busy
qa.e: Endless busyness keeps us from understanding ourselves.

qa.q: In an extract MCQ, 'a huge silence' most likely means
qa.a: a deep pause for reflection
qa.e: It is a meaningful pause, not permanent silence.

qa.q: Which short answer best links silence and peace?
qa.a: Silence calms us and stops harm to others
qa.e: Pausing ends rush, war and harm, leading to peace.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The earth is used as a symbol in the poem.
Reason (R): It shows that life can exist beneath apparent death.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; R gives the symbolic meaning.

qa.q: Case: A school starts each day with one minute of silence before classes. Which idea from the poem does this reflect?
qa.a: A shared pause brings calm and reflection
qa.e: It applies the poem's call for silence and introspection.

qa.q: Who wrote 'A Thing of Beauty'?
qa.a: John Keats
qa.e: The lines are by John Keats.

qa.q: These lines are taken from Keats's poem
qa.a: Endymion
qa.e: They form the opening of 'Endymion'.

qa.q: According to Keats, the loveliness of a thing of beauty
qa.a: keeps increasing
qa.e: Its loveliness increases and never passes into nothingness.

qa.q: What does a thing of beauty keep for us, according to the poem?
qa.a: A quiet bower
qa.e: It keeps a quiet bower, a peaceful shelter, for us.

qa.q: A 'bower' is
qa.a: a shady, sheltered place
qa.e: A bower is a shelter made by trees or plants.

qa.q: Besides sweet dreams, what else does beauty give us?
qa.a: Health and quiet breathing
qa.e: Beauty gives a sleep full of sweet dreams, health and quiet breathing.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The poem is written in heroic couplets.
Reason (R): Each pair of lines rhymes and follows iambic pentameter.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; R is the definition of a heroic couplet.

qa.q: Iambic pentameter has how many stressed beats in a line?
qa.e: Penta means five: five iambs, five stressed beats, about ten syllables.

qa.q: What do we weave every morning, according to Keats?
qa.a: A flowery band binding us to the earth
qa.e: The flowery band of beautiful things binds us to life on earth.

qa.q: The 'flowery band' binds us to
qa.a: the earth
qa.e: It keeps us attached to life on earth.

qa.q: 'Despondence' means
qa.a: a state of hopelessness
qa.e: It means deep despair or low spirits.

qa.q: 'Inhuman dearth of noble natures' refers to
qa.a: a lack of good, noble people
qa.e: Dearth means scarcity; noble natures are good people.

qa.q: What is a 'pall'?
qa.a: A dark cloth spread over a coffin
qa.e: Here the pall stands for sadness covering our spirits.

qa.q: What removes the pall from our dark spirits?
qa.a: Some shape of beauty
qa.e: A beautiful thing lifts the gloom from our minds.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Beauty helps us despite suffering.
Reason (R): Some shape of beauty moves away the pall from our dark spirits.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; R shows how beauty helps in times of gloom.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Keats lists despondence and gloomy days as sources of suffering.
Reason (R): Keats says beauty cannot help us when life is gloomy.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: R is false: beauty helps in spite of gloom. A is true.

qa.q: Who enjoy the shade of the trees in the poem?
qa.a: Simple sheep
qa.e: Trees sprout a shady boon for simple sheep.

qa.q: What do the clear rills make for themselves?
qa.a: A cool shelter against the hot season
qa.e: They create a cool shelter against the heat.

qa.q: What is the 'mid-forest brake' rich with?
qa.a: Musk-rose blooms
qa.e: It has a sprinkling of fair musk-rose blooms.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT listed as a thing of beauty?
qa.a: Tall city buildings
qa.e: Keats lists nature and stories, not buildings.

qa.q: 'The grandeur of the dooms we have imagined for the mighty dead' refers to
qa.a: the glorious fates of great people of old
qa.e: It means the grand fates and achievements of past heroes.

qa.q: What image does Keats use for the endless bounty of beauty?
qa.a: An endless fountain of immortal drink
qa.e: Beauty is like an endless fountain pouring from heaven's brink.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Keats includes 'lovely tales that we have heard or read' among things of beauty.
Reason (R): Beauty can come from human imagination as well as nature.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; R explains why tales are included.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The 'endless fountain' suggests that beauty is limited.
Reason (R): The fountain pours from heaven's brink.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: 'endless' shows beauty is unlimited. R is true.

qa.q: What is the main theme of 'A Thing of Beauty'?
qa.a: Beauty gives lasting joy
qa.e: Beauty is a joy for ever and makes life bearable.

qa.q: How does nature help us, according to Keats?
qa.a: It heals and soothes our suffering
qa.e: Nature's beauty lifts our sorrow.

qa.q: What does 'immortal drink' refer to?
qa.a: Nectar, the drink of the gods
qa.e: Immortal drink is the nectar that gives eternal life.

qa.q: Where does the endless fountain pour from?
qa.a: Heaven's brink
qa.e: It pours from heaven's brink, showing beauty is divine.

qa.q: The 'flowery band' is a metaphor for
qa.a: beauty that keeps us attached to life
qa.e: Beauty binds us to the earth and to life.

qa.q: Why is beauty called a divine gift?
qa.a: It pours from heaven like a fountain
qa.e: The fountain image shows beauty flows from heaven to us.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Keats sees beauty as a divine gift.
Reason (R): He describes it as pouring to us from heaven's brink.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; the image of heaven's brink supports A.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A pall is a dark cloth spread over a coffin.
Reason (R): The 'pall' in the poem stands for happiness.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: R is false: the pall stands for gloom. A is true.

qa.q: 'Simple sheep' is an example of
qa.a: alliteration
qa.e: The repeated 's' sound at the start of words is alliteration.

qa.q: 'Are we wreathing' instead of 'we are wreathing' is an example of
qa.a: inversion
qa.e: Reversing normal word order is inversion.

qa.q: Which word in the poem is an example of archaic (old-fashioned) diction?
qa.a: o'er
qa.e: 'O'er' is an old poetic form of 'over'.

qa.q: The rhyme scheme of the poem follows
qa.a: rhyming couplets (aabb...)
qa.e: Each pair of lines rhymes, as in heroic couplets.

qa.q: Which is a cause of suffering listed by Keats?
qa.a: The dearth of noble natures
qa.e: A lack of good people is one cause of suffering.

qa.q: Which pair are both things of beauty in the poem?
qa.a: Daffodils and lovely tales
qa.e: Both daffodils and tales are listed as beautiful.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): 'Noble natures' is an example of alliteration.
Reason (R): The lines come from the opening of Keats's 'Endymion'.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both are true, but the source of the lines does not explain why the phrase is alliteration.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The poem is written in blank verse.
Reason (R): Its lines rhyme in pairs.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: blank verse does not rhyme; this poem uses rhyming couplets. R is true.

qa.q: What does 'wreathing a flowery band to bind us to the earth' suggest?
qa.a: Beauty keeps us attached to life
qa.e: The band of beautiful things ties us to life on earth.

qa.q: According to Keats, what makes humans love life despite troubles?
qa.a: Some shape of beauty
qa.e: Beauty removes the pall from our dark spirits.

qa.q: Why is grandeur associated with the mighty dead?
qa.a: Their glorious fates inspire us
qa.e: Great people of the past met grand fates that we imagine with awe.

qa.q: Which phrase shows that suffering is part of life in the poem?
qa.a: Gloomy days
qa.e: Gloomy days are among the troubles of life.

qa.q: The phrase 'bind us to the earth' means
qa.a: keep us attached to life
qa.e: It means beauty keeps us connected to life.

qa.q: The 'lovely tales that we have heard or read' show that beauty can be found in
qa.a: literature and stories
qa.e: Stories, too, are things of beauty.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Humans continue to love life despite suffering.
Reason (R): Beauty removes the pall of sorrow from their spirits.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; R gives the reason.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Keats speaks of the glorious fates we imagine for the great people of the past.
Reason (R): Keats links grandeur with the mighty dead because of their large tombs.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: R is false: grandeur comes from their glorious fates, not tombs. A is true.

qa.q: Do things of beauty make a lasting impression, according to Keats?
qa.a: Yes, their joy lasts for ever
qa.e: Their loveliness increases and never passes into nothingness.

qa.q: What image does Keats use for the bounty of the earth?
qa.a: An endless fountain of immortal drink
qa.e: Beauty pours endlessly like a heavenly fountain.

qa.q: In an extract question, 'it will never pass into nothingness' means
qa.a: beauty will never die
qa.e: It stresses the permanence of beauty.

qa.q: Which device is in 'flowery band'?
qa.a: Metaphor
qa.e: Beauty is described as a band of flowers without 'like' or 'as'.

qa.q: What is the tone of the poem?
qa.a: Joyful and uplifting
qa.e: It celebrates beauty and its lasting joy.

qa.q: A short answer on nature and beauty must include
qa.a: nature's power to heal sorrow
qa.e: Keats shows that nature's beauty lifts sorrow.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Keats believes the impression of beauty lasts for ever.
Reason (R): He says its loveliness increases and never passes into nothingness.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; R is the evidence for A.

qa.q: Case: A student remembers a sunrise at Kanyakumari from years ago and still feels joyful thinking of it. Which line of Keats does this prove?
qa.a: A thing of beauty is a joy for ever
qa.e: The lasting joy of a beautiful memory is exactly the first line's claim.

qa.q: Who wrote 'A Roadside Stand'?
qa.a: Robert Frost
qa.e: Robert Frost, the American poet, wrote it.

qa.q: Robert Frost is best known for poems about
qa.a: rural New England
qa.e: Frost wrote mainly about rural New England.

qa.q: Where is the roadside stand placed?
qa.a: At the road's edge, before an old house
qa.e: A new shed stands at the road's edge in front of a little old house.

qa.q: What do the rural folk hope to get from the stand?
qa.a: Some city money to live better
qa.e: They want city money to improve their lives.

qa.q: The poem mainly deals with
qa.a: the plight of the rural poor
qa.e: It describes the poverty and neglect of rural people.

qa.q: What kind of poem is 'A Roadside Stand'?
qa.a: Narrative and reflective
qa.e: It tells of the stand and reflects on its meaning.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The rural people set up a stand by the road.
Reason (R): They hoped to earn some of the city's money.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Both true; R gives the reason for A.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The stand is located in a crowded market.
Reason (R): It is at the edge of a road where traffic speeds by.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: it is at the roadside, not in a market. R is true.

qa.q: What does 'polished traffic' refer to?
qa.a: Rich city people in shiny cars
qa.e: It means the gleaming cars of well-off city people.

qa.q: 'With a mind ahead' means the travellers are
qa.a: thinking only of their destination
qa.e: They are focused on where they are going and ignore the stand.

qa.q: What do the city people complain about?
qa.a: Badly painted signs that spoil the view
qa.e: The crude signs with N and S turned wrong mar the scenery.

qa.q: Which letters are painted the wrong way on the signs?
qa.a: N and S
qa.e: The signs have S turned wrong and N turned wrong.

qa.q: Which of these is offered for sale at the stand?
qa.a: Wild berries in wooden quarts
qa.e: Wild berries in wooden quarts are on sale.

qa.q: What is the poet's real complaint?
qa.a: The trusting, unsaid sorrow of the poor
qa.e: The hurt to the scenery is not his concern; the silent sorrow is.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The city travellers barely notice the roadside stand.
Reason (R): Robert Frost wrote about rural New England.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
